title: German A1
description: German from your first word to CEFR level A1, the level of the Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1. Grammar lessons cover sounds and spelling, greetings, numbers, the present tense, articles and plurals, the accusative and a first look at the dative, modal and separable verbs, the imperative and the perfect tense. About 700 everyday words are learned through typed vocabulary reviews with pronunciation, and a reading list points to graded readers you can try on your own.
author: Erudior
changelog: Fixed the word "am" not accepting "on" as an answer.

lessons.title: Sounds, letters and spelling
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

German is spelled far more regularly than English. Once you know how the letters sound, you can
read almost any German word out loud, and you can usually write a word you hear. This lesson
gives you that key: the alphabet and its letter names, the vowels (including the three with
dots), the letter ß, the letter groups that trip up English speakers, and where the stress
falls. Along the way you'll learn the first words everyone needs: *ja*, *nein*, *bitte*,
*danke* and the everyday greetings, and how to spell your name when someone asks.

Read every example aloud: pronunciation is learned with your mouth, not your eyes.

## The alphabet

German uses the same 26 letters as English, plus *ä*, *ö*, *ü* and *ß*. The letter names are
different, and you need them to spell your name on the phone or at a counter. The respellings
below are approximate English sounds.

| Letter | Name | Letter | Name | Letter | Name |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | ah | J | yot | S | ess |
| B | bay | K | kah | T | tay |
| C | tsay | L | ell | U | oo |
| D | day | M | emm | V | fow (rhymes with *cow*) |
| E | ay | N | enn | W | vay |
| F | eff | O | oh | X | iks |
| G | gay (hard g) | P | pay | Y | üpsilon |
| H | hah | Q | koo | Z | tset |
| I | ee | R | air (roughly) | ß | ess-tset |

The letters English speakers mix up most are A (ah), E (ay), I (ee) and J (yot). English
"ay" is the German name of E, and English "ee" is the German name of I, so if you spell *Jane*
the English way ("jay, ay, en, ee"), a German writes down something like "?, E, N, I".
Practise your own name until the German letter names come without thinking.

## Vowels: long and short

Every German **[[vowel]]** (a, e, i, o, u) can be long or short, and the difference can change the
meaning of a word. Some rough rules for spotting a long vowel:

- a vowel followed by *h* is long: *Jahr*, *wohnen*, *sehr*;
- a doubled vowel is long: *Tee* (tea), *Boot* (boat);
- *ie* is a long "ee": *sie*, *wie*, *vier*.

A vowel before a double **[[consonant]]** (*ll*, *mm*, *ss*, *tt*…) is short: *Hallo*, *kommen*,
*bitte*. Short vowels are clipped, as in English *bit* or *hot*; long vowels are held, with no
glide at the end. Long *e* in *Tee* is a pure, steady "ay" that doesn't slide into "ee" the way English
"ay" does.

| Short | Long |
|---|---|
| *Stadt* (city) | *Tag* (day) |
| *bitte* (please) | *sie* (she) |
| *Wort* (word) | *wohnen* (to live) |

An unstressed *e* at the end of a word is never silent. *Name* has two syllables: "NAH-meh".
*Danke* is "DAHN-keh". 

## The umlauts ä, ö, ü

The two dots are called an **[[umlaut]]**. They change the sound of the vowel:

- *ä* sounds like *e* in English *bed* (long *ä* as in *Käse* is a longer version of that);
- *ö*: say "ay", then round your lips as if to whistle, keeping your tongue where it is;
- *ü*: say "ee", then round your lips the same way.

You know *Tschüss* (bye). Try *Österreich* (Austria) and *Grüß Gott* (hello, in the south). The
umlaut is part of the spelling, not decoration: *schon* (already) and *schön* (beautiful) are
different words.

Typing them: in this app, use the buttons under the answer box. On a Windows US keyboard,
hold Alt and type 0228 (ä), 0246 (ö), 0252 (ü), 0223 (ß) on the number pad, or switch to the
US-International layout. On a Mac, press Option+u and then the vowel; Option+s gives ß. On a
phone, press and hold the vowel. Germans write *ae*, *oe*, *ue* (*Oesterreich*) only when
they can't type the real letter.

## ß and ss

The letter *ß* is called *Eszett* (ess-tset) or *scharfes S*. It always sounds like a
sharp *s* as in *kiss*. The rule for when to use it:

- after a long vowel or a **[[diphthong]]** (two vowels gliding together, like *ei* or *au*),
  write *ß*: *Straße*, *heißen*, *Grüß Gott*;
- after a short vowel, write *ss*: *Tschüss*, *dass*, *Wasser*.

Switzerland doesn't use *ß* at all and writes *ss* everywhere. No German word begins with
*ß*, so you never need it as a capital at the start of a word; in text written all in capitals,
*ß* becomes *SS* (*STRASSE*).

## Vowel pairs: ei, ie, eu, äu, au

These are the pairs English speakers swap most often.

| Spelling | Sounds like | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *ei* | English *eye* | *nein* (no), *heißen* (to be called) |
| *ie* | English *ee* | *Wie bitte?* (pardon?), *Wiedersehen* |
| *eu*, *äu* | *oy* as in *boy* | *Deutschland*, *Häuser* (houses) |
| *au* | *ow* as in *cow* | *auf*, *Frau* |

Memory hook: in *ei* and *ie*, say the English name of the second letter. *Nein* ends in
*i*, so you say "eye"; *wie* ends in *e*, so you say "ee". *Wein* (wine) and *Wien* (Vienna)
are a good pair to practise.

## Consonants that differ from English

| Spelling | Sound | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *w* | English *v* | *wie*, *Wort*, *wohnen* |
| *v* | usually English *f* | *Vorname*, *vier* |
| *j* | English *y* | *ja*, *Jahr* |
| *z* | *ts* as in *cats* | *zehn* (ten), *zwei* (two) |
| *s* before a vowel | English *z* | *sie*, *Sonne* (sun), *langsam* |
| *sch* | English *sh* | *schreiben*, *schön* |
| *sp*, *st* at the start of a word or part | *shp*, *sht* | *sprechen*, *Stadt*, *buchstabieren* |
| *ch* after a, o, u, au | rough sound at the back of the throat | *Nacht* (night), *noch* (still), *Buchstabe* (letter) |
| *ch* after other letters | soft hiss, like the *h* in *huge* | *ich*, *nicht* (not) |
| *-ig* at the end | like *ich* | *zwanzig* (twenty) |
| *qu* | *kv* | *Quatsch* (nonsense) |
| *th* | plain *t* | *Theater* |

The two *ch* sounds deserve practice. After *a*, *o*, *u* and *au* (*Nacht*, *noch*, *auch*),
it's the scraping sound in Scottish *loch*. After everything else (*ich*, *nicht*, *Milch*),
it's softer, made at the front of the mouth: say "hue" and stretch the h. (*Milch* means milk.) Never turn either
into an English *k* or *ch* as in *church*.

At the end of a word or syllable, *b*, *d* and *g* lose their voice and
sound like *p*, *t* and *k*. This is called **[[final devoicing]]**: *Tag* sounds like "tahk", *und* like "oont", *gelb* (yellow) like
"gelp". The spelling doesn't change.

The German *r*: at the start of a syllable, *r* is made at the back of the throat, close to a
light gargle: *richtig* (right), *Grüß Gott*. After a vowel, it mostly melts into a short
"uh": *der* (the) sounds close to "dare-uh", and the *r* in *Wort* is barely heard. If the throat *r* is hard at first, a
rolled *r* is understood everywhere, and many southern speakers use one.

## Where the stress falls

**[[Word stress]]** in German is usually on the first syllable: *DAN-ke*, *BIT-te*, *SCHREI-ben*,
*VOR-na-me*. Important exceptions:

- words beginning with *be-*, *ent-*, *ver-* and a few other short prefixes stress the next
  syllable: *Ent-SCHUL-di-gung*, *ver-STE-hen*;
- verbs ending in *-ieren* stress the *ie*: *buch-sta-BIE-ren*;
- many words borrowed from other languages stress the end: *Al-pha-BET*, *Ad-RES-se*;
- *Auf Wiedersehen* is stressed on *WIE*, and *Tschüss* has one syllable.

## Nouns have capital letters

Every German **[[noun]]** starts with a capital letter, wherever it is in the sentence: *der Name*,
*das Wort*, *mein Vorname*. That's a gift for readers: you can spot the nouns at a glance. Other
words are lowercase unless they start a sentence. The pronoun *ich* (I) is always lowercase,
unlike English *I*.

*Mein Name ist Lena.* — My name is Lena.
*Wie ist Ihr Familienname?* — What is your surname?
*Das Wort ist neu.* — The word is new.

## Spelling your name

When you give your name in Germany, people will often ask you to spell it. The question is *Wie
schreibt man das?* (literally "How does one write that?"), and the answer is the letters,
said one by one with the verb *buchstabieren* (to spell):

*Wie schreibt man das?* — How do you spell that?
*Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren?* — Could you spell that, please?
*M – Ü – Double-L – E – R.* In German: *em, ü, zwei el* or *doppel-el, e, er.*

A double letter is often said as *zwei* (two) or *Doppel-* plus the letter.

## Polite words and greetings

Greetings change with the time of day. *Guten Morgen* is used until about 10 or 11 o'clock,
*Guten Tag* through the day, *Guten Abend* from about 6 p.m. *Gute Nacht* is only for going to
bed. *Hallo* is friendly and works almost anywhere; *Grüß Gott* is the standard greeting in
Bavaria and Austria. For goodbye, *Auf Wiedersehen* is polite and *Tschüss* is casual.

*Danke!* — *Bitte!* is the everyday exchange: thanks, you're welcome. *Bitte* also means
"please" and "here you are". *Danke schön* and *Bitte schön* are a little warmer.
*Entschuldigung* means "excuse me" (to get attention) and "sorry". *Wie bitte?* asks someone
to repeat what they said: "pardon?". If you need it again and slower, say *Noch einmal,
bitte. Langsam, bitte.*

## Dialogue: at a reception desk

> Frau Brandt: Guten Morgen!
>
> Tom: Guten Morgen. Mein Name ist Tom Weaver.
>
> Frau Brandt: Wie bitte? Noch einmal, bitte. Langsam, bitte.
>
> Tom: Tom Weaver. Mein Vorname ist Tom, mein Familienname ist Weaver.
>
> Frau Brandt: Danke. Wie schreibt man das?
>
> Tom: W – E – A – V – E – R.
>
> Frau Brandt: W, E, A, V wie Vogel, E, R?
>
> Tom: Ja, richtig.
>
> Frau Brandt: Danke schön, Herr Weaver.
>
> Tom: Bitte schön. Auf Wiedersehen!

Good morning! — Good morning. My name is Tom Weaver. — Pardon? Again, please. Slowly, please.
— Tom Weaver. My first name is Tom, my surname is Weaver. — Thank you. How do you spell that? —
W-E-A-V-E-R. — W, E, A, V as in *Vogel* (bird), E, R? — Yes, right. — Thank you very much, Mr
Weaver. — You're welcome. Goodbye!

Notice that Tom says the letter names the German way: *vay, ay, ah, fow, ay, air*.
Germans clarify a letter with a word that starts with it ("V as in Vogel"), much like "B as
in Bravo".

## Pronunciation

- *Entschuldigung*: stress on *SCHUL*; *-ung* is a short "oo" plus the *ng* of English *sing*,
  with no hard g: "oong".
- *Tschüss*: one syllable; start with "ch" as in *church*, then *ü*.
- *Wiedersehen*: "VEE-der-zay-en", with *w* as v and *s* as z.
- *buchstabieren*: *ch* at the back (after *u*), *st* as "sht", stress on *BIE*.
- *schreiben*: "SHRY-ben", *ei* as in *eye*.
- *Familienname*: stress on *MI*; *-lien* is one syllable, "lyen": "fa-MEE-lyen-nah-meh".

## Common mistakes

- Reading *w* as English w. *Wie* is "vee", *Wort* is "vort".
- Swapping *ei* and *ie*. *nein* is "nine", *sie* is "zee". Use the second-letter hook.
- A silent final *e*. *Danke*, *bitte*, *Name*: always pronounce the last *e*.
- Using *Gute Nacht* as a greeting in the evening. It means goodbye at bedtime; say *Guten
  Abend* when you arrive.
- Leaving off the umlaut. *schon* and *schön* are different words; write the dots.
- Lowercase nouns. *das wort* is wrong; nouns are always capitalized: *das Wort*.
- Spelling with English letter names. Practise *E* = ay, *I* = ee, *J* = yot, *V* = fow,
  *W* = vay.

## Key points

- German spelling is regular: learn the sounds of the letters once and you can read aloud.
- *w* = v, *v* = f, *j* = y, *z* = ts, *s* before a vowel = z, *sp/st* = shp/sht.
- *ei* = "eye", *ie* = "ee", *eu/äu* = "oy"; two *ch* sounds; final *b/d/g* sound like *p/t/k*.
- *ä, ö, ü* are separate sounds; write *ß* after long vowels and diphthongs, *ss* after short ones.
- Stress is usually on the first syllable, except after *be-, ent-, ver-*, in *-ieren* verbs
  and in many borrowed words.
- All nouns start with a capital letter.
- *Wie schreibt man das?* — answer with German letter names.

lessons.title: Greetings and introductions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In the last lesson you learned to say hello, thank you and goodbye, and to spell your name. Now
you'll hold a first real conversation: say who you are, where you're from and where you live,
ask the same of someone else, and ask how they are. To do that you need four verbs (*sein*,
*heißen*, *kommen*, *wohnen*), four question words, and one decision German makes you take in
every conversation: *du* or *Sie*?

## du or Sie?

English has one word for "you". German has two for talking to one person:

| | Use it with | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *du* | friends, family, children, classmates, people your age in casual settings, pets | *Wie heißt du?* |
| *Sie* | adults you don't know, shop and office staff, your boss, older people, anyone you call *Herr* or *Frau* | *Wie heißen Sie?* |

*du* is the **[[informal]]** "you"; *Sie* is the **[[formal]]** "you". *Sie* is always written with a
capital S, even in the middle of a sentence; that's how you tell it apart from *sie* (she,
they), which you'll meet in Lesson 4.

The two go with different ways of naming people. With *du*, people use first names: *Hallo,
Lena!* With *Sie*, they use *Herr* (Mr) or *Frau* (Mrs or Ms) and the surname: *Guten Tag,
Frau Schulz.* *Frau* is used for every adult woman, married or not; there's no German
equivalent of "Miss" in everyday use.

When in doubt, start with *Sie*. Switching from *Sie* to *du* is a small social step, and
usually the older person or the one in a senior position offers it: *Wir können gern du
sagen.* (We can say *du* to each other, if you like.) Among students, young people and in many workplaces, *du* is normal from
the first minute.

## The verb sein (to be)

A **[[verb]]** is a word for an action or state, like *to be*, *to live* or *to come*. The form
you find in a dictionary is the **[[infinitive]]**: *sein* (to be), *wohnen* (to live). In a
sentence, the verb changes its ending to match its **[[subject]]**, the person or thing doing it.
*sein* is irregular, as "to be" is in English, so learn these forms by heart:

| | sein |
|---|---|
| ich (I) | *bin* |
| du (you, informal) | *bist* |
| Sie (you, formal) | *sind* |
| er (he) / sie (she) | *ist* |

*Ich bin Paul.* — I'm Paul.
*Bist du Lena?* — Are you Lena?
*Sind Sie Herr Fischer?* — Are you Mr Fischer?
*Frau Ahmadi ist sehr nett.* — Ms Ahmadi is very nice.

You'll see the full table (we, you all, they) in Lesson 4.

## heißen, kommen, wohnen

Most German verbs are regular. You take the infinitive, remove *-en* to get the stem, and add
an ending. For now you need three forms:

| | heißen (to be called) | kommen (to come) | wohnen (to live) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | *heiße* | *komme* | *wohne* |
| du | *heißt* | *kommst* | *wohnst* |
| Sie | *heißen* | *kommen* | *wohnen* |

The *du* form ends in *-st*. *heißen* is the exception you can already see: its stem ends in
*ß*, so *du* adds only *-t* (*du heißt*, not *du heißst*). The *Sie* form is always the same as
the infinitive, which makes formal German easy.

*heißen* is how Germans give their name. Literally *Ich heiße Anna* is "I am called Anna". You
can also say *Ich bin Anna* or *Mein Name ist Anna* (my name is Anna).

*kommen* goes with *aus* (from) for where you come from:
*Ich komme aus Deutschland.* — I'm from Germany.
*Kommst du aus Österreich?* — Are you from Austria?
*Herr Meier kommt aus der Schweiz.* — Mr Meier is from Switzerland.

*wohnen* goes with *in* for where you live now:
*Ich wohne in Hamburg.* — I live in Hamburg.
*Wohnen Sie in der Stadt?* — Do you live in the city?

Most country names, like *Deutschland* and *Österreich*, have no article. A few do, and *die
Schweiz* is the one you need now: say *aus der Schweiz* and *in der Schweiz* as fixed chunks.
The *der* is explained when you learn the dative in Lesson 18.

One more verb is useful straight away, *sprechen* (to speak), though you'll study it properly
in Lesson 7. Notice the *du* form changes its vowel: *Ich spreche Englisch. Sprichst du
Deutsch? Sprechen Sie Englisch?*

## Asking questions with wer, wie, woher, wo

A **[[W-question]]** starts with a question word, and in German almost all of them begin with *w*.
The verb comes straight after the question word, and the subject follows the verb:

| Question word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *wer* | who | *Wer ist das?* — Who is that? |
| *wie* | how; what (with names) | *Wie heißt du?* — What's your name? |
| *woher* | where from | *Woher kommen Sie?* — Where are you from? |
| *wo* | where | *Wo wohnst du?* — Where do you live? |

Careful: *wer* means "who" and *wo* means "where". English speakers constantly swap them
because *wer* looks like "where". And *wie* is "how", even where English uses "what": *Wie
heißen Sie?* is "What's your name?", literally "How are you called?"

*woher* asks about origin and needs *aus* in the answer; *wo* asks about location and needs
*in*:
*Woher kommst du? — Aus Kanada.* — Where are you from? — From Canada.
*Wo wohnst du? — In Berlin.* — Where do you live? — In Berlin.

## How are you?

| Informal | Formal |
|---|---|
| *Wie geht's?* | *Wie geht es Ihnen?* |
| *Gut, danke. Und dir?* | *Gut, danke. Und Ihnen?* |

*Wie geht's?* is short for *Wie geht es?* (literally "How goes it?"). *Ihnen* and *dir* mean
"to you"; for now, learn the questions and answers as whole chunks. Possible answers, from
best to worst:

*Sehr gut, danke!* — Very well, thanks!
*Gut.* — Fine / good.
*Auch gut.* — Fine too (after the other person has said they're fine and asked *Und dir?*).
*Es geht.* — So-so.
*Nicht so gut.* — Not so good.

*Wie geht's?* is a real question between friends, not just "hi": Germans may tell you how
they actually are. In a shop or with strangers, people say *Guten Tag* and skip it.

When you meet someone, say *Freut mich* (nice to meet you), literally "pleases me". The other
person often answers *Mich auch* (me too).

## Introducing someone else

Use *Das ist …* (this is …) to introduce a third person: *Das ist Jonas. Er kommt aus Bremen.*
(This is Jonas. He's from Bremen.) *er* means he, *sie* means she; both take *ist*, *kommt*,
*wohnt*, *heißt*. Lesson 4 covers these forms in full.

## Dialogue 1: at a language course (du)

> Mia: Hallo! Ich bin Mia. Wie heißt du?
>
> Ben: Hallo, Mia. Ich heiße Ben. Freut mich!
>
> Mia: Freut mich auch. Woher kommst du, Ben?
>
> Ben: Ich komme aus Irland. Und du?
>
> Mia: Ich komme aus Österreich, aus Graz. Aber ich wohne jetzt in Leipzig.
>
> Ben: Leipzig ist eine schöne Stadt!

Hi! I'm Mia. What's your name? — Hi, Mia. I'm Ben. Nice to meet you! — Nice to meet you too.
Where are you from, Ben? — I'm from Ireland. And you? — I'm from Austria, from Graz. But I live
in Leipzig now. — Leipzig is a beautiful city!

## Dialogue 2: at a hotel (Sie)

> Herr Wolf: Guten Abend! Wie geht es Ihnen, Frau Novak?
>
> Frau Novak: Danke, sehr gut. Und Ihnen, Herr Wolf?
>
> Herr Wolf: Auch gut, danke. Wer ist das?
>
> Frau Novak: Das ist Herr Costa. Er kommt aus Portugal.
>
> Herr Wolf: Guten Abend, Herr Costa. Freut mich. Wo wohnen Sie?
>
> Herr Costa: In Lissabon. Lissabon ist eine Stadt in Portugal.

Good evening! How are you, Ms Novak? — Very well, thank you. And you, Mr Wolf? — Fine too,
thanks. Who is that? — This is Mr Costa. He's from Portugal. — Good evening, Mr Costa. Pleased
to meet you. Where do you live? — In Lisbon. Lisbon is a city in Portugal.

(*aber* means "but", *jetzt* means "now", *schön* means "beautiful" and *eine* means "a"; you'll
learn these properly later.)

## Countries and places

*das Land* (country) and *die Stadt* (city, town) are your first two nouns with articles. Every
German noun has one of three articles, *der*, *die* or *das*, and you'll learn why in Lesson 5.
For now, learn each noun together with its article as one unit.

*Deutschland ist ein Land.* — Germany is a country.
*Wien ist eine Stadt in Österreich.* — Vienna is a city in Austria.
*Die Schweiz ist klein.* — Switzerland is small.

## Pronunciation

- *heißen*: *ei* as in "eye", *ß* as a sharp *s*: "HY-sen".
- *wohnen*: *w* = v, long *o*, silent *h*: "VOH-nen".
- *woher*: stress on the second syllable, "vo-HAIR".
- *Österreich*: stress on *Ö*; *eich* ends with the soft *ch* of *ich*.
- *die Schweiz*: "shvites", one syllable, *z* = ts.
- *Wie geht's?*: "vee gates".

## Common mistakes

- Mixing *du* and *Sie* in one conversation (*Wie heißen du?*). Pick one and keep its forms:
  *Wie heißt du?* or *Wie heißen Sie?*
- *Wer* for "where". *Wer* is who, *wo* is where.
- *Wie ist dein Name?* is fine, but *Was ist dein Name?* sounds like a translation from English.
- *Ich komme von Deutschland.* Origin takes *aus*: *Ich komme aus Deutschland.*
- *Ich bin gut* for "I'm fine". Say *Mir geht's gut* or just *Gut, danke*. *Ich bin gut* means
  "I'm good at something" or "I'm a good person".
- Writing the formal *Sie* in lowercase. It's always *Sie*.
- *Du heißst*. The stem ends in *ß*, so it's *du heißt*.

## Key points

- *du* for friends, family and children; *Sie* (capital S) for adults you don't know and
  anyone you call *Herr* or *Frau*.
- *sein*: *ich bin, du bist, Sie sind, er/sie ist*.
- Regular verbs: *ich -e, du -st, Sie -en*; *du heißt* is the exception.
- *kommen aus* for origin, *wohnen in* for where you live now.
- *wer* = who, *wie* = how, *woher* = where from, *wo* = where; the verb follows the question word.
- *Wie geht's?* (informal), *Wie geht es Ihnen?* (formal); *Freut mich* when you meet someone.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Numbers, age and phone numbers
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now say who you are and where you're from. The next things people ask are how old you
are, your phone number and your address, and the answers are all numbers. This lesson teaches
the numbers from 0 to 100, the one big surprise in how German says them, and how to give your
age, phone number, postcode and e-mail address. You'll also meet a second key verb, *haben*
(to have).

## 0 to 12

These have to be learned one by one, as in English.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 *null* | 1 *eins* | 2 *zwei* | 3 *drei* |
| 4 *vier* | 5 *fünf* | 6 *sechs* | 7 *sieben* |
| 8 *acht* | 9 *neun* | 10 *zehn* | 11 *elf* |
| 12 *zwölf* | | | |

Watch the sounds from Lesson 1: *zwei* and *zehn* start with "ts", *vier* starts with "f",
*neun* rhymes with "coin", and *sechs* sounds like "zex". *elf* looks
like the English creature, but it's eleven.

On the phone and in announcements, people often say *zwo* instead of *zwei*, so it can't be
confused with *drei*. You'll hear *zwo* at train stations and in phone numbers; both are correct.

## 13 to 19

Like English "-teen", German adds *-zehn* (ten) to the unit:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 13 *dreizehn* | 14 *vierzehn* | 15 *fünfzehn* |
| 16 *sechzehn* | 17 *siebzehn* | 18 *achtzehn* |
| 19 *neunzehn* | | |

Two spelling traps: *sechzehn* drops the *s* of *sechs*, and *siebzehn* drops the *-en* of
*sieben*.

## The tens

The tens end in *-zig*, which is pronounced like "-tsich" with the soft *ch* of *ich*. (In
southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland you'll hear "-tsik".)

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 20 *zwanzig* | 30 *dreißig* | 40 *vierzig* |
| 50 *fünfzig* | 60 *sechzig* | 70 *siebzig* |
| 80 *achtzig* | 90 *neunzig* | 100 *hundert* |

*dreißig* is the odd one: it ends in *-ßig*, not *-zig*. *sechzig* and *siebzig* lose letters,
just like 16 and 17. *hundert* can also be *einhundert*.

## 21 to 99: the units come first

This is the big difference from English. German says the unit first, then *und* (and), then
the ten, all as one word:

| Number | German | Literally |
|---|---|---|
| 21 | *einundzwanzig* | one-and-twenty |
| 34 | *vierunddreißig* | four-and-thirty |
| 47 | *siebenundvierzig* | seven-and-forty |
| 58 | *achtundfünfzig* | eight-and-fifty |
| 66 | *sechsundsechzig* | six-and-sixty |
| 99 | *neunundneunzig* | nine-and-ninety |

Memory hook: think of the old English nursery rhyme "four-and-twenty blackbirds". German
always counts this way. When you hear a number, hold the first part in your head until the
ten arrives: *dreiundsiebzig* — you hear 3, then 70, and you write 73. Practise by reading numbers off
car number plates or prices until you stop reversing them.

*eins* becomes *ein* inside a longer number: *einundzwanzig*, *einunddreißig*. On its own, or
at the end, it's *eins*: *hunderteins* (101). And *sechs* keeps its *s* in *sechsundzwanzig*,
*sechsundsechzig*; only 16 and 60 drop it.

## How old are you?

*alt* means "old". To ask someone's age:

*Wie alt bist du?* — How old are you? (informal)
*Wie alt sind Sie?* — How old are you? (formal)
*Ich bin 29 Jahre alt.* — I'm 29 years old.
*Ich bin 29.* — I'm 29.

*das Jahr* is "the year", and its plural is *die Jahre*: *ein Jahr*, *zwei Jahre*. German
uses *sein* (to be) for age, just like English, so *Ich habe 29 Jahre* is wrong. The opposite
of *alt* is *jung* (young): *Das Kind ist sehr jung.* (The child is very young.)

## The verb haben (to have)

*haben* is the second most important German verb. Like *sein*, it's slightly irregular:

| | haben |
|---|---|
| ich | *habe* |
| du | *hast* |
| Sie | *haben* |
| er / sie | *hat* |

The *du* and *er/sie* forms drop the *b*: *du hast*, *er hat*. You'll see *haben* in full
in Lesson 6.

*Hast du eine Telefonnummer?* — Do you have a phone number?
*Ich habe eine Handynummer.* — I have a mobile number.
*Haben Sie eine E-Mail-Adresse?* — Do you have an e-mail address?

(*eine* means "a" here; more on that in Lesson 5.)

## Phone numbers

*die Telefonnummer* is a phone number in general; *die Handynummer* is a mobile number (*das
Handy* is the German word for a mobile phone). *die Nummer* is a number used as a label, like
a phone, room or house number; *die Zahl* is a number as a quantity or figure: *Sieben ist eine
Zahl.*

Germans usually say phone numbers digit by digit, or in pairs: 0176 48 25 93 can be *null eins
sieben sechs, achtundvierzig, fünfundzwanzig, dreiundneunzig*. Asking someone to repeat is
normal: *Noch einmal, bitte. Langsam, bitte.*

*Wie ist deine Telefonnummer?* — What's your phone number? (informal)
*Wie ist Ihre Handynummer?* — What's your mobile number? (formal)
*Meine Nummer ist 0151 23 40 17.* — My number is 0151 23 40 17.

*deine*, *Ihre* and *meine* mean "your" and "my"; Lesson 6 explains them.

## Addresses and e-mail

A German address puts the street first and the house number after it, then the postcode
before the town:

> Lisa Krämer
>
> Lindenstraße 14
>
> 04107 Leipzig

*die Adresse* is the address, *die Hausnummer* the house number, *die Postleitzahl* the postcode
(often shortened to *PLZ*). German postcodes have five digits; Austrian and Swiss ones have four.

*Wie ist Ihre Adresse? — Lindenstraße 14, 04107 Leipzig.*
*Die Hausnummer ist vierzehn.* — The house number is fourteen.
*Die Postleitzahl ist null-vier-eins-null-sieben.* — The postcode is 04107.

For an e-mail address, @ is said like English "at", the dot is *Punkt*, and the hyphen is
*Bindestrich*. *die E-Mail* is both "the e-mail" (the message) and,
in everyday speech, short for *die E-Mail-Adresse*.

*Meine E-Mail ist lisa.kraemer@post.de.* — "lisa Punkt kraemer at post Punkt de"

Notice the address uses *ae* for *ä*, because many e-mail addresses can't contain umlauts.

## Dialogue: signing up at a gym

> Mitarbeiter: Guten Tag! Wie ist Ihr Name, bitte?
>
> Frau Okafor: Okafor, Grace Okafor.
>
> Mitarbeiter: Und wie alt sind Sie, Frau Okafor?
>
> Frau Okafor: Ich bin 34 Jahre alt.
>
> Mitarbeiter: Wie ist Ihre Adresse?
>
> Frau Okafor: Bergstraße 72, 50667 Köln.
>
> Mitarbeiter: Zweiundsiebzig oder siebenundzwanzig?
>
> Frau Okafor: Zweiundsiebzig. Sieben, zwei.
>
> Mitarbeiter: Danke. Haben Sie eine Handynummer?
>
> Frau Okafor: Ja, die Nummer ist 0172 58 39 61.

Hello! What's your name, please? — Okafor, Grace Okafor. — And how old are you, Ms Okafor? —
I'm 34 years old. — What's your address? — Bergstraße 72, 50667 Cologne. — Seventy-two or
twenty-seven? — Seventy-two. Seven, two. — Thank you. Do you have a mobile number? — Yes, the
number is 0172 58 39 61.

(*der Mitarbeiter* is the employee; *oder* means "or".) The question "72 or 27?" is exactly the
confusion German numbers cause, even among Germans: saying the digits separately settles it.

## Pronunciation

- *zwanzig*, *dreißig*, *vierzig*: stress on the first syllable; *-ig* like *ich*.
- *dreißig*: *ei* as in "eye", then a sharp *s*: "DRY-sich".
- *sieben*: "ZEE-ben" (*s* before a vowel is z; *ie* is ee).
- *fünf*: round your lips for *ü*; don't say "funf".
- *zwölf*: *ö* with rounded lips, *z* = ts: "tsvölf".
- *Postleitzahl*: *st* in the middle of a word is a plain "st"; stress on *POST*.
- *achtzig*: the *ch* is the throaty one, as in *Nacht*.

## Common mistakes

- Reversing two-digit numbers: writing 52 for *fünfundzwanzig* (25). Units first, then tens.
- Writing *dreizig* or *dreissig*. It's *dreißig* (or *dreissig* only in Switzerland).
- Writing *sechszehn*, *siebenzehn*, *sechszig*, *siebenzig*. Correct: *sechzehn*, *siebzehn*,
  *sechzig*, *siebzig*.
- *eins und zwanzig* as separate words. Numbers under a million are one word: *einundzwanzig*.
- *Ich habe 30 Jahre.* German uses *sein* for age: *Ich bin 30 Jahre alt.*
- *du habst*, *er habt*. The forms are *du hast*, *er hat*.

## Key points

- Learn 0–12 by heart; 13–19 add *-zehn*; tens end in *-zig*, except *dreißig*.
- *sechzehn, sechzig, siebzehn, siebzig* drop letters.
- 21–99: unit + *und* + ten, written as one word: *vierundfünfzig* = 54.
- *zwo* is an alternative to *zwei*, common on the phone.
- Age: *Wie alt bist du? Ich bin … Jahre alt.*
- *haben*: *ich habe, du hast, Sie haben, er/sie hat*.
- Addresses: street + number, then postcode + town.

lessons.title: The present tense and asking questions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far you've used verbs with *ich*, *du* and *Sie*, plus *er/sie ist*. This lesson completes
the picture: all the people a verb can go with, the endings for every one of them, the full
forms of *sein*, and the two rules of German word order that you'll use in every sentence
from now on: the verb comes second in a statement, and first in a yes/no question. Once you
have these, you can talk about what people do, and ask about it.

## Personal pronouns

A **[[personal pronoun]]** is a short word that stands for a person or thing: I, you, she, we…

| | Singular | | Plural | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st person | *ich* | I | *wir* | we |
| 2nd person | *du* | you (informal, one person) | *ihr* | you (informal, two or more) |
| 3rd person | *er* / *sie* / *es* | he / she / it | *sie* | they |
| formal | *Sie* | you (formal, one or more) | *Sie* | you (formal) |

Three things to notice:

- German has a separate plural "you": *ihr* is what you say to two or more friends, like
  "you guys" or "y'all". Formal *Sie* is the same for one person or many.
- *sie* has three jobs. Lowercase *sie* means "she" or "they"; capital *Sie* means formal
  "you". The verb ending tells "she" apart from "they": *sie wohnt* (she lives), *sie wohnen*
  (they live).
- *er*, *sie* and *es* also mean "it", depending on the noun's gender (Lesson 5). For people,
  *er* is he and *sie* is she.

## Regular verb endings

To use a verb in a sentence you **[[conjugate]]** it: you take its **[[stem]]** (the infinitive minus
*-en*) and add the **[[ending]]** that matches the subject. *machen* (to do, to make) has the stem
*mach-*:

| | Ending | machen | wohnen | spielen (to play) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | -e | *mache* | *wohne* | *spiele* |
| du | -st | *machst* | *wohnst* | *spielst* |
| er / sie / es | -t | *macht* | *wohnt* | *spielt* |
| wir | -en | *machen* | *wohnen* | *spielen* |
| ihr | -t | *macht* | *wohnt* | *spielt* |
| sie / Sie | -en | *machen* | *wohnen* | *spielen* |

Memory hook: say the endings as a chant, *e, st, t, en, t, en*. Two pairs look the same: the
*wir* and *sie/Sie* forms are both the infinitive, and the *er* and *ihr* forms both end in
*-t*. The pronoun tells you which one you mean.

The **[[present tense]]** covers all of English "I play", "I'm playing" and "I do play". There's no
"-ing" form in German: *Ich lerne Deutsch* is both "I learn German" and "I'm learning German".
With a time word it can also mean the future: *Heute spielen wir Tennis.* (We're playing tennis
today.)

## Stems ending in -t or -d

If the stem ends in *-t* or *-d*, German adds an *e* before *-st* and *-t*, because *arbeitt*
or *antwortst* can't be pronounced clearly:

| | arbeiten (to work) | antworten (to answer) |
|---|---|---|
| ich | *arbeite* | *antworte* |
| du | *arbeitest* | *antwortest* |
| er / sie / es | *arbeitet* | *antwortet* |
| wir | *arbeiten* | *antworten* |
| ihr | *arbeitet* | *antwortet* |
| sie / Sie | *arbeiten* | *antworten* |

*Er arbeitet hier.* — He works here.
*Antwortest du?* — Are you answering?

## Stems ending in -s, -ß or -z

If the stem ends in an *s* sound (*-s*, *-ß*, *-z*), the *du* form adds only *-t*, so it looks
like the *er* form: *du heißt*, *er heißt*. The same happens with *tanzen* (to dance): *du
tanzt*.

## sein in full

| | sein (to be) |
|---|---|
| ich | *bin* |
| du | *bist* |
| er / sie / es | *ist* |
| wir | *sind* |
| ihr | *seid* |
| sie / Sie | *sind* |

Don't confuse *ihr seid* (you are) with *seit* (since), which sounds the same. *ist* is easy to
remember: it's English "is" with a *t*.

*Wir sind hier.* — We're here.
*Seid ihr aus Berlin?* — Are you (all) from Berlin?
*Sie sind jetzt in Wien.* — They're in Vienna now. / You're in Vienna now.

## A few verbs to know

*gehen* (to go, on foot), *kommen* (to come), *hören* (to hear, to listen to), *fragen* (to
ask), *sagen* (to say), *lernen* (to learn), *studieren* (to study at university), *leben*
(to live, to be alive) and *verstehen* (to understand) are all regular in the present tense.

*lernen* vs *studieren*: *lernen* is learning anything, including revising for a test;
*studieren* is studying a subject at a university. *Ich studiere Biologie* (I'm a biology
student), but *Ich lerne Deutsch* (I'm learning German).

*wohnen* vs *leben*: *wohnen* is where your home is (*Ich wohne in der Goethestraße*), *leben*
is living in a wider sense (*Wir leben in Deutschland. Er lebt allein.* — He lives alone).

## Rule 1: the verb comes second

In a German **[[statement]]**, the conjugated verb is always the second element. The first element
can be the subject, but it can also be a time word, a place or an object. When something else
comes first, the subject moves to just after the verb:

| 1 | 2 (verb) | rest |
|---|---|---|
| *Ich* | *arbeite* | *heute in Köln.* |
| *Heute* | *arbeite* | *ich in Köln.* |
| *In Köln* | *arbeite* | *ich heute.* |

All three mean "I'm working in Cologne today". This is the **[[verb-second rule]]**, and it's the
biggest difference from English word order. English says "Today I work"; German must say
*Heute arbeite ich*. Starting with a time word is very common and sounds natural:

*Jetzt lernen wir.* — Now we're studying.
*Oft hört sie Musik.* — She often listens to music.
*Hier wohnt Familie Klein.* — The Klein family lives here.

Adverbs such as *oft* (often), *immer* (always) and *gern* usually come right after the verb:
*Ich spiele oft Tennis. Er arbeitet immer.* *gern* is how German says "like doing": *Ich lerne
gern Deutsch.* (I like learning German.) *Wir spielen gern.* (We like playing.)

## Rule 2: questions

For a **[[yes/no question]]**, put the verb first and the subject second:

*Du wohnst hier.* → *Wohnst du hier?* — Do you live here?
*Er arbeitet heute.* → *Arbeitet er heute?* — Is he working today?
*Ihr versteht das.* → *Versteht ihr das?* — Do you (all) understand that?

There's no "do" in German questions. Just swap the verb to the front.

For a W-question, the question word comes first and the verb second, exactly as in Lesson 2.
Three new question words:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| *was* | what | *Was machst du heute?* — What are you doing today? |
| *warum* | why | *Warum lernst du Deutsch?* — Why are you learning German? |
| *wann* | when | *Wann arbeitet Lara?* — When does Lara work? |

*wann* only asks questions about time. It looks like English "when" but isn't used for
"when I was young"; that's a different word you'll meet later.

*hier* (here), *dort* (there), *jetzt* (now) and *heute* (today) are useful in answers:
*Wo ist Max? — Dort.* *Wann lernst du? — Jetzt.*

## Dialogue: a new flatmate

> Lukas: Hallo! Bist du Sara? Ich bin Lukas. Ich wohne hier.
>
> Sara: Hallo, Lukas! Ja, ich bin Sara. Was machst du? Studierst du?
>
> Lukas: Nein, ich arbeite. Ich bin Koch. Und du?
>
> Sara: Ich studiere Musik. Ich spiele Klavier.
>
> Lukas: Toll! Spielst du oft?
>
> Sara: Ja, immer. Heute spiele ich auch. Warum fragst du?
>
> Lukas: Ich höre gern Musik. Und Jonas und Mira, sie spielen Gitarre.
>
> Sara: Wann sind Jonas und Mira hier?
>
> Lukas: Jetzt sind sie dort, im Park. Gehen wir?

Hi! Are you Sara? I'm Lukas. I live here. — Hi, Lukas! Yes, I'm Sara. What do you do? Are you a
student? — No, I work. I'm a cook. And you? — I study music. I play the piano. — Great! Do you
play often? — Yes, all the time. I'm playing today too. Why do you ask? — I like listening to
music. And Jonas and Mira, they play the guitar. — When are Jonas and Mira here? — Right now
they're over there, in the park. Shall we go?

(*der Koch* is a cook, *das Klavier* a piano, *die Gitarre* a guitar, *toll* means "great", and
*im Park* "in the park". Notice: no article before a job: *Ich bin Koch*.)

## Pronunciation

- *arbeiten*: "AR-by-ten"; *ei* as in "eye".
- *verstehen*: stress on *STE*; *st* = "sht" because it starts the root.
- *studieren*: "shtoo-DEE-ren"; *-ieren* verbs are stressed on *ie*.
- *warum*: stress on *RUM*: "va-ROOM".
- *ihr seid*: "eer zite"; same sound as *seit*.
- *jetzt*: *j* = y, *tzt* is one quick "tst": "yetst".

## Common mistakes

- English word order after a time word: *Heute ich arbeite.* Correct: *Heute arbeite ich.*
- Adding a helper verb the way English adds "do": *Tust du hier wohnen?* Just put the verb
  first: *Wohnst du hier?*
- Using *-st* with *ihr*: *ihr wohnst*. The *ihr* ending is *-t*: *ihr wohnt*.
- Forgetting the extra *e*: *er arbeitt*, *du antwortst*. Correct: *er arbeitet*, *du
  antwortest*.
- *ihr sind*, *wir seid*. Correct: *wir sind*, *ihr seid*.
- Translating "I am learning" word for word: *Ich bin lernen.* German uses one verb: *Ich lerne.*
- Using *studieren* for school homework. Say *Ich lerne* for revising.

## Key points

- Pronouns: *ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie*.
- Endings: *-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en*; stems in *-t/-d* add *e* (*arbeitest*); stems in
  *-s/-ß/-z* take only *-t* with *du* (*heißt*).
- *sein*: *bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind*.
- One German present form covers "I play", "I'm playing" and "I do play".
- Statements: the verb is second; if something else comes first, the subject follows the verb.
- Yes/no questions: the verb comes first. W-questions: question word, then verb.
- *gern* after the verb means "like doing".

lessons.title: Nouns, gender and articles
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Module 1 you learned to greet people, give your name, count and build simple sentences with
verbs. Now you start talking about *things*: the pen on the desk, the phone in your bag, the
keys you can't find. To do that in German you need to know three facts about every noun:
its gender, its article and its plural.

By the end of this lesson you can point at an object and ask *Was ist das?* (What is that?),
answer *Das ist ein Stift* (That's a pen), and talk about more than one thing: *Das sind
Stifte* (Those are pens).

## Every noun has a gender

English has one word for "the". German has three, because every German noun belongs to one of
three groups called **[[gender]]**: **[[masculine]]**, **[[feminine]]** and **[[neuter]]**. The word for "the"
— the **[[definite article]]** — changes with the gender:

| Gender | "the" | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | der | *der Tisch* (the table), *der Stuhl* (the chair), *der Schlüssel* (the key) |
| feminine | die | *die Lampe* (the lamp), *die Tür* (the door), *die Tasche* (the bag) |
| neuter | das | *das Buch* (the book), *das Fenster* (the window), *das Handy* (the mobile phone) |

Grammatical gender is a label for the word, not a fact about the object. A table isn't male
and a door isn't female; *der* and *die* simply tell you which group the word is in. Even
words for people can surprise you: *das Kind* (the child) is neuter.

The gender matters because many other words have to agree with it — the article now, and
later possessives (*mein*, *meine*), adjective endings and pronouns. If you know the gender,
all of these fall into place.

The golden rule: never learn a noun without its article. Don't learn *Tisch = table*;
learn *der Tisch = the table*. Say it aloud as one unit — *derTisch, dieLampe, dasBuch* — until
the article feels like part of the word. Your vocabulary cards always show nouns with their
article, and you'll be asked to type it.

A memory hook many learners like: picture every masculine noun in blue, every feminine noun
in red and every neuter noun in green. When you learn *die Uhr* (the clock), imagine a red
clock.

## The indefinite article: ein and eine

The **[[indefinite article]]** means "a" or "an". It has two forms in the basic (subject) form:

| Gender | "the" | "a / an" |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | der Stift | ein Stift |
| feminine | die Brille | eine Brille |
| neuter | das Heft | ein Heft |

Masculine and neuter share *ein*; feminine adds *-e*: *eine*. So *ein* alone doesn't tell you
whether a noun is masculine or neuter — another reason to learn nouns with *der/die/das*.

- *Das ist ein Kuli.* — That's a ballpoint pen.
- *Das ist eine Zeitung.* — That's a newspaper.
- *Das ist ein Foto.* — That's a photo.
- *Ist das eine Uhr?* — Is that a clock?

Just like English "a", *ein/eine* has no plural. For more than one thing you simply drop it:
*ein Buch* → *Bücher* (books).

## Was ist das? Das ist … / Das sind …

The question *Was ist das?* means "What is that?" or "What is this?" — German uses the same
word for both. The answer starts with *Das ist …* for one thing and *Das sind …* for several:

- *Was ist das?* — *Das ist ein Schlüssel.* — What's that? — That's a key.
- *Und das?* — *Das sind Schlüssel.* — And that? — Those are keys.
- *Das ist die Tasche von Anna.* — That's Anna's bag. (Literally "the bag of Anna".)

Notice that the *das* in *Das ist* never changes. It means "this" or "that" and points at
something, whatever its gender: *Das ist der Tisch. Das ist die Lampe. Das sind Stühle.* Only
the article in front of the noun shows the gender.

## Gender hints

You can't guess every gender, but some endings are reliable:

| Ending | Gender | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft | feminine (always) | *die Zeitung*, *die Freiheit* (freedom), *die Möglichkeit* (possibility) |
| -ion, -tät | feminine | *die Information*, *die Universität* |
| -chen, -lein (small things) | neuter (always) | *das Mädchen* (girl), *das Brötchen* (bread roll) |
| -e | usually feminine | *die Lampe*, *die Tasche*, *die Brille* — but *der Name* |
| -er (for a person or a machine that does something) | usually masculine | *der Computer*, *der Lehrer* (teacher) — but *das Fenster* |

Two more hints:

- Words borrowed from English that end in *-y* are often neuter (*das Handy*, *das Hobby*,
  *das Baby*), but not always: *die Party*.
- In a **[[compound noun]]** — two nouns joined into one word — the *last* part decides the gender.
  *das Haus* (house) + *die Tür* = *die Haustür* (the front door). *das Handy* + *die Nummer* =
  *die Handynummer*. The first part only adds meaning.

Use the hints to check yourself, but the article you memorised always wins.

## Plurals: one article, many endings

Here is the good news: in the plural every noun takes the same article: *die*.

- *der Tisch* → *die Tische*
- *die Lampe* → *die Lampen*
- *das Buch* → *die Bücher*

The bad news: German has several ways to form the **[[plural]]**, so you learn each noun's plural
with it, just like the article. The main patterns:

| Pattern | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| -e | der Tisch, das Heft, der Stift | die Tische, die Hefte, die Stifte |
| umlaut + -e | der Stuhl | die Stühle |
| -er | das Kind | die Kinder |
| umlaut + -er | das Buch | die Bücher |
| -n / -en | die Lampe, die Tür, die Zeitung | die Lampen, die Türen, die Zeitungen |
| -s | das Handy, das Foto, der Kuli | die Handys, die Fotos, die Kulis |
| no ending | der Schlüssel, das Fenster, der Computer | die Schlüssel, die Fenster, die Computer |

Patterns that help:

- Most feminine nouns add *-n* or *-en*: *die Tasche → die Taschen*, *die Uhr → die Uhren*.
- Masculine and neuter nouns ending in *-er*, *-el* or *-en* usually add nothing: *der
  Schlüssel → die Schlüssel*. The article tells you it's plural: *der Schlüssel* (one key),
  *die Schlüssel* (keys).
- Short words ending in a vowel other than *-e*, and many English loanwords, add *-s*:
  *das Handy → die Handys*.
- An umlaut can appear in the plural: *der Stuhl → die Stühle*. The vowel sound changes, so
  listen for it.

A useful word for anything: *das Ding*, plural *die Dinge* — "the thing". *Was ist das Ding
hier?* — What's this thing here?

## Dialogue: the first day in the shared office

Lena helps Tom, a new colleague from Canada, find his way around the desk they share.

> Tom: *Was ist das?*
>
> Lena: *Das ist ein Schlüssel. Der Schlüssel ist für die Tür hier.*
>
> Tom: *Danke! Und das? Ist das eine Lampe?*
>
> Lena: *Ja, das ist die Lampe. Und das sind Stifte, Kulis und Papier.*
>
> Tom: *Super. Ist das dein Handy?*
>
> Lena: *Nein, das ist das Handy von Max. Mein Handy ist hier in der Tasche.*
>
> Tom: *Und die Zeitung?*
>
> Lena: *Die Zeitung ist für alle. Das Fenster ist auch für alle!*

Translation:

> Tom: What's that?
>
> Lena: That's a key. The key is for the door here.
>
> Tom: Thanks! And that? Is that a lamp?
>
> Lena: Yes, that's the lamp. And those are pens, ballpoints and paper.
>
> Tom: Great. Is that your phone?
>
> Lena: No, that's Max's phone. My phone is here in the bag.
>
> Tom: And the newspaper?
>
> Lena: The newspaper is for everyone. The window is for everyone too!

(*dein* = your, *mein* = my, *für* = for, *alle* = everyone. You'll learn *mein* and *dein*
properly in the next lesson; *in der Tasche* means "in the bag" and the form *der* there is
explained in lesson 19.)

## Pronunciation

- *Stuhl*: a long *u* — the *h* isn't pronounced, it only shows the vowel is long.
- *Tür*, *Bücher*, *Stühle*, *Schlüssel*: round your lips for *u* and say *ee* — that's *ü*.
  It's long in *Tür* and *Bücher*, short in *Schlüssel*.
- *Zeitung*: *z* sounds like *ts* and *ei* like English "eye": TSAI-tung.
- *Uhr* sounds close to English "poor" without the *p*: a long *u* and a soft *r*.
- *Handy* is said much like English "Henny" with a *d*; *Computer* keeps the English stress
  (kom-PYOO-ter).
- *Brille*: a short *i* and a double *l* — BRIL-le.

## Common mistakes

- Translating "the" as *die* everywhere. *Die* is only feminine and plural. *der Tisch*,
  not ~~die Tisch~~.
- Guessing the plural with -s. English adds *-s*; German usually doesn't. ~~die Tischs~~ →
  *die Tische*; ~~die Buchs~~ → *die Bücher*.
- Lowercase nouns. Every German noun starts with a capital letter, in the middle of a
  sentence too: *Das ist eine Uhr*, not ~~eine uhr~~.
- Thinking *die Brille* is plural. English says "glasses", but *die Brille* is one pair,
  feminine singular: *Das ist meine Brille.* Two pairs are *zwei Brillen*.
- Changing *Das ist* to match the noun. It's always *Das ist die Lampe*, never
  ~~Die ist die Lampe~~ for "That's the lamp".
- The *Handy* trap. In German *das Handy* means a mobile (cell) phone, not something useful.

## Key points

- Every noun is masculine (*der*), feminine (*die*) or neuter (*das*). Learn each one with its
  article and plural.
- "A" is *ein* for masculine and neuter, *eine* for feminine. There's no plural "a".
- All plurals take *die*. Plural endings vary: *-e, ¨e, -er, ¨er, -(e)n, -s* or none.
- Endings like *-ung, -heit, -keit* (feminine) and *-chen* (neuter) give reliable hints; in a
  compound the last part decides.
- *Was ist das?* — *Das ist …* (one thing) / *Das sind …* (several).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Family and possessives
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In the last lesson you learned that every noun has a gender and an article: *der Stift, die
Tasche, das Handy*. Now you'll use that knowledge to talk about the people in your life — and
to say whose they are. *My* brother, *your* sister, *our* dog: words like these are called
**[[possessive articles]]**, and they take the place of *der/die/das* or *ein/eine*.

You'll also learn all forms of *haben* (to have), so you can say *Ich habe zwei Brüder* or
*Wir haben eine Katze*.

## Family words

| Masculine | Feminine | Neuter, plural and others |
|---|---|---|
| der Vater (father) | die Mutter (mother) | die Eltern (parents — plural only) |
| der Sohn (son) | die Tochter (daughter) | das Kind, die Kinder (child, children) |
| der Bruder (brother) | die Schwester (sister) | die Geschwister (brothers and sisters, siblings) |
| der Großvater / der Opa (grandfather / grandpa) | die Großmutter / die Oma (grandmother / grandma) | das Baby (baby) |
| der Mann (man; husband) | die Frau (woman; wife) | die Familie (family) |
| der Freund (friend; boyfriend) | die Freundin (friend; girlfriend) | die Person (person) |

Some notes:

- *die Frau* means "the woman" and also "the wife". Without an article, *Frau Klein* is "Mrs
  (or Ms) Klein", as you learned in lesson 2. In the same way *der Mann* is "the man" and *mein
  Mann* is "my husband".
- *die Eltern* and *die Geschwister* are used only in the plural. German has a handy single
  word for "brothers and sisters": *Hast du Geschwister?* — Do you have any siblings?
- *Opa* and *Oma* are the everyday words. *Großvater* and *Großmutter* sound a bit more formal.
- Many family plurals take an umlaut: *die Mütter, die Väter, die Brüder, die Töchter, die
  Söhne*. *die Schwester* becomes *die Schwestern*.

Pets count as family too: *der Hund* (dog), *die Katze* (cat), and the general word *das Tier*
(animal).

## Possessive articles: whose is it?

Here are the possessive articles, one for each person you met in lesson 4:

| Pronoun | Possessive | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| ich | mein | my |
| du | dein | your (one person, informal) |
| er | sein | his |
| sie | ihr | her |
| es | sein | its |
| wir | unser | our |
| ihr | euer | your (several people, informal) |
| sie | ihr | their |
| Sie | Ihr | your (formal, one or more people) |

Note two things. First, *ihr* has several meanings: "her", "their", and with a capital *I*,
the formal "your" (*Ihr*). Context makes it clear. Second, the pronoun *ihr* (you, plural)
and the possessive *ihr* (her/their) look identical but are different words.

## The endings: same as ein and eine

A possessive article takes exactly the same endings as *ein*: no ending for masculine and
neuter, *-e* for feminine. Unlike *ein*, it also has a plural form, also with *-e*.

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a | ein Bruder | eine Schwester | ein Kind | — |
| my | mein Bruder | meine Schwester | mein Kind | meine Eltern |
| your | dein Bruder | deine Schwester | dein Kind | deine Eltern |
| his | sein Bruder | seine Schwester | sein Kind | seine Eltern |
| her | ihr Bruder | ihre Schwester | ihr Kind | ihre Eltern |
| our | unser Bruder | unsere Schwester | unser Kind | unsere Eltern |
| your (pl.) | euer Bruder | eure Schwester | euer Kind | eure Eltern |
| their | ihr Bruder | ihre Schwester | ihr Kind | ihre Eltern |
| your (formal) | Ihr Bruder | Ihre Schwester | Ihr Kind | Ihre Eltern |

*euer* drops its second *e* when an ending is added: *eure*, not ~~euere~~.

These are the forms for the subject of the sentence, the person or thing doing the action or
being described. Grammar calls this form the **[[nominative]]**: it's the first of German's four
**[[cases]]**, the forms that show a noun's job in the sentence. You'll meet the next case in
lesson 9.

### Two questions, two decisions

English speakers often get stuck on *sein* versus *ihr*. Use two steps:

1. Who owns it? That chooses the word: a man or boy → *sein*; a woman or girl → *ihr*;
   several people → *ihr*.
2. What is owned? Its gender and number choose the ending: masculine or neuter → no ending;
   feminine or plural → *-e*.

- *Paul und seine Mutter* — Paul and his mother (Paul owns → *sein*; *Mutter* is feminine → *-e*)
- *Anna und ihr Vater* — Anna and her father (Anna owns → *ihr*; *Vater* is masculine → no ending)
- *Anna und ihre Mutter* — Anna and her mother
- *Die Kinder und ihr Hund* — The children and their dog

Step 1 is the same as in English. Step 2 is the new part: the ending agrees with the thing
owned, not the owner.

## Wer ist das?

To ask about a person, use *wer* (who); for a thing, *was* (what):

- *Wer ist das?* — *Das ist mein Bruder Jonas.* — Who's that? — That's my brother Jonas.
- *Wer sind die Leute auf dem Foto?* — *Das sind meine Eltern.* — Who are the people in the
  photo? — Those are my parents. (*die Leute* = people; *auf dem Foto* = in the photo.)
- *Ist das deine Freundin?* — *Nein, das ist meine Schwester.* — Is that your girlfriend? —
  No, that's my sister.

As in the last lesson, *das* in *Das ist / Das sind* never changes.

## haben in full

You know *ich habe, du hast, Sie haben*. Here is the whole verb. Watch the *er/sie/es* form:
it's *hat*, not ~~habt~~.

| | haben |
|---|---|
| ich | habe |
| du | hast |
| er / sie / es | hat |
| wir | haben |
| ihr | habt |
| sie / Sie | haben |

- *Wir haben zwei Kinder, einen Sohn und eine Tochter.* — We have two children, a son and a
  daughter.
- *Hat sie Geschwister?* — Does she have siblings?
- *Habt ihr ein Tier?* — Do you (all) have a pet?
- *Mein Vater hat eine Katze.* — My father has a cat.

One small preview: after *haben*, a masculine noun takes *einen* instead of *ein*: *Ich habe
einen Bruder* (I have a brother), *Er hat einen Hund*. The same happens to the possessives:
*Ich habe meinen Schlüssel*. Feminine, neuter and plural don't change. Lesson 9 explains why;
for now, treat *einen* as the "after *haben*" form of *ein* for masculine nouns.

## Married, single, divorced

To give your marital status, use *sein* + the word, with no ending:

- *Ich bin verheiratet.* — I'm married.
- *Mein Bruder ist ledig.* — My brother is single.
- *Meine Eltern sind geschieden.* — My parents are divorced.

## Dialogue: photos on the phone

Sara shows her colleague Mehmet some photos.

> Mehmet: *Wer ist das? Ist das deine Familie?*
>
> Sara: *Ja. Das ist mein Vater und das ist meine Mutter.*
>
> Mehmet: *Und das Baby?*
>
> Sara: *Das ist Lukas, der Sohn von meiner Schwester. Meine Schwester ist verheiratet. Ihr Mann heißt Jan.*
>
> Mehmet: *Hast du auch einen Bruder?*
>
> Sara: *Nein, ich habe nur eine Schwester. Und du? Hast du Geschwister?*
>
> Mehmet: *Ja, zwei Brüder. Wir haben auch einen Hund. Sein Name ist Kebab!*
>
> Sara: *Kebab? Euer Hund heißt Kebab? Toll!*

Translation:

> Mehmet: Who's that? Is that your family?
>
> Sara: Yes. That's my father and that's my mother.
>
> Mehmet: And the baby?
>
> Sara: That's Lukas, my sister's son. My sister is married. Her husband is called Jan.
>
> Mehmet: Do you have a brother too?
>
> Sara: No, I only have one sister. And you? Do you have siblings?
>
> Mehmet: Yes, two brothers. We have a dog too. His name is Kebab!
>
> Sara: Kebab? Your dog is called Kebab? Great!

(*nur* = only; *toll* = great. *der Sohn von meiner Schwester* is a common spoken way to say
"my sister's son"; *meiner* is a form you'll learn with the dative in lesson 18.)

Notice *Sein Name*: the dog is *der Hund*, so "his" is *sein*. German refers to animals and
things by their grammatical gender: a masculine noun is "he" (*er*) and takes *sein*.

## Pronunciation

- *Vater* begins with an *f* sound: FAH-ter. The *v* in German words is usually an *f*.
- *Tochter* and its plural *Töchter*: the *ch* after *o* is the throaty *ach*-sound;
  after *ö* it's the soft *ich*-sound.
- *Eltern*, *Geschwister*, *verheiratet*, *geschieden*: stress *EL-tern*, *ge-SCHWIS-ter*,
  *ver-HEI-ra-tet*, *ge-SCHIE-den*. *ei* sounds like "eye", *ie* like "ee".
- *Familie* has three syllables, stressed on *MI*: "fa-MEE-lyeh". The final *-ie* is a
  quick "yeh", not "ee".
- *Baby* is said much as in English, "BAY-bee", but with a pure, steady German *e*.

## Common mistakes

- Using the owner's gender for the ending. ~~Anna und ihre Vater~~ → *Anna und ihr Vater*:
  *Vater* is masculine, so no ending.
- Translating "her" as *sie*. *sie* is "she / they"; the possessive "her" is *ihr*: *ihr Bruder*.
- Saying ~~euere~~. The form is *eure*.
- Writing *Ihr* (formal your) in lower case, or the plural pronoun *ihr* with a capital.
  *Wie ist Ihr Name?* (formal) vs *Wo wohnt ihr?* (you all).
- Saying ~~er habt~~. It's *er hat*; *habt* belongs to *ihr*.
- Counting *Eltern* as one person. *Meine Eltern sind …* — always plural, with *sind*.
- Calling a friend *mein Freund* when you don't mean a partner: *mein Freund* and *meine
  Freundin* usually suggest a boyfriend or girlfriend. For a plain friend Germans often say
  *ein Freund von mir* (a friend of mine).

## Key points

- Possessive articles: *mein, dein, sein, ihr, sein, unser, euer, ihr, Ihr*.
- They take the same endings as *ein*: none for masculine and neuter, *-e* for feminine, and
  *-e* in the plural (*meine Eltern*).
- The owner chooses the word (*sein* or *ihr*); the thing owned chooses the ending.
- *haben*: *habe, hast, hat, haben, habt, haben*. After *haben*, masculine *ein* becomes
  *einen* (explained in lesson 9).
- *Wer ist das? — Das ist meine Mutter. Wer sind die Leute? — Das sind meine Eltern.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Jobs, languages and countries
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

After your name, where you're from and your family, the next thing people ask is what you do
and which languages you speak. This lesson gives you the words for common jobs, workplaces,
languages and countries, and three grammar points:

- how to say your job — with no article: *Ich bin Lehrerin*;
- how German makes a woman's job title from a man's with *-in*;
- the full forms of *sprechen*, your first **[[stem-changing verb]]**.

## Asking about jobs

The standard question, formal and informal:

- *Was sind Sie von Beruf?* — What do you do (for a living)? Literally "What are you by
  profession?"
- *Was bist du von Beruf?* — the same, informal.
- *Was machst du beruflich?* — a relaxed alternative (*beruflich* = for work).

And the answer:

- *Ich bin Lehrer.* — I'm a teacher. (a man)
- *Ich bin Ärztin.* — I'm a doctor. (a woman)
- *Mein Bruder ist Koch.* — My brother is a cook.
- *Sie ist Studentin.* — She's a student.

Notice what's missing: there's no *ein* or *eine*. English says "I'm *a* teacher"; German
says *Ich bin Lehrer*. With jobs (and *Student*, *Schüler*) after *sein*,
German leaves the article out. ~~Ich bin ein Lehrer~~ isn't wrong grammar, but it
sounds odd — like stressing "I'm a teacher (and not something else)".

Other useful patterns:

- *Ich arbeite als Kellner.* — I work as a waiter. (*als* = as)
- *Ich studiere Englisch.* — I'm studying English (at university).
- *Meine Firma ist in Hamburg.* — My company is in Hamburg.

If you don't work, you can say *Ich arbeite nicht* (I don't work) or *Ich bin Schüler* (I'm a
school pupil). Note the difference: a *Student* or *Studentin* is at university; a *Schüler*
or *Schülerin* is at school.

## Jobs for men and women: the -in ending

Most job nouns have a masculine form and a feminine form. The feminine is made by adding
*-in*, and some words also take an umlaut:

| Masculine (der) | Feminine (die) | English |
|---|---|---|
| der Lehrer | die Lehrerin | teacher |
| der Student | die Studentin | (university) student |
| der Schüler | die Schülerin | pupil, school student |
| der Verkäufer | die Verkäuferin | salesperson, shop assistant |
| der Kellner | die Kellnerin | waiter / waitress |
| der Ingenieur | die Ingenieurin | engineer |
| der Polizist | die Polizistin | police officer |
| der Arzt | die Ärztin | doctor |
| der Koch | die Köchin | cook, chef |

The feminine forms are always *die* and always form the plural with *-nen*: *die Lehrerin →
die Lehrerinnen*. The masculine plurals follow the patterns from lesson 5: *die Lehrer, die
Studenten, die Ärzte, die Köche, die Polizisten, die Ingenieure*.

When you talk about yourself, choose the form that fits you: a woman says *Ich bin Ingenieurin*,
a man *Ich bin Ingenieur*. Your vocabulary cards ask for the masculine form unless the prompt
says "female".

## Places of work

- *das Büro* — office: *Ich arbeite im Büro.* — I work in an office. (*im* = in the; a short
  form explained in lesson 19.)
- *die Firma* (plural *die Firmen*) — company, firm.
- *die Schule* — school; *die Universität* — university, often shortened to *die Uni*.
- *die Arbeit* — work, the job: *Die Arbeit ist interessant.* — The work is interesting.
- *der Beruf* — profession, occupation.

## Countries and languages

Most country names are neuter and are used without an article: *Ich komme aus Spanien. Ich
wohne in Frankreich.*

A few countries always take an article. You'll meet them in fixed phrases:

| Country | "I come from …" | "I live in …" |
|---|---|---|
| die Schweiz | Ich komme aus der Schweiz. | Ich wohne in der Schweiz. |
| die Türkei | Ich komme aus der Türkei. | Ich wohne in der Türkei. |
| die USA (plural) | Ich komme aus den USA. | Ich wohne in den USA. |

(After *aus* and *in*, *die* turns into *der* or *den*. That's the dative case, taught in lesson
18 — for now learn these as set phrases.)

Many language names end in *-isch* and are written with a capital letter when they name the
language. They're used without an article:

| Country | Language |
|---|---|
| Deutschland, Österreich, die Schweiz | Deutsch |
| England, die USA | Englisch |
| Spanien | Spanisch |
| Frankreich | Französisch |
| Italien | Italienisch |
| Polen | Polnisch |
| die Türkei | Türkisch |

The Swiss also speak French, Italian and Romansh, and Austria is German-speaking, so
*Deutsch* covers three countries. Something that crosses borders is *international*:
*Meine Firma ist international.*

## sprechen: a verb that changes its vowel

*sprechen* (to speak) has regular endings, but in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms the vowel of
the stem changes from *e* to *i*:

| | sprechen |
|---|---|
| ich | spreche |
| du | sprichst (changed) |
| er / sie / es | spricht (changed) |
| wir | sprechen |
| ihr | sprecht |
| sie / Sie | sprechen |

The stem is the part of the verb before the ending: *sprech-*. In a stem-changing verb, only
*du* and *er/sie/es* change; *ich*, *wir*, *ihr* and *sie/Sie* stay regular. You'll meet more
verbs like this in lesson 13 (*essen → isst*, *lesen → liest*, *fahren → fährt*), always in
the same two places.

- *Welche Sprachen sprichst du?* — Which languages do you speak? (*welche* = which)
- *Ich spreche Englisch und ein bisschen Deutsch.* — I speak English and a bit of German.
- *Mein Vater spricht Polnisch.* — My father speaks Polish.
- *Sprechen Sie Französisch?* — Do you speak French?
- *Wir sprechen hier Deutsch.* — We speak German here.

## Dialogue: at a language café

Two people meet at a conversation evening in Munich.

> Mia: *Hallo, ich bin Mia. Woher kommst du?*
>
> Daniel: *Ich komme aus den USA, aus Chicago. Und du?*
>
> Mia: *Ich komme aus Polen, aber ich wohne jetzt hier in München. Was bist du von Beruf?*
>
> Daniel: *Ich bin Ingenieur. Meine Firma ist international. Und du?*
>
> Mia: *Ich bin Lehrerin. Ich arbeite an einer Schule. Welche Sprachen sprichst du?*
>
> Daniel: *Englisch, Spanisch und ein bisschen Deutsch. Du sprichst sehr gut Deutsch!*
>
> Mia: *Danke! Ich spreche Polnisch, Deutsch und Englisch. Mein Mann spricht auch Italienisch.*
>
> Daniel: *Toll! Ist er auch Lehrer?*
>
> Mia: *Nein, er ist Koch.*

Translation:

> Mia: Hi, I'm Mia. Where are you from?
>
> Daniel: I'm from the USA, from Chicago. And you?
>
> Mia: I'm from Poland, but I live here in Munich now. What do you do for a living?
>
> Daniel: I'm an engineer. My company is international. And you?
>
> Mia: I'm a teacher. I work at a school. Which languages do you speak?
>
> Daniel: English, Spanish and a bit of German. You speak German very well!
>
> Mia: Thanks! I speak Polish, German and English. My husband speaks Italian too.
>
> Daniel: Great! Is he a teacher too?
>
> Mia: No, he's a cook.

(*aber* = but; *ein bisschen* = a bit; *an einer Schule* = at a school, another dative set
phrase.)

## Pronunciation

- *Ingenieur* is a French loanword: in-zhe-NYÖR, with *g* like the *s* in "measure".
- *Arzt* ends in *-tst*: ARTST. *Ärztin*: AIRTS-tin.
- *Polizist*, *Universität*, *Büro*, *international* are stressed on the last syllable:
  po-li-TSIST, u-ni-ver-si-TÄT, bü-RO, in-ter-na-tsio-NAL. *z* and *-ti-* sound like *ts*.
- *Koch*: the throaty *ach*-sound. *Köchin* and *sprichst*: the soft *ich*-sound.
- *Spanien*, *sprechen*, *Sprache*, *Student*: *sp* and *st* at the start of a word sound like
  *shp* and *sht*: SHPAH-nyen, shtu-DENT (*Student* is stressed on the second syllable).
- *Türkei* is stressed at the end: tür-KAI.

## Common mistakes

- Adding an article to a job: ~~Ich bin eine Ärztin~~ → *Ich bin Ärztin*.
- Forgetting the feminine *-in*. A woman says *Ich bin Studentin*, not ~~Ich bin Student~~.
- Using the English names: ~~Ich spreche German~~ → *Ich spreche Deutsch*; ~~Ich komme aus
  Germany~~ → *aus Deutschland*.
- Writing languages in lower case: *Ich spreche Englisch* (capital *E*).
- Keeping the *e* in the *du/er* forms: ~~er sprecht~~ → *er spricht*; ~~du sprechst~~ → *du
  sprichst*. And don't change *ich*: ~~ich spriche~~ → *ich spreche*.
- Leaving out the article with *die Schweiz*, *die Türkei* and *die USA*: *aus der Türkei*, not
  ~~aus Türkei~~.

## Key points

- *Was sind Sie von Beruf?* — *Ich bin Lehrer / Lehrerin.* No article before a job.
- Feminine job titles add *-in* (sometimes with an umlaut): *der Arzt → die Ärztin*. Plural
  *-innen*.
- Most countries need no article; *die Schweiz, die Türkei, die USA* do.
- Languages: *Deutsch, Englisch, Spanisch, Französisch …*, capitalized, no article.
- *sprechen*: *spreche, sprichst, spricht, sprechen, sprecht, sprechen* — the stem vowel
  changes only for *du* and *er/sie/es*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Describing things: adjectives and negation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now name things (*die Tasche*), say whose they are (*meine Tasche*) and say what
people do. This lesson lets you describe them — big or small, new or old, cheap or too
expensive, red or blue — and say what something is *not*. You'll learn:

- **[[adjectives]]** after *sein*: *Die Tasche ist neu.*
- words that make adjectives stronger or weaker: *sehr, ziemlich, zu*;
- colours;
- the two ways German says "not": *nicht* and *kein*;
- *doch*, the little word that says "yes" to a negative question.

## Adjectives after sein: no endings

An adjective describes a noun. When it comes after *sein* (to be), it never changes. It's the
same for every gender and in the plural:

- *Der Tisch ist neu.* — The table is new.
- *Die Lampe ist neu.* — The lamp is new.
- *Das Handy ist neu.* — The phone is new.
- *Die Stühle sind neu.* — The chairs are new.

That's all you need for A1. (When an adjective stands *before* a noun — "a new table" — it
does take endings. That comes at A2; for now, put your adjectives after *ist* and *sind*.)

You can also refer back to a noun with a pronoun. Germans use *er*, *sie* or *es* by the
noun's gender, even for things:

- *Wie ist der Film?* — *Er ist interessant.* — How's the film? — It's interesting.
- *Und die Zeitung?* — *Sie ist langweilig.* — And the newspaper? — It's boring.
- *Das Buch? Es ist toll.* — The book? It's great.

*Wie ist …?* (What's … like? / How is …?) is the question for a description.

## Opposites

Adjectives are easiest to learn in pairs:

| Adjective | Opposite |
|---|---|
| groß (big, tall) | klein (small, short) |
| neu (new) | alt (old) |
| gut (good) | schlecht (bad) |
| lang (long) | kurz (short) |
| teuer (expensive) | billig (cheap) |
| richtig (right, correct) | falsch (wrong) |
| leicht (easy; light) | schwer (difficult; heavy) |
| schnell (fast, quick) | langsam (slow) |
| interessant (interesting) | langweilig (boring) |
| schön (beautiful, nice) | — |
| toll (great) | — |
| kaputt (broken) | — |

Some adjectives have two meanings. *leicht* is "easy" and "light (not heavy)"; *schwer* is
"difficult" and "heavy". *groß* is "big" for things and "tall" for people: *Mein Bruder ist
sehr groß.* *schön* is "beautiful" for a place or person and "nice" in general: *Das ist
schön!* — That's nice!

*kaputt* is the everyday word for "broken": *Mein Handy ist kaputt.* In casual speech *Ich bin
kaputt* means "I'm exhausted".

## sehr, ziemlich, zu

Put these directly before the adjective:

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| sehr | very | *Die Uhr ist sehr schön.* — The watch is very beautiful. |
| ziemlich | quite, fairly, rather | *Der Test ist ziemlich leicht.* — The test is fairly easy. |
| zu | too (more than you want) | *Die Tasche ist zu teuer.* — The bag is too expensive. |
| nicht so | not so, not very | *Der Film ist nicht so gut.* — The film isn't that good. |

*zu* is always negative: something is too much for you. *Das Auto ist zu teuer* means you
won't buy it. Don't use *zu* to mean "very".

## Colours

*die Farbe* (plural *die Farben*) means "the colour". Colours work like any other adjective
after *sein*:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| rot — red | blau — blue | grün — green |
| gelb — yellow | schwarz — black | weiß — white |
| grau — grey | braun — brown | |

- *Welche Farbe hat dein Handy?* — *Es ist schwarz.* — What colour is your phone? — It's black.
  (Literally "Which colour has your phone?")
- *Die Tür ist rot und das Fenster ist weiß.* — The door is red and the window is white.
- *Meine Katze ist grau.* — My cat is grey.

## Two ways to say "not": nicht and kein

English uses "not" for almost everything. German has two words, and the choice depends on
what you're negating. This is called **[[negation]]**.

### kein: "not a", "no"

Use *kein* to negate a noun that would have *ein/eine* or no article at all. It's the
**[[negative article]]**, and it takes the same endings as *ein* — plus a plural form, like
*mein*:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| positive | ein Stift | eine Uhr | ein Buch | Bücher |
| negative | kein Stift | keine Uhr | kein Buch | keine Bücher |

- *Das ist kein Heft, das ist ein Buch.* — That's not a notebook, that's a book.
- *Das ist keine Katze!* — That's not a cat!
- *Das sind keine Fotos.* — Those aren't photos.
- *Ich habe keine Zeit.* — I don't have (any) time. (*die Zeit* = time)
- *Wir haben keine Kinder.* — We don't have any children.

Think of *kein* as "not + ein" glued together: never say ~~nicht ein~~.

As with *ein*, a masculine noun after *haben* gets *-en*: *Ich habe keinen Hund* (I don't have
a dog). Lesson 9 explains this.

### nicht: everything else

Use *nicht* to negate a verb, an adjective, or a noun with *der/die/das* or a possessive:

- *Ich arbeite heute nicht.* — I'm not working today.
- *Das Buch ist nicht interessant.* — The book isn't interesting.
- *Das ist nicht mein Schlüssel.* — That isn't my key.
- *Das ist nicht die Tür, das ist das Fenster!* — That's not the door, that's the window!

### Where does nicht go?

Two basic rules for now:

1. To negate the whole sentence, *nicht* usually goes at the end: *Ich verstehe das nicht.* —
   I don't understand that. *Er kommt heute nicht.* — He's not coming today.
2. To negate an adjective or one part, *nicht* goes right before it: *Der Kaffee ist nicht
   teuer. Das ist nicht mein Handy.*

German never uses a helper like English "do" in negation: ~~Ich nicht verstehe~~, ~~Ich
tue nicht verstehen~~ → *Ich verstehe nicht.*

## Doch: yes, to a negative

English answers a negative question with "yes" or "no" and hopes the listener understands.
German has a special word. If someone asks or says something *negative* and you want to
contradict it, answer *doch* instead of *ja*:

- *Ist das nicht dein Handy?* — *Doch, das ist mein Handy.* — Isn't that your phone? — Yes, it
  is.
- *Du hast keine Brille, oder?* — *Doch!* — You don't have glasses, do you? — Yes, I do! (*oder*
  at the end = right?)
- *Das ist nicht richtig.* — *Doch, das ist richtig!* — That's not right. — Yes, it is!

To agree with a negative, use *nein*: *Ist das nicht dein Handy?* — *Nein, das ist nicht mein
Handy.* *Doch* is a small word called a **[[particle]]**; you'll hear it constantly.

## Dialogue: buying a second-hand bike

Jonas looks at a second-hand bike that Frau Weber is selling.

> Jonas: *Guten Tag! Ist das das Fahrrad?*
>
> Frau Weber: *Ja. Es ist ziemlich neu und sehr schnell.*
>
> Jonas: *Es ist schön. Ist es nicht zu klein für mich?*
>
> Frau Weber: *Nein, es ist groß. Sie sind ja auch groß!*
>
> Jonas: *Und das Licht hier? Ist das kaputt?*
>
> Frau Weber: *Nein, nein, das ist nicht kaputt. Es ist nur alt.*
>
> Jonas: *Hm. Die Farbe ist toll — grün und schwarz. Aber 300 Euro? Das ist zu teuer.*
>
> Frau Weber: *Zu teuer? Nein, das ist billig!*
>
> Jonas: *Ich habe leider nicht so viel Geld. 250?*
>
> Frau Weber: *Na gut, 250.*

Translation:

> Jonas: Good afternoon! Is that the bike?
>
> Frau Weber: Yes. It's quite new and very fast.
>
> Jonas: It's nice. Isn't it too small for me?
>
> Frau Weber: No, it's big. You're tall too, after all!
>
> Jonas: And the light here? Is that broken?
>
> Frau Weber: No, no, that's not broken. It's just old.
>
> Jonas: Hmm. The colour is great — green and black. But 300 euros? That's too expensive.
>
> Frau Weber: Too expensive? No, that's cheap!
>
> Jonas: Unfortunately I don't have that much money. 250?
>
> Frau Weber: Oh, all right, 250.

(*das Fahrrad* = bicycle; *das Licht* = light; *für mich* = for me; *nur* = only, just;
*leider* = unfortunately; *viel Geld* = much money; *na gut* = oh, all right. The *ja* in
*Sie sind ja auch groß* means "after all, as we can see".)

## Pronunciation

- *teuer*: *eu* sounds like English "oy": TOY-er.
- *weiß*: like English "vice" — *w* is a *v* sound, *ß* a sharp *s*.
- *grün*: long *ü*; *schwarz* ends in *-rts*.
- *billig*, *richtig*, *langweilig*, *ziemlich*: final *-ig* is pronounced like *-ich* (soft
  *ich*-sound) in standard German: BIL-lich, RICH-tich.
- *interessant* is stressed at the end: in-te-res-SANT. *kaputt* too: ka-PUTT.
- *doch* has the throaty *ach*-sound and is said short and firmly.

## Common mistakes

- Adding endings after *sein*: ~~Das Auto ist roter~~ → *Das Auto ist rot.*
- Saying ~~nicht ein~~: ~~Das ist nicht ein Hund~~ → *Das ist kein Hund.*
- Doubling the negative: ~~Ich habe nicht keine Zeit~~ → *Ich habe keine Zeit.*
- Answering *ja* to contradict a negative question: *Hast du keinen Hund?* — *Doch!* (not
  *Ja!*)
- Using *zu* for "very": ~~Das Essen ist zu gut~~ sounds like a complaint. Say *sehr gut*.
- Saying ~~Ich bin langweilig~~ for "I'm bored". It means "I'm boring"! Say *Mir ist
  langweilig* — a fixed phrase meaning "I'm bored".
- *billig* can sound like "cheap and nasty". For a good price Germans often say *günstig*
  (good value).

## Key points

- After *sein*, adjectives never change: *Der Tisch / Die Lampe / Die Stühle … ist/sind neu.*
- *sehr* = very, *ziemlich* = quite, *zu* = too (negative), *nicht so* = not very.
- Colours: *rot, blau, grün, gelb, schwarz, weiß, grau, braun*.
- *kein/keine* negates nouns with *ein* or no article; *nicht* negates everything else.
- *nicht* goes at the end to negate a whole sentence, and before an adjective or a specific part.
- *Doch!* says "yes" to contradict a negative question or statement.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Food, drink and the accusative
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far your sentences have mostly described people and things: *Das ist ein Tisch.* *Meine Schwester ist Lehrerin.* *Der Computer ist kaputt.* In this lesson people start doing things to things: eating bread, drinking coffee, ordering a cake. To talk like that, German needs a new form of the article, the **[[accusative]]**. The good news is that the change is small: only masculine words change.

You will also learn the verbs you need at the table (*essen*, *trinken*, *nehmen*, *möchten*), how *essen* and *nehmen* change their vowel, and how to order politely in a café. By the end you can say what you like to eat and order breakfast in German.

## Food and drink

Learn every food word with its article, as always. Many drinks are masculine, which matters in a moment.

| der (masculine) | die (feminine) | das (neuter) |
|---|---|---|
| der Kaffee — coffee | die Milch — milk | das Wasser — water |
| der Tee — tea | die Butter — butter | das Bier — beer |
| der Saft — juice | die Wurst — sausage | das Brot — bread |
| der Wein — wine | die Kartoffel — potato | das Brötchen — bread roll |
| der Käse — cheese | die Nudeln — pasta (plural) | das Ei — egg |
| der Fisch — fish | | das Fleisch — meat |
| der Apfel — apple | | das Gemüse — vegetables |
| der Reis — rice | | das Obst — fruit |
| der Salat — salad | | das Essen — food, meal |
| der Kuchen — cake | | |

The three meals are all neuter: *das Frühstück* (breakfast), *das Mittagessen* (lunch) and *das Abendessen* (dinner). *Mittag* means midday and *Abend* means evening, so the words explain themselves.

Two words name whole groups, and German treats them as one uncountable thing, like English *fruit*: *das Obst* (fruit) and *das Gemüse* (vegetables). So *Gemüse ist gesund* — "vegetables are healthy" — uses a singular verb. (*gesund* means healthy.)

German also builds long food words by sticking nouns together. The last part decides the gender: *der Apfel + der Saft = der Apfelsaft* (apple juice), *der Käse + das Brot = das Käsebrot* (cheese sandwich), *der Apfel + der Kuchen = der Apfelkuchen* (apple cake).

## Subject and object: what the accusative is

In "The woman drinks the coffee", the woman does the drinking: she is the subject. The coffee is what gets drunk: it is the **[[direct object]]**, the thing the action is done to. English shows this by word order alone. German also marks it on the article, and the form it uses for a direct object is the accusative.

In lesson 6 you met the nominative, the case of the subject (and of anything after *sein*). The accusative is the second of German's four cases; from lesson 18 you'll add a third, the dative.

### Only the masculine changes

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
