| nominative (subject) | der / ein / kein | die / eine / keine | das / ein / kein | die / – / keine |
| accusative (object) | den / einen / keinen | die / eine / keine | das / ein / kein | die / – / keine |

Feminine, neuter and plural forms are exactly the same in both cases. Only the masculine gets an -n: *der* becomes *den*, *ein* becomes *einen*, *kein* becomes *keinen*. A memory hook: the masculine is the only one that changes, and it always picks up an *n*: *den, einen, keinen*.

- *Der Kaffee ist heiß.* — The coffee is hot. (subject: nominative)
- *Ich trinke den Kaffee.* — I'm drinking the coffee. (object: accusative)
- *Ein Apfel kostet nicht viel.* — An apple doesn't cost much. (subject)
- *Er isst einen Apfel.* — He's eating an apple. (object)
- *Ich habe keinen Saft.* — I don't have any juice. (object, negative)
- *Sie trinkt eine Cola.* — She's drinking a cola. (feminine: no change)
- *Wir essen das Brot.* — We're eating the bread. (neuter: no change)
- *Ich kaufe die Eier.* — I'm buying the eggs. (plural: no change; *kaufen* = to buy)

Possessives follow *ein*: *mein* becomes *meinen* for a masculine object. *Ich trinke meinen Tee.* — I'm drinking my tea.

### Which verbs take the accusative?

Most verbs that act on something take a direct object in the accusative: *essen*, *trinken*, *nehmen*, *möchten*, *haben*, *machen*, *hören*, *lernen*, *fragen* and many more. One verb never does: *sein*. After *sein* you keep the nominative, because nothing is being done to anything: *Das ist ein Kuchen* but *Ich esse einen Kuchen*.

## The verbs: essen, trinken, nehmen

*trinken* (to drink) is regular. *essen* (to eat) and *nehmen* (to take; when ordering, to have) change their vowel in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms: e becomes i.

| | trinken | essen | nehmen |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | trinke | esse | nehme |
| du | trinkst | isst | nimmst |
| er / sie / es | trinkt | isst | nimmt |
| wir | trinken | essen | nehmen |
| ihr | trinkt | esst | nehmt |
| sie / Sie | trinken | essen | nehmen |

Notice three details. *du isst* has no extra *s* ending, because the stem already ends in *ss*. *er isst* sounds exactly like *er ist* (he is); only the spelling is different. *nehmen* loses its *h* and doubles the *m*: *du nimmst, er nimmt*.

- *Was isst du gern?* — What do you like to eat?
- *Paul nimmt einen Tee.* — Paul is having a tea.
- *Ihr esst viel Obst.* — You (all) eat a lot of fruit.

## möchten: the polite "would like"

*möchten* means "would like". It is the most useful word in any café or shop, and much more polite than "I want".

| | möchten |
|---|---|
| ich | möchte |
| du | möchtest |
| er / sie / es | möchte |
| wir | möchten |
| ihr | möchtet |
| sie / Sie | möchten |

Watch out: *ich möchte* and *er möchte* are identical — there is no *-t* on the *er* form. The object after *möchten* is accusative, like after any other verb:

- *Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.* — I'd like a coffee, please.
- *Möchten Sie ein Wasser?* — Would you like a water?
- *Sie möchte keinen Fisch.* — She doesn't want any fish.

You can also put a verb at the end: *Ich möchte Kuchen essen* (I'd like to eat cake). Lesson 14 explains this pattern; for now, use *möchten* with a noun.

## Saying what you like: gern

To say you like doing something, add *gern* after the verb. *Ich trinke Tee* is "I drink tea"; *Ich trinke gern Tee* is "I like drinking tea". For dislikes, use *nicht gern*.

- *Ich esse gern Nudeln.* — I like eating pasta.
- *Mein Bruder isst nicht gern Gemüse.* — My brother doesn't like eating vegetables.
- *Trinkst du gern Wein?* — Do you like wine?

When you talk about food in general, you usually leave out the article: *Ich esse gern Fisch* (fish in general), but *Ich esse den Fisch* (that particular fish).

## Hunger and thirst

German says "I have hunger": *Ich habe Hunger* (I'm hungry) and *Ich habe Durst* (I'm thirsty). There is no article. Ask *Hast du Hunger?* — Are you hungry? If food tastes good, it is *lecker*: *Der Kuchen ist lecker!*

## Ordering in a café

| Situation | German | English |
|---|---|---|
| The waiter asks | *Was möchten Sie?* / *Was nehmen Sie?* | What would you like? |
| You order | *Ich nehme einen Tee.* / *Ich möchte ein Brötchen, bitte.* | I'll have a tea. / I'd like a roll, please. |
| Asking about something | *Haben Sie Apfelkuchen?* | Do you have apple cake? |
| With / without | *mit Milch* / *ohne Milch* | with milk / without milk |

*mit* (with) and *ohne* (without) are useful here as set phrases; *Kaffee mit Milch*, *Tee ohne Zucker* (*der Zucker* = sugar).

## Dialogue: In the café

*Kellnerin* is a female waiter.

> Kellnerin: Guten Morgen! Was möchten Sie?
>
> Herr Weber: Ich nehme einen Kaffee mit Milch, bitte.
>
> Kellnerin: Und Sie?
>
> Frau Weber: Ich habe Durst. Ich möchte einen Orangensaft und ein Wasser.
>
> Kellnerin: Möchten Sie auch etwas essen? Das Frühstück ist heute sehr gut.
>
> Frau Weber: Ja, gern. Ein Brötchen mit Butter und Käse, bitte. Haben Sie auch Eier?
>
> Kellnerin: Ja, natürlich. Und Sie, Herr Weber? Nehmen Sie auch ein Brötchen?
>
> Herr Weber: Nein, ich habe keinen Hunger. Aber der Apfelkuchen dort sieht toll aus …
>
> Frau Weber: Paul! Du isst jeden Morgen Kuchen!
>
> Herr Weber: Ja, Kuchen ist lecker. Einen Apfelkuchen, bitte.

In English:

> Waitress: Good morning! What would you like?
>
> Mr Weber: I'll have a coffee with milk, please.
>
> Waitress: And you?
>
> Mrs Weber: I'm thirsty. I'd like an orange juice and a water.
>
> Waitress: Would you like something to eat too? The breakfast is very good today.
>
> Mrs Weber: Yes, please. A roll with butter and cheese, please. Do you have eggs too?
>
> Waitress: Yes, of course. And you, Mr Weber? Are you having a roll too?
>
> Mr Weber: No, I'm not hungry. But the apple cake there looks great …
>
> Mrs Weber: Paul! You eat cake every morning!
>
> Mr Weber: Yes, cake is delicious. An apple cake, please.

Look at the objects: *einen Kaffee*, *einen Orangensaft* and *einen Apfelkuchen* are masculine, so they take *einen*; *ein Wasser* and *ein Brötchen* are neuter and stay *ein*. *Ich habe keinen Hunger* uses *keinen* because *Hunger* is masculine. (*etwas* = something, *natürlich* = of course, *jeden Morgen* = every morning, *sieht … aus* = looks.) In a café, *einen Apfelkuchen, bitte* means a slice, not the whole cake; you can also say *ein Stück Apfelkuchen* (lesson 10).

## Pronunciation

- *Brötchen*: the *ö* is made by saying "ay" with rounded lips; *-chen* has the soft *ch* of *ich*.
- *Käse*: long *ä*, like the vowel in English "air" without the r: KÄ-se.
- *Ei* rhymes with English "eye"; *Eier* (eggs) is "EYE-er".
- *Gemüse* is stressed on the middle: ge-MÜ-se. *Kartoffel* too: kar-TOF-fel.
- *Frühstück*: stress on the first part, FRÜH-stück; the *h* is silent and makes the *ü* long.
- *isst* and *ist* sound the same; *nimmt* has a short *i*.

## Common mistakes

- *Ich möchte ein Kaffee.* — Wrong. *Kaffee* is masculine and the object, so: *Ich möchte einen Kaffee.*
- *Ich nehme einen Wasser.* — Wrong in the other direction. Only masculine words get *-en*; *Wasser* is neuter: *ein Wasser*.
- *Er esst Brot.* / *Du nehmst …* — Use the stem change: *er isst*, *du nimmst*.
- *Er möchtet …* — No *-t*: *er möchte*.
- *Ich bin Hunger.* / *Ich habe ein Hunger.* — Say *Ich habe Hunger*, with no article.
- *Ich gern esse Fisch.* — The verb comes second: *Ich esse gern Fisch.*
- *Das ist einen Apfel.* — After *sein*, no accusative: *Das ist ein Apfel.*

## Key points

- The accusative marks the direct object. Only masculine articles change: *den, einen, keinen* (and *meinen*, *deinen* …).
- Feminine, neuter and plural look the same as the nominative.
- *sein* is never followed by the accusative.
- *essen* and *nehmen* change e→i in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms: *isst, nimmt*.
- *möchte* has no *-t* in the *er/sie/es* form. Use it to order politely.
- *gern* after the verb says you like doing something; *Ich habe Hunger / Durst* has no article.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Shopping and prices
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 9 you learned to order food and drink with the accusative: *Ich nehme einen Kaffee.* Now you go shopping. You will learn the big numbers (from 100 up to a million), how Germans write and say prices, how to ask what something costs, how to ask for a kilo, a litre or a bottle of something, and how to point at things with *dieser* (this) and ask about them with *welcher* (which). You will also meet *es gibt* (there is, there are), one of the most useful phrases in the language.

## Numbers from 100 up

You already know 0 to 100 (lesson 3). Bigger numbers follow the same logic and are written as one word, however long.

| Number | German |
|---|---|
| 100 | hundert / einhundert |
| 101 | hunderteins |
| 110 | hundertzehn |
| 125 | hundertfünfundzwanzig |
| 200 | zweihundert |
| 350 | dreihundertfünfzig |
| 999 | neunhundertneunundneunzig |
| 1.000 | tausend / eintausend |
| 1.500 | tausendfünfhundert / eintausendfünfhundert |
| 2.480 | zweitausendvierhundertachtzig |
| 10.000 | zehntausend |
| 100.000 | hunderttausend |
| 1.000.000 | eine Million |
| 3.000.000 | drei Millionen |

The pattern is: hundreds, then the rest exactly as you learned it. So 347 is *dreihundert* + *siebenundvierzig* = *dreihundertsiebenundvierzig*. Inside the last two digits the order is still "units and tens": 47 = *sieben-und-vierzig*.

Only *Million* is a separate word, and it is a feminine noun with a plural: *eine Million, zwei Millionen*.

### Writing numbers

German swaps the English comma and point:

- A point (or a small space) separates thousands: *1.000* or *1 000* = one thousand.
- A comma marks decimals: *2,5* = two point five, read *zwei Komma fünf*.

So *1.250* is one thousand two hundred and fifty, not one and a quarter. This matters a lot when you read prices.

## Prices: Euro and Cent

Germany, Austria and most EU countries pay in *Euro* (*der Euro*) and *Cent* (*der Cent*). Prices are written with a comma, and the euro sign usually comes after the number: *3,50 €*.

| Written | Said |
|---|---|
| 1,00 € | ein Euro |
| 3,50 € | drei Euro fünfzig |
| 12,99 € | zwölf Euro neunundneunzig |
| 0,80 € | achtzig Cent |
| 249,00 € | zweihundertneunundvierzig Euro |

Two habits to copy. First, you don't say "and" or "Cent" in the middle: 3,50 € is just *drei Euro fünfzig*. Second, *Euro* doesn't take a plural ending after a number: *zehn Euro*, never *zehn Euros*. The same goes for *Cent*: *fünfzig Cent*.

### Asking what it costs

There are two equally common questions:

- *Was kostet das Brot?* / *Wie viel kostet das Brot?* — How much is the bread?
- *Was kosten die Äpfel?* / *Wie viel kosten die Äpfel?* — How much are the apples?

The verb agrees with the thing: one thing *kostet*, several things *kosten*. The answer: *Das Brot kostet 2,80 €.* *Die Äpfel kosten 3,20 € das Kilo* (3.20 a kilo). At the till you'll hear the total as *Das macht 8,40 €* — That's 8.40.

*wie viel* (how much, how many) is two words. You also use it for other quantities: *Wie viel Geld hast du?* — How much money do you have?

## Quantities: no "of"

To buy a kilo of apples, say *ein Kilo Äpfel*. German puts the amount straight in front of the food, with no word for "of".

| German | English |
|---|---|
| ein Kilo Äpfel | a kilo of apples |
| 200 Gramm Käse | 200 grams of cheese |
| ein Liter Milch | a litre of milk |
| eine Flasche Wein | a bottle of wine |
| eine Packung Nudeln | a packet of pasta |
| ein Stück Kuchen | a piece of cake |

Measures that are masculine or neuter (*das Kilo*, *das Gramm*, *der Liter*, *das Stück*) stay singular after a number: *zwei Kilo Kartoffeln, drei Liter Wasser, zwei Stück Kuchen*. Feminine containers take their plural: *zwei Flaschen Wasser, drei Packungen Reis*. An easy rule of thumb: if it ends in *-e* or *-ung* like *Flasche* or *Packung*, use the plural.

The amount and the food together are one object, so the article of the measure word changes as usual: *Ich kaufe einen Liter Milch* (der Liter → einen).

## dieser and welcher

*dieser* means "this" (or "that", when you point); a pointing word like this is called a **[[demonstrative]]**. *welcher* means "which". Both take the same endings as *der, die, das* — compare the last letters.

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| article | der / den | die | das | die |
| nominative | dieser / welcher | diese / welche | dieses / welches | diese / welche |
| accusative | diesen / welchen | diese / welche | dieses / welches | diese / welche |

Once again only the masculine changes in the accusative, and it gets the same *-n* as *den*: *der → den*, *dieser → diesen*, *welcher → welchen*.

- *Welcher Käse ist gut?* — Which cheese is good? *Dieser Käse ist sehr gut.* — This cheese is very good.
- *Welchen Wein möchten Sie?* — Which wine would you like? *Ich nehme diesen Wein.* — I'll take this wine.
- *Welche Flasche kostet 4 Euro?* — Which bottle costs 4 euros? *Diese.* — This one.
- *Welches Brot ist frisch?* — Which bread is fresh? (*frisch* = fresh) *Dieses Brot hier.* — This bread here.

You can drop the noun when it's clear: *Ich nehme diesen.* — I'll take this one (a masculine thing).

## es gibt: there is, there are

*es gibt* means "there is" or "there are". It never changes for plural, and the thing that exists is in the accusative.

- *Hier gibt es einen Supermarkt.* — There's a supermarket here.
- *Gibt es hier eine Bäckerei?* — Is there a bakery here?
- *Heute gibt es Fisch.* — There's fish today.
- *Es gibt keinen Reis mehr.* — There's no rice left. (*mehr* = more, any more)
- *Es gibt viele Geschäfte.* — There are many shops. (*viele* = many)

Use *es gibt* for what exists or is available somewhere. Use *Das ist …* to identify a thing in front of you.

## Shopping verbs

All of these take an accusative object.

| German | English | Example |
|---|---|---|
| kaufen | to buy | *Ich kaufe einen Apfel.* — I'm buying an apple. |
| brauchen | to need | *Wir brauchen Brot und Milch.* — We need bread and milk. |
| suchen | to look for | *Ich suche den Markt.* — I'm looking for the market. |
| bezahlen | to pay (for) | *Er bezahlt den Kaffee.* — He's paying for the coffee. |
| kosten | to cost | *Das kostet 5 Euro.* — That costs 5 euros. |

Note that *suchen* and *bezahlen* need no preposition: "look *for*" and "pay *for*" are just *suchen* and *bezahlen* plus the object.

Some useful little words: *viel* (a lot, much), *wenig* (little, not much), *alles* (everything), *zusammen* (together). *Das kostet viel.* — That costs a lot. *Ich habe wenig Geld.* — I have little money. *Ist das alles?* — Is that everything? In a café the waiter asks *Zusammen oder getrennt?* — Together or separately? (*getrennt* = separately.)

## Dialogue: At the market

> Verkäuferin: Guten Tag! Was brauchen Sie?
>
> Lena: Guten Tag! Was kosten die Äpfel?
>
> Verkäuferin: Welche? Diese hier kosten 2,40 € das Kilo, und diese dort 3,10 €.
>
> Lena: Dann nehme ich die hier. Ein Kilo, bitte. Und 200 Gramm Käse.
>
> Verkäuferin: Gern. Welchen Käse möchten Sie? Der Gouda ist heute im Angebot: 100 Gramm kosten nur 1,20 €.
>
> Lena: Super, dann 200 Gramm Gouda. Gibt es auch Eier?
>
> Verkäuferin: Ja, natürlich. Zehn Stück kosten 3,20 €.
>
> Lena: Gut, zehn Eier, bitte. Das ist alles. Was macht das zusammen?
>
> Verkäuferin: Das macht zusammen acht Euro.
>
> Lena: Hier sind zehn Euro.
>
> Verkäuferin: Und zwei Euro zurück. Vielen Dank und einen schönen Tag noch!

In English:

> Saleswoman: Hello! What do you need?
>
> Lena: Hello! How much are the apples?
>
> Saleswoman: Which ones? These here are 2.40 a kilo, and those there 3.10.
>
> Lena: Then I'll take these here. A kilo, please. And 200 grams of cheese.
>
> Saleswoman: Sure. Which cheese would you like? The Gouda is on special offer today: 100 grams cost only 1.20.
>
> Lena: Great, 200 grams of Gouda then. Are there eggs too?
>
> Saleswoman: Yes, of course. Ten cost 3.20.
>
> Lena: Good, ten eggs, please. That's everything. What does that come to altogether?
>
> Saleswoman: That's eight euros altogether.
>
> Lena: Here's ten euros.
>
> Saleswoman: And two euros back. Thank you and have a nice day!

Check the maths: 2,40 + 2,40 + 3,20 = 8,00 €. *Verkäuferin* is a female shop assistant (lesson 7 had *der Verkäufer*). *im Angebot* means "on special offer"; take it as a fixed phrase. *zurück* = back; *einen schönen Tag noch* = have a nice day.

## Places to shop

*das Geschäft* is the general word for a shop. *der Supermarkt* is a supermarket, *der Markt* an open-air market, *die Bäckerei* a bakery (from *der Bäcker*, the baker). In a supermarket you pay at *die Kasse*, the checkout, and you look for *das Angebot*, the special offer. *der Preis* is the price: *Der Preis ist gut.*

## Pronunciation

- *Euro* is "OY-ro": *eu* sounds like the *oy* in "boy".
- *Bäckerei* is stressed on the last syllable: bä-cke-REI. Most words ending in *-ei* do this.
- *Supermarkt*: stress on the first syllable, SU-per-markt, and say the *k* and the *t*.
- *Million* is mil-YOHN, stressed on the last syllable.
- *Gramm* and *Kilo*: short *a* in *Gramm*, long *i* in *Kilo*.

## Common mistakes

- *zehn Euros*, *zwei Kilos* — No plural after a number: *zehn Euro, zwei Kilo*.
- *ein Kilo von Äpfeln* — No *von* after a measure: *ein Kilo Äpfel*.
- *Wie viel kosten das?* — One thing, singular verb: *Wie viel kostet das?*
- Reading *1.500 €* as "one and a half euros". The point is the thousands separator: 1,500 euros.
- *Welche Käse möchten Sie?* — *Käse* is masculine and the object: *Welchen Käse …?*
- *Es gibt ein Supermarkt.* — *es gibt* takes the accusative: *einen Supermarkt*.
- *Ich suche für eine Bäckerei.* — No preposition: *Ich suche eine Bäckerei.*

## Key points

- Big numbers are one word: *dreihundertsiebenundvierzig*. Only *Million* is separate.
- A point separates thousands, a comma marks decimals and cents: *1.000*, *3,50 €*.
- Say prices as *drei Euro fünfzig*; no plural after numbers: *zehn Euro*.
- Amount + food with no "of": *ein Kilo Äpfel, eine Flasche Wasser*.
- *dieser* and *welcher* take the endings of *der/die/das*; masculine accusative is *diesen, welchen*.
- *es gibt* + accusative = there is / there are.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Days, times and the clock
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can count, order food and pay. Now you need to say when things happen: what time it is, when the shop opens, on which day you work, and how often you do something. This lesson teaches the clock (the official 24-hour way and the everyday way), the days of the week and the parts of the day, the little prepositions *um*, *am*, *von … bis* that go with them, and a few words for how often. The numbers you need are 0 to 59, which you know from lesson 3.

## What time is it?

There are two ways to ask, and both are everyday German:

- *Wie spät ist es?* — What time is it? (literally "How late is it?")
- *Wie viel Uhr ist es?* — What time is it? (literally "How much clock is it?")

The answer always starts with *Es ist …*: *Es ist acht Uhr.* — It's eight o'clock.

*die Uhr* is the clock or watch from lesson 5. In times it means "o'clock", and it never takes a plural: *Es ist zehn Uhr*, not *zehn Uhren*.

## The official time

Timetables, radio, shops, appointments and anything written use the 24-hour clock. You say the hour, then *Uhr*, then the minutes:

| Written | Said | English |
|---|---|---|
| 7:00 | sieben Uhr | 7 a.m. |
| 8:15 | acht Uhr fünfzehn | 8:15 a.m. |
| 12:30 | zwölf Uhr dreißig | 12:30 p.m. |
| 14:05 | vierzehn Uhr fünf | 2:05 p.m. |
| 19:45 | neunzehn Uhr fünfundvierzig | 7:45 p.m. |
| 0:20 | null Uhr zwanzig | 12:20 a.m. |

*Uhr* sits between the hours and the minutes, where English writes the colon. Germans often write *14.05 Uhr* with a point, or *14:05 Uhr*.

## The everyday time

When people talk, they normally use the 12-hour clock and count minutes *nach* (after, past) and *vor* (before, to) the hour.

| Time | Said |
|---|---|
| 3:00 | drei (Uhr) |
| 3:05 | fünf nach drei |
| 3:10 | zehn nach drei |
| 3:15 | Viertel nach drei |
| 3:20 | zwanzig nach drei |
| 3:30 | halb vier |
| 3:40 | zwanzig vor vier |
| 3:45 | Viertel vor vier |
| 3:50 | zehn vor vier |
| 3:55 | fünf vor vier |

*das Viertel* is a quarter. *Viertel nach drei* is a quarter past three and *Viertel vor vier* a quarter to four, just like English.

### The famous trap: halb

*halb vier* does not mean half past four. It means "half (of the way) to four", so 3:30. Think of the hour you are moving towards: at 3:30 you are halfway to four. *halb eins* is 12:30, *halb acht* is 7:30.

People also count from *halb*: *fünf vor halb vier* is 3:25 and *fünf nach halb vier* is 3:35. You don't have to say these yourself, but you will hear them.

In parts of southern and eastern Germany and in Austria you may also hear *viertel vier* for 3:15 and *drei viertel vier* (also written *dreiviertel vier*) for 3:45, counting quarters towards the next hour like *halb*. Everyone understands *Viertel nach* and *Viertel vor*, so use those.

### One o'clock

With *Uhr*, one is *ein*: *Es ist ein Uhr.* Without *Uhr*, it is *eins*: *Es ist eins.* Never say *eins Uhr*.

### Uhr or Stunde?

*Uhr* tells you the time on the clock. *die Stunde* is an hour as a length of time, and *die Minute* a minute.

- *Es ist zwei Uhr.* — It's two o'clock.
- *Der Film ist zwei Stunden lang.* — The film is two hours long.
- *Ich warte zehn Minuten.* — I'm waiting ten minutes. (*warten* = to wait)

To ask how long, say *Wie lange?*: *Wie lange arbeitest du heute?* — *Acht Stunden.*

## Days, parts of the day and the week

All days are masculine and capitalized, because they are nouns.

| Day | Short | Memory hook |
|---|---|---|
| der Montag | Mo | moon day, like Monday |
| der Dienstag | Di | |
| der Mittwoch | Mi | *Mitte* = middle: mid-week |
| der Donnerstag | Do | *Donner* = thunder: Thor's day, like Thursday |
| der Freitag | Fr | like Friday |
| der Samstag | Sa | in northern Germany also *der Sonnabend* |
| der Sonntag | So | *Sonne* = sun: Sunday |

*die Woche* is the week and *das Wochenende* the weekend (*Ende* = end). *der Tag* is the day.

The parts of the day are masculine too, except the night:

| German | Roughly | English |
|---|---|---|
| der Morgen | 5 to 9 | the morning |
| der Vormittag | 9 to 12 | the late morning, before noon |
| der Mittag | 12 to 14 | noon, midday |
| der Nachmittag | 14 to 18 | the afternoon |
| der Abend | 18 to 23 | the evening |
| die Nacht | 23 to 5 | the night |

*vor* means before and *nach* means after, so *Vormittag* is "before midday" and *Nachmittag* "after midday".

### Today, tomorrow, yesterday

*heute* (today, lesson 4), *morgen* (tomorrow) and *gestern* (yesterday) combine with the parts of the day: *heute Abend* (this evening), *gestern Abend* (last night, yesterday evening), *morgen Nachmittag* (tomorrow afternoon). Careful: *morgen* in small letters is tomorrow, *der Morgen* with a capital is the morning. Tomorrow morning is *morgen früh*, not *morgen Morgen* (*früh* = early).

## When? um, am, von … bis

| Preposition | Used with | Example |
|---|---|---|
| um | clock times | *um acht Uhr* — at eight o'clock |
| am | days, parts of the day, the weekend | *am Montag, am Abend, am Wochenende* — on Monday, in the evening, at the weekend |
| in der | the night | *in der Nacht* — at night |
| von … bis | from … until | *von neun bis fünf* — from nine to five |

*am* is short for *an dem*, but you can learn it as one word. Notice that the night is the exception: not *am Nacht* but *in der Nacht*.

- *Der Kurs beginnt um halb neun.* — The course starts at half past eight. (*beginnen* = to begin)
- *Am Freitag arbeite ich nicht.* — I don't work on Friday.
- *Am Nachmittag lerne ich Deutsch.* — In the afternoon I study German.
- *Die Bäckerei ist von sieben bis achtzehn Uhr offen.* — The bakery is open from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. (*offen* = open)
- *Ich arbeite bis fünf.* — I work until five.
- *Wann kommst du? — Um sieben.* — When are you coming? — At seven.

When a time phrase comes first, the verb stays in second place and the subject moves after it: *Am Freitag arbeite ich nicht.* You met verb-second word order in lesson 4; lesson 12 practises it in detail.

## How often?

A **[[frequency adverb]]** says how often something happens. You know *immer* (always) and *oft* (often) from lesson 4; add *manchmal* (sometimes) and *nie* (never).

| immer | oft | manchmal | nie |
|---|---|---|---|
| always | often | sometimes | never |

They usually come straight after the verb, or after the subject when the subject follows the verb:

- *Am Morgen trinke ich immer Kaffee.* — In the morning I always drink coffee.
- *Wir essen oft Nudeln.* — We often eat pasta.
- *Am Sonntag schlafe ich manchmal bis zehn.* — On Sundays I sometimes sleep until ten. (*schlafen* = to sleep)
- *Er kommt nie zu spät.* — He's never late. (*zu spät* = too late)

*nie* is already negative, so never add *nicht* to it. *früh* (early) and *spät* (late) are the opposites you need here: *Es ist schon spät.* — It's already late.

For "every day" German uses the accusative from lesson 9: *jeden Tag* (der Tag → jeden), *jede Woche*, *jedes Wochenende*.

## Dialogue: Do you have time on Saturday?

> Anna: Hallo Tom! Hast du am Samstag Zeit?
>
> Tom: Am Samstag? Am Vormittag arbeite ich. Aber am Nachmittag habe ich Zeit.
>
> Anna: Super! Möchtest du einen Kaffee trinken?
>
> Tom: Gern! Wann denn? Um zwei?
>
> Anna: Um zwei habe ich noch Deutschkurs. Der Kurs ist von zehn bis halb drei.
>
> Tom: Dann um drei?
>
> Anna: Ja, um drei. Und ich habe Zeit bis sechs. Am Abend kommt meine Schwester.
>
> Tom: Gut. Dann bis Samstag um drei!
>
> Anna: Bis Samstag! Tschüss!

In English:

> Anna: Hi Tom! Do you have time on Saturday?
>
> Tom: On Saturday? In the morning I work. But in the afternoon I have time.
>
> Anna: Great! Would you like to have a coffee?
>
> Tom: I'd love to! When? At two?
>
> Anna: At two I still have my German course. The course is from ten until half past two.
>
> Tom: At three, then?
>
> Anna: Yes, at three. And I have time until six. In the evening my sister is coming.
>
> Tom: Good. See you on Saturday at three, then!
>
> Anna: See you Saturday! Bye!

*die Zeit* means time in general: *Hast du Zeit?* — Do you have time? *denn* in *Wann denn?* just makes the question sound friendlier. *Bis Samstag!* (until Saturday) is how you say "see you on Saturday".

## Pronunciation

- *Viertel*: the *v* is an *f* and the *ie* is short here: FIR-tel.
- *Uhr* sounds like "oor" with a long *u*.
- *Abend* and *Tag* end in a *t* and a *k* sound: AH-bent, tahk. That's the final devoicing from lesson 1.
- *Mittwoch* is stressed on the first syllable: MIT-voch, with the *ch* of *Bach*. *Nacht* has the same *ch*.
- *Dienstag*: long *ie*, DEENS-tahk. Don't confuse it with *Donnerstag*, DON-ners-tahk.
- *gestern*: GES-tern, with a hard *g*.

## Common mistakes

- *halb drei* is 2:30, not 3:30. Count towards the next hour.
- *am acht Uhr* — Clock times take *um*: *um acht Uhr*.
- *in Montag*, *an Montag* — Days take *am*: *am Montag*.
- *am Nacht* — The exception: *in der Nacht*.
- *Ich lerne zwei Uhr.* — For a length of time use *Stunden*: *Ich lerne zwei Stunden.*
- *Es ist eins Uhr.* — Say *ein Uhr* or just *eins*.
- *morgen Morgen* — Say *morgen früh*.
- *Ich nicht nie esse Fisch.* — *nie* is enough, and the verb is second: *Ich esse nie Fisch.*

## Key points

- Ask *Wie spät ist es?* or *Wie viel Uhr ist es?* and answer *Es ist …*.
- Official time: hours + *Uhr* + minutes (*vierzehn Uhr zehn*). Everyday time: *nach*, *vor*, *Viertel*, *halb*.
- *halb* points to the next hour: *halb vier* = 3:30.
- *um* + clock time, *am* + day or part of the day, *in der Nacht*, *von … bis*.
- *Uhr* = o'clock, *Stunde* = an hour of time.
- Days and parts of the day are masculine nouns (except *die Nacht*); *morgen* = tomorrow, *der Morgen* = morning.
- Frequency: *immer, oft, manchmal, nie*, usually after the verb.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: A day in my life: separable verbs and word order
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

With the clock and the days from lesson 11 you can say when things happen. Now you'll describe a whole day: getting up, showering, going to work, shopping, watching TV. Many of these everyday actions are expressed in German by a special kind of verb that splits in two, the **[[separable verb]]**. You'll also practise putting a time word first (*Um sieben stehe ich auf*) and linking actions with *zuerst*, *dann* and *danach*.

## Separable verbs: the verb that splits

Look at the verb *aufstehen* (to get up). In the dictionary it is one word. In a sentence it breaks apart:

- *Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.* — I get up at seven o'clock.

The main part, *stehen*, is conjugated and sits in its usual place, second. The small front part, *auf*, jumps to the very end of the sentence. That front part is called the **[[separable prefix]]**. English does something similar with phrasal verbs: "I get *up*", "I pick you *up*", "Call me *back*". German simply pushes the little word all the way to the end.

| | aufstehen | anfangen | fernsehen |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | stehe … auf | fange … an | sehe … fern |
| du | stehst … auf | fängst … an | siehst … fern |
| er / sie / es | steht … auf | fängt … an | sieht … fern |
| wir | stehen … auf | fangen … an | sehen … fern |
| ihr | steht … auf | fangt … an | seht … fern |
| sie / Sie | stehen … auf | fangen … an | sehen … fern |

The verb part keeps all its habits. *fangen* changes a→ä (*du fängst, er fängt*) and *sehen* changes e→ie (*du siehst, er sieht*), so *anfangen* and *fernsehen* do too.

### The separable verbs in this lesson

| Verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| aufstehen | to get up | *Wir stehen früh auf.* — We get up early. |
| anfangen | to begin, to start | *Der Film fängt um acht an.* — The film starts at eight. |
| einkaufen | to go shopping | *Am Samstag kaufe ich ein.* — On Saturday I go shopping. |
| anrufen | to phone | *Ich rufe meine Mutter an.* — I'm phoning my mother. |
| fernsehen | to watch TV | *Siehst du oft fern?* — Do you often watch TV? |
| aufräumen | to tidy up | *Er räumt die Küche auf.* — He's tidying the kitchen. |
| mitkommen | to come along | *Kommst du mit?* — Are you coming along? |
| abholen | to pick up | *Ich hole das Kind um vier ab.* — I pick up the child at four. |
| ankommen | to arrive | *Der Zug kommt um neun an.* — The train arrives at nine. |

(*die Küche* = kitchen, *der Zug* = train.)

The prefixes often carry a hint of their meaning: *auf* = up, *an* = on or at, *ein* = in, *mit* = with or along, *ab* = off or away, *fern* = far (*fernsehen* is literally "far-see", like "tele-vision").

### Where everything goes

The rule is the same in statements and in questions: the conjugated verb in its usual place, the prefix at the very end, everything else in between.

- *Ich rufe heute Abend meine Schwester an.* — I'm calling my sister this evening.
- *Wann stehst du am Sonntag auf?* — When do you get up on Sundays?
- *Räumst du dein Zimmer auf?* — Are you tidying your room? (*das Zimmer* = room)
- *Wir kaufen nicht ein.* — We're not going shopping. (*nicht* comes before the prefix.)

When the verb is in the infinitive, for example after *möchte*, it stays in one piece at the end: *Ich möchte heute einkaufen.* — I'd like to go shopping today.

### Not every verb splits

Only these little prefixes split off. Ordinary verbs stay whole, even when they look long:

- *frühstücken* (to have breakfast) is not separable: *Ich frühstücke um acht.* Never *Ich stücke früh*.
- *duschen* (to shower), *kochen* (to cook), *putzen* (to clean) are regular: *Ich dusche, du duschst; ich koche; du putzt.*
- *schlafen* (to sleep) and *waschen* (to wash) change a→ä: *du schläfst, er schläft; du wäschst, er wäscht.*

## Word order: time first, verb second

You learned the verb-second rule in lesson 4: in a statement the verb is the second element, and the first place does not have to be the subject. When a time phrase comes first, the subject moves behind the verb. This swap is called **[[inversion]]**, and it is how Germans tell a day in order:

| Position 1 | Position 2 (verb) | Subject | Rest | End |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ich | stehe | | um sieben | auf. |
| Um sieben | stehe | ich | | auf. |
| Am Montag | arbeite | ich | bis fünf. | |
| Normalerweise | frühstücke | ich | um acht. | |
| Dann | rufe | ich | meine Mutter | an. |

German speakers start sentences with a time phrase all the time; it sounds natural and lets you tell a day in order. The subject still comes right after the verb, and the prefix still goes to the end.

### Telling things in order

These words put actions in a sequence, and each one fills position 1 on its own:

- *zuerst* — first (of all)
- *dann* — then
- *danach* — after that, afterwards
- *später* — later

*Zuerst dusche ich, dann frühstücke ich. Danach räume ich auf, und später kaufe ich ein.* — First I shower, then I have breakfast. After that I tidy up, and later I go shopping.

Note the last part: *und* doesn't count as a position, so after *und später* the verb comes next: *und später kaufe ich ein*.

*normalerweise* (normally, usually) works the same way: *Normalerweise sehe ich am Abend fern.*

## Reading: Jonas's day

> Ich heiße Jonas und ich bin Koch. Normalerweise stehe ich um neun Uhr auf. Zuerst dusche ich, dann frühstücke ich: ein Kaffee und ein Brötchen. Danach räume ich die Wohnung auf, und um elf kaufe ich ein. Meine Arbeit fängt um zwölf Uhr an. Ich koche bis drei, dann habe ich zwei Stunden Pause. Am Abend ist das Restaurant immer voll. Um elf Uhr habe ich Feierabend. Dann bin ich sehr müde. Ich sehe noch eine Stunde fern und gehe um eins ins Bett. Am Montag arbeite ich nicht. Dann rufe ich meine Eltern an, oder ich hole meine Freundin ab und wir kochen zusammen.

In English:

> My name is Jonas and I'm a cook. Normally I get up at nine o'clock. First I shower, then I have breakfast: a coffee and a roll. After that I tidy the flat, and at eleven I go shopping. My work starts at twelve. I cook until three, then I have a two-hour break. In the evening the restaurant is always full. At eleven I finish work. Then I'm very tired. I watch TV for another hour and go to bed at one. On Mondays I don't work. Then I phone my parents, or I pick up my girlfriend and we cook together.

(*die Wohnung* = flat, apartment; *die Pause* = break; *voll* = full; *noch eine Stunde* = for another hour; *ins Bett* = to bed.)

*der Feierabend* is the time after work, and *Ich habe Feierabend* means "I've finished work for the day". It's a very German word and a very popular one. *der Alltag* is everyday life, the normal routine: *Mein Alltag ist ziemlich ruhig* (*ruhig* = quiet).

## Dialogue: Are you coming along?

> Lukas: Wann stehst du morgen auf?
>
> Sara: Um halb sechs. Mein Zug kommt um acht in Köln an.
>
> Lukas: So früh! Ich habe morgen frei. Zuerst schlafe ich lange, dann räume ich die Küche auf.
>
> Sara: Und danach?
>
> Lukas: Danach kaufe ich ein. Und am Abend gehen Tim und ich ins Kino. Kommst du mit?
>
> Sara: Wann fängt der Film an?
>
> Lukas: Um acht.
>
> Sara: Nein danke, morgen Abend bin ich sicher müde. Ich gehe früh ins Bett.
>
> Lukas: Schade! Vielleicht am Samstag?
>
> Sara: Ja, am Samstag komme ich gern mit!

In English:

> Lukas: When are you getting up tomorrow?
>
> Sara: At half past five. My train arrives in Cologne at eight.
>
> Lukas: So early! I've got the day off tomorrow. First I'll sleep in, then I'll tidy the kitchen.
>
> Sara: And after that?
>
> Lukas: After that I'll do the shopping. And in the evening Tim and I are going to the cinema. Are you coming along?
>
> Sara: When does the film start?
>
> Lukas: At eight.
>
> Sara: No thanks, tomorrow evening I'll surely be tired. I'm going to bed early.
>
> Lukas: Pity! Maybe on Saturday?
>
> Sara: Yes, on Saturday I'd love to come along!

German often uses the present tense for the future when a time word makes it clear: *Morgen kaufe ich ein* — Tomorrow I'll go shopping. (*frei haben* = to have the day off, *ins Kino* = to the cinema, *sicher* = surely, *schade* = pity, *vielleicht* = maybe.)

*fertig* means finished or ready: *Ich bin fertig!* — I'm done! / I'm ready! In casual speech it can also mean exhausted.

## Pronunciation

- Separable verbs are stressed on the prefix: AUF-stehen, AN-rufen, FERN-sehen, EIN-kaufen, MIT-kommen, AB-holen. *frühstücken* is also stressed at the front (FRÜH-stücken) but never splits, because *früh* is not a separable prefix. Stress alone doesn't tell you, so learn which verbs split.
- In a sentence the prefix at the end keeps a strong stress: *Ich stehe um sieben AUF.*
- *duschen*: the *sch* is like English "sh"; the *u* is short in some regions and long in others (DU-shen or DOO-shen), and both are fine.
- *müde*: long *ü*; round your lips as for "oo" and say "ee".
- *Feierabend*: FEI-er-ah-bent; *ei* as in "eye".

## Common mistakes

- *Ich aufstehe um sieben.* — Split it: *Ich stehe um sieben auf.*
- *Ich stehe auf um sieben.* — The prefix goes to the very end: *Ich stehe um sieben auf.*
- *Um sieben ich stehe auf.* — After a time phrase the verb comes next: *Um sieben stehe ich auf.*
- *Ich rufe an meine Mutter.* — The person goes in the middle: *Ich rufe meine Mutter an.*
- *Er fangt um acht an.* — Keep the stem change: *er fängt an*.
- *Ich stücke früh.* — *frühstücken* doesn't split: *Ich frühstücke.*
- *Dann ich dusche.* — *dann* takes position 1, so: *Dann dusche ich.*

## Key points

- A separable verb splits in a statement or question: the verb part is second (or first in a yes/no question), the prefix goes to the end.
- The prefix is stressed: AUF-stehen.
- The verb part keeps its stem change: *er fängt an, du siehst fern*.
- In the infinitive (after *möchte*) the verb stays together: *Ich möchte einkaufen.*
- A time phrase or *zuerst, dann, danach, später, normalerweise* can fill position 1; then the verb comes second and the subject follows it.
- *und* doesn't count as a position: *und dann frühstücke ich*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Hobbies and stem-changing verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 4 is about free time and plans. In this first lesson you learn to talk about your
hobbies: what you do in your free time, what you like, what you like more, and what you like
most of all.

On the way you meet an important group of verbs. In lesson 4 you learned the regular present
tense endings (-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en), and you have already seen a few verbs that change
their vowel, such as *sprechen* (du sprichst) in lesson 7 and *essen* and *nehmen* in lesson 9.
Here that pattern gets a name and a full explanation, because many of the most common German
verbs, including several hobby verbs, behave this way.

## Talking about hobbies

The easiest way to ask about free time is with *gern*, which you know from lesson 4. *Gern*
goes right after the verb (after a short pronoun like *das* if there is one: *Ich mache das
gern*) and before the rest: *Ich spiele gern Gitarre.* It means that you like doing it.

- *Was machst du gern?* — What do you like doing?
- *Was machen Sie in der Freizeit?* — What do you do in your free time?
- *Hast du ein Hobby?* — Do you have a hobby?
- *Mein Hobby ist Musik.* — My hobby is music.
- *Ich lese gern.* — I like reading.
- *Ich tanze nicht gern.* — I don't like dancing.

*In der Freizeit* means "in (your) free time". Learn it as a fixed chunk for now; the
grammar behind *der* after *in* comes in lesson 18.

Many hobbies are just verbs: *lesen* (to read), *schwimmen* (to swim), *tanzen* (to dance),
*singen* (to sing), *reisen* (to travel), *wandern* (to hike), *joggen* (to jog), *malen* (to
paint), *fotografieren* (to take photos). Others use *spielen* or *fahren* with a noun:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *Fußball spielen* | to play football (soccer) |
| *Gitarre spielen* | to play the guitar |
| *Fahrrad fahren* | to ride a bike, to cycle |
| *Musik hören* | to listen to music |
| *Filme sehen* | to watch films |
| *Freunde treffen* | to meet friends |
| *spazieren gehen* | to go for a walk |
| *ins Kino gehen* | to go to the cinema |

Two small notes. German drops the article with sports and instruments here: *Ich spiele
Fußball* (no *den*), *Ich spiele Gitarre*. And *ins Kino*, *ins Theater* and *ins Konzert* are
fixed chunks for going somewhere; you will see why in later lessons.

## Stem-changing verbs

The **[[stem]]** of a verb is the infinitive without *-en*: *mach-en*, *lern-en*, *fahr-en*. In
regular verbs the stem never changes. A **[[stem-changing verb]]** changes the vowel of its stem,
but only in the du form and the er/sie/es form. Every other form is regular. There are
three patterns at A1.

### Pattern 1: a → ä

| | fahren (to go by vehicle) | schlafen (to sleep) |
|---|---|---|
| ich | fahre | schlafe |
| du | *fährst* | *schläfst* |
| er/sie/es | *fährt* | *schläft* |
| wir | fahren | schlafen |
| ihr | fahrt | schlaft |
| sie/Sie | fahren | schlafen |

*Waschen* (du wäschst, er wäscht) follows the same pattern.

### Pattern 2: e → i

| | sprechen | geben (to give) | helfen (to help) | treffen (to meet) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | spreche | gebe | helfe | treffe |
| du | *sprichst* | *gibst* | *hilfst* | *triffst* |
| er/sie/es | *spricht* | *gibt* | *hilft* | *trifft* |
| wir | sprechen | geben | helfen | treffen |
| ihr | sprecht | gebt | helft | trefft |
| sie/Sie | sprechen | geben | helfen | treffen |

*Essen* (du isst, er isst) and *nehmen* (du nimmst, er nimmt) belong here too. *Nehmen* also
changes its consonants (*du nimmst, er nimmt*), so learn those two forms by heart; *treffen*
keeps its double *f* (*du triffst, er trifft*).

### Pattern 3: e → ie

| | lesen (to read) | sehen (to see) |
|---|---|---|
| ich | lese | sehe |
| du | *liest* | *siehst* |
| er/sie/es | *liest* | *sieht* |
| wir | lesen | sehen |
| ihr | lest | seht |
| sie/Sie | lesen | sehen |

*Lesen* has one more twist: its stem ends in -s, so du gets only -t (*du liest*, not
"du liesst"), just like *heißen* (du heißt) in lesson 4.

### A memory hook

Think of the change as a "spotlight" on the two singular persons you talk to or about: *du*
and *er/sie/es*. The plural forms, and *ich*, stay in the dark and keep the plain vowel. If you
know the er form, you know the du form: *er fährt → du fährst*, *er liest → du liest*.

You can't see from the infinitive whether a verb changes, so the vocabulary list notes every
stem change. Many common verbs with *e* or *a* do not change: *gehen*, *lernen*, *machen*,
*spielen*, *wandern*, *malen*, *tanzen*.

Examples:

- *Mein Vater fährt am Wochenende Fahrrad.* — My father cycles at the weekend.
- *Liest du gern?* — Do you like reading?
- *Anna sieht jeden Abend einen Film.* — Anna watches a film every evening.
- *Wann triffst du deine Freunde?* — When are you meeting your friends?
- *Er hilft oft im Garten.* — He often helps in the garden.
- *Was gibt es heute im Kino?* — What's on at the cinema today? (*es gibt*, lesson 10)
- *Wir fahren zusammen, und ihr fahrt allein.* — We're going together, and you're going alone.

## gern, lieber, am liebsten

*Gern* has two more forms for comparing. *Lieber* is its **[[comparative]]** ("rather, prefer")
and *am liebsten* its **[[superlative]]** ("most of all, like best").

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| *gern* | like doing | *Ich schwimme gern.* — I like swimming. |
| *lieber* | prefer, would rather | *Ich jogge lieber.* — I prefer jogging. |
| *am liebsten* | like most of all | *Am liebsten tanze ich.* — Most of all I like dancing. |

They all sit where *gern* sits, after the verb:

- *Ich sehe gern Filme, aber ich lese lieber.* — I like watching films, but I prefer reading.
- *Trinkst du lieber Kaffee oder Tee?* — Do you prefer coffee or tea?
- *Ich höre am liebsten Musik.* — Most of all I like listening to music.

When *am liebsten* comes first in the sentence, remember the rule from lesson 4: the verb stays
in position 2 and the subject moves behind it. *Am liebsten wandere ich* (not "Am liebsten ich
wandere").

*Lieber* also works for choosing between things: *Ich sehe gern Filme, aber ich gehe lieber
ins Konzert.* — I like watching films, but I'd rather go to a concert. (For liking a thing
itself, German uses *mögen*, which you meet properly in the next lesson.)

## Dialogue: Was machst du gern?

Jonas and Mia are new in a German course and chat in the break.

> Jonas: Was machst du gern in der Freizeit, Mia?
>
> Mia: Ich lese viel, und ich male gern. Und du?
>
> Jonas: Ich spiele gern Fußball, aber am liebsten fahre ich Fahrrad.
>
> Mia: Fährst du allein?
>
> Jonas: Nein, mein Bruder fährt auch gern. Wir fahren am Sonntag immer zusammen.
>
> Mia: Ich fahre nicht so gern Fahrrad. Ich wandere lieber.
>
> Jonas: Siehst du auch gern Filme?
>
> Mia: Ja! Ich treffe am Freitag Freunde, und wir gehen ins Kino. Kommst du mit?
>
> Jonas: Gern! Wann fängt der Film an?
>
> Mia: Um acht. Und danach singen wir Karaoke!

Translation:

> Jonas: What do you like doing in your free time, Mia?
>
> Mia: I read a lot, and I like painting. And you?
>
> Jonas: I like playing football, but most of all I like cycling.
>
> Mia: Do you ride alone?
>
> Jonas: No, my brother likes cycling too. We always ride together on Sundays.
>
> Mia: I don't like cycling so much. I prefer hiking.
>
> Jonas: Do you like watching films too?
>
> Mia: Yes! I'm meeting friends on Friday and we're going to the cinema. Are you coming?
>
> Jonas: I'd love to! When does the film start?
>
> Mia: At eight. And afterwards we're singing karaoke!

Notice *Fährst du …?* and *mein Bruder fährt* with ä, but *wir fahren* without it.

## Pronunciation

- *fährt, schläft*: ä is pronounced like the e in English "bed" (long here: "fairt").
- *liest, sieht*: ie is a long "ee". The h in *sieht* is silent; it only shows that the vowel
  is long.
- *Theater*: the th is a plain t, and the stress is on the second syllable: the-A-ter.
- *fotografieren*: verbs ending in -ieren are stressed on *-ie-*: fo-to-gra-FIE-ren.
- *Konzert*: the z sounds like "ts"; stress on the second syllable: kon-ZERT.
- *joggen* is an English loanword, but the j is said like English "dj" by most speakers and the
  -en is German.

## Common mistakes

- Putting the change in the wrong person. *Ich fähre* and *wir sprichen* are wrong: only
  du and er/sie/es change. *Ich fahre, wir sprechen.*
- Adding the umlaut to ihr. *Ihr fahrt* (no ä), *ihr lest*, *ihr seht*.
- Using the English word order with gern. Not "Ich gern lese" but *Ich lese gern*.
- Saying "mehr gern" for "more". The comparative of *gern* is *lieber*: *Ich schwimme
  lieber* (not "Ich schwimme mehr gern").
- "I play the guitar" with an article. In German: *Ich spiele Gitarre*.
- Using *gehen* for travel by vehicle. *Gehen* is on foot. For bikes, cars, trains and so
  on use *fahren*: *Ich fahre nach Berlin.* — I'm going to Berlin.

## Key points

- A stem-changing verb changes its vowel only in the du and er/sie/es forms: a → ä (*fahren,
  schlafen*), e → i (*sprechen, essen, geben, helfen, treffen, nehmen*), e → ie (*lesen,
  sehen*).
- Learn the er form with each verb: *er fährt, er gibt, er liest*.
- *gern* = like doing, *lieber* = prefer, *am liebsten* = like most of all; all go after the
  verb.
- With sports and instruments there's no article: *Ich spiele Fußball / Gitarre.*
- Ask *Was machst du gern?* or *Hast du ein Hobby?*

lessons.title: Modal verbs: können, wollen, möchten
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In the last lesson you talked about what you like doing. Now you learn to say what you can
do, what you want to do and what you would like to do: *Ich kann schwimmen*, *Ich will
Gitarre lernen*, *Ich möchte eine Party feiern*. These sentences need a new kind of verb and a
new word order, and both are central to German. Once you have them, you can also make plans
and invitations.

## What a modal verb does

A **[[modal verb]]** adds an attitude to another verb: ability (can), wish (want, would like),
obligation (must) or permission (may). In English: "I *can* swim", "I *want to* travel". In
German it works the same way, with one big difference in word order:

- *Ich kann schwimmen.* — I can swim.
- *Ich will reisen.* — I want to travel.
- *Ich möchte tanzen.* — I'd like to dance.

The modal verb is conjugated and sits in position 2. The second verb stays in the infinitive
(the form ending in -en, as in the dictionary) and goes to the very end of the sentence. There
is no "zu" (no "to") in front of it.

This lesson covers *können*, *wollen*, *mögen* and *möchten*. Lesson 15 adds *müssen*,
*dürfen* and *sollen*.

## The forms

Modal verbs are irregular in the singular. Three things are true of all of them:

1. The ich and er/sie/es forms are the same and have no ending: *ich kann, er kann*.
   (*möchten* is the one exception: *ich möchte, er möchte* are the same but end in *-e*.)
2. Most of them change their vowel in the singular: *können → ich kann*.
3. The plural is regular, built from the infinitive: *wir können, ihr könnt, sie können*.

| | können (can) | wollen (want) | mögen (like) | möchten (would like) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | kann | will | mag | möchte |
| du | kannst | willst | magst | möchtest |
| er/sie/es | kann | will | mag | möchte |
| wir | können | wollen | mögen | möchten |
| ihr | könnt | wollt | mögt | möchtet |
| sie/Sie | können | wollen | mögen | möchten |

You know *möchte* from ordering food in lesson 9 (*Ich möchte einen Kaffee*). It is really a
polite form of *mögen*, but at A1 treat it as its own verb. Note that its er form is *er möchte*,
with no -t.

Memory hook: *ich* and *er* are twins with modal verbs. If you remember *ich kann*, you
already know *er kann*.

## The sentence bracket

German puts the two parts of the verb at two fixed points and fills the middle with
everything else. This is called the **[[sentence bracket]]**: the modal verb opens it in
position 2, the infinitive closes it at the end.

| Position 1 | Position 2 (modal) | middle | end (infinitive) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ich | kann | gut | kochen. |
| Mein Bruder | will | am Samstag eine Party | feiern. |
| Am Sonntag | möchten | wir | wandern. |
| Was | kannst | du | spielen? |

In English the two verbs stay together ("I can cook well"). In German they separate: *Ich
kann gut kochen*, never "Ich kann kochen gut".

Yes/no questions start with the modal; the infinitive is still at the end:

- *Kannst du Ski fahren?* — Can you ski?
- *Willst du am Wochenende Freunde treffen?* — Do you want to meet friends at the weekend?
- *Möchten Sie etwas trinken?* — Would you like something to drink?

*Nicht* usually goes just before the infinitive: *Ich kann heute nicht kommen.* — I can't come
today.

You already know a bracket from lesson 12: *Ich stehe um sieben auf.* With a modal verb, a
separable verb comes back together as one word at the end: *Ich will um sieben aufstehen.*
*Kommst du mit?* becomes *Willst du mitkommen?* And *einladen* (to invite): *Ich möchte
meine Freunde einladen.*

## können: ability and possibility

*Können* says that you are able to do something, or that something is possible:

- *Ich kann ein bisschen Gitarre spielen.* — I can play the guitar a bit.
- *Kannst du gut kochen?* — Can you cook well? / Are you a good cook?
- *Meine Schwester kann Klavier spielen, aber sie kann nicht singen.* — My sister can play the
  piano, but she can't sing.
- *Kannst du am Freitag?* — Can you (make it) on Friday?
- *Wir können zusammen Auto fahren.* — We can drive together.

For languages, German often leaves out the second verb: *Ich kann Deutsch* — I can speak
German. *Kannst du Englisch?* — Do you speak English?

To say how well, use *gut, sehr gut, ein bisschen, nicht so gut, nicht*, and put it before the
infinitive (or before the noun that goes with it): *Ich kann sehr gut schwimmen.*

## wollen and möchten: wishes and plans

Both express a wish, but they feel different:

- *möchte* is polite and soft: "would like". Use it with strangers, in shops, and whenever you
  ask for something.
- *will* is direct and firm: "want". Fine for plans and for talking about yourself with
  friends, but *Ich will einen Kaffee* to a waiter sounds pushy, like a child saying "I want…".

Examples:

- *Ich will im Sommer nach Spanien reisen.* — I want to travel to Spain in the summer.
- *Was willst du heute machen?* — What do you want to do today?
- *Ich möchte bitte zwei Brötchen.* — I'd like two rolls, please.

False friend warning: *Ich will* does not mean "I will". It means "I want". The English future
"I will" is a different verb that you meet after A1.

## mögen: liking things and people

*Mögen* mostly takes a noun, not an infinitive: *Ich mag Pizza.* — I like pizza. *Magst du
Jazz?* — Do you like jazz? *Ich mag meine Kollegen.* — I like my colleagues. For liking
activities, keep using *gern* from lesson 13: *Ich tanze gern* (I like dancing).

## Useful little words for plans

| German | English | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *natürlich* | of course | *Natürlich kann ich helfen.* — Of course I can help. |
| *vielleicht* | maybe | *Vielleicht komme ich später.* — Maybe I'll come later. |
| *leider* | unfortunately | *Ich kann leider nicht.* — Unfortunately I can't. |
| *schon* | already | *Kannst du schon Auto fahren?* — Can you drive already? |
| *noch* | still | *Ich lerne noch.* — I'm still learning. |
| *noch nicht* | not yet | *Ich kann noch nicht Ski fahren.* — I can't ski yet. |
| *gleich* | right away, in a moment | *Ich komme gleich!* — I'm coming right away! |
| *wirklich* | really | *Das ist wirklich toll.* — That's really great. |
| *sicher* | sure, certainly | *Sie kommt sicher.* — She's sure to come. |

Two useful nouns: *die Lust* (desire, being in the mood) and *der Spaß* (fun).

- *Hast du Lust auf eine Party?* — Do you feel like a party? (*auf* is part of the chunk.)
- *Ich habe keine Lust.* — I don't feel like it.
- *Tanzen macht Spaß.* — Dancing is fun.

## Dialogue: Eine Idee

Lea calls her friend Max.

> Lea: Du, Max, ich habe eine Idee. Ich will am Samstag eine Party machen.
>
> Max: Super! Was möchtest du feiern?
>
> Lea: Das Wochenende! Ich möchte alle Freunde aus dem Kurs einladen. Kannst du kommen?
>
> Max: Natürlich! Kann ich helfen? Ich kann ein bisschen kochen.
>
> Lea: Ja, gern. Und du spielst Gitarre, oder? Kannst du etwas spielen?
>
> Max: Hm, ich lerne noch. Ich kann noch nicht wirklich gut spielen.
>
> Lea: Egal! Wir wollen ja nur singen und tanzen.
>
> Max: Okay, dann bringe ich die Gitarre mit. Kommt Jana auch?
>
> Lea: Vielleicht. Ich frage sie gleich.
>
> Max: Toll, ich habe wirklich Lust auf eine Party!

Translation:

> Lea: Hey, Max, I've got an idea. I want to have a party on Saturday.
>
> Max: Great! What would you like to celebrate?
>
> Lea: The weekend! I'd like to invite all my friends from the course. Can you come?
>
> Max: Of course! Can I help? I can cook a bit.
>
> Lea: Yes, please. And you play the guitar, don't you? Can you play something?
>
> Max: Hm, I'm still learning. I can't really play well yet.
>
> Lea: Doesn't matter! We only want to sing and dance anyway.
>
> Max: Okay, then I'll bring the guitar. Is Jana coming too?
>
> Lea: Maybe. I'll ask her right away.
>
> Max: Great, I'm really in the mood for a party!

New in passing: *egal* (it doesn't matter), *oder?* at the end of a sentence ("…, don't
you?"), *mitbringen* (to bring along, separable like *mitkommen*).

## Pronunciation

- *können, möchten, mögen*: ö is made by saying "e" with rounded lips. Don't flatten it to
  "o": *können* with ö (we can) and *kann* with a (I can) sound clearly different.
- *will* has a short i, like English "will"; the w is a German w, which sounds like English v:
  "vill".
- *Klavier*: the v sounds like English v here (it's a foreign word), and the stress is at the
  end: kla-VIER. *Gitarre* is stressed on the second syllable: gi-TAR-re. *Instrument*: in-stru-MENT.
- *Lust*: the u is short, as in English "put", and the st is said "st", not "sht".

## Common mistakes

- Keeping the two verbs together, as in English: "Ich kann spielen Gitarre". Correct: *Ich
  kann Gitarre spielen.*
- Adding "zu": "Ich will zu reisen". Modal verbs never take *zu*: *Ich will reisen.*
- Adding endings to ich and er: "ich kanne", "er kannt", "er möchtet". Correct: *ich kann, er
  kann, er möchte.*
- Conjugating both verbs: "Ich kann schwimme". Only the modal changes; the other verb stays in
  the infinitive.
- Reading *Ich will* as "I will". It means "I want".
- Using *will* when ordering. Say *Ich möchte …* to be polite.
- Using *mögen* for activities: "Ich mag schwimmen" is understood but sounds odd at this level;
  say *Ich schwimme gern*.

## Key points

- Modal verbs: *können* (can), *wollen* (want), *mögen* (like), *möchten* (would like).
- ich and er/sie/es forms are identical: *ich kann, er kann; ich will, er will; ich möchte, er
  möchte* (no ending, except the *-e* of *möchte*).
- Sentence bracket: modal in position 2, infinitive at the end, everything else in between.
- Questions: *Kannst du …?* with the infinitive at the end. *Nicht* goes before the infinitive.
- Separable verbs join up again at the end: *Willst du mitkommen?*
- *möchte* is polite, *will* is direct; *will* never means "will".
- *Hast du Lust?* and *Das macht Spaß* are everyday phrases for plans.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Modal verbs: müssen, dürfen, sollen — rules and obligations
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 14 you met the modal verbs *können, wollen, mögen* and *möchten* and the sentence
bracket (modal in position 2, infinitive at the end). This lesson adds the other three modal
verbs: *müssen* (must, have to), *dürfen* (may, be allowed to) and *sollen* (should, be supposed
to). With them you can talk about rules, signs, appointments and paperwork, which is exactly
what you meet when you live in a German-speaking country, and you can ask politely for
permission.

## The forms

The pattern is the one you already know: ich and er/sie/es are the same with no ending, the
singular has its own vowel, and the plural is regular.

| | müssen (must) | dürfen (may) | sollen (should) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | muss | darf | soll |
| du | musst | darfst | sollst |
| er/sie/es | muss | darf | soll |
| wir | müssen | dürfen | sollen |
| ihr | müsst | dürft | sollt |
| sie/Sie | müssen | dürfen | sollen |

Watch the spelling: *muss* and *musst* have ss (short u), and the umlaut disappears in the
singular: *müssen → ich muss*, *dürfen → ich darf*. *Sollen* doesn't change its vowel at all.

The word order is the same as in lesson 14:

| Position 1 | Position 2 (modal) | middle | end |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ich | muss | morgen früh | arbeiten. |
| Hier | darf | man nicht | parken. |
| Sie | müssen | das Formular | ausfüllen. |
| | Soll | ich das Fenster | öffnen? |

*Ausfüllen* (to fill in) is separable, so it stays together at the end, as you saw with
*mitkommen* in lesson 14. *Unterschreiben* (to sign) is not separable: *Sie unterschreibt
hier* and *Sie muss hier unterschreiben.*

## müssen: necessity

*Müssen* says that something is necessary, because of a rule, a situation or your own
feeling:

- *Ich muss um sieben aufstehen.* — I have to get up at seven.
- *Du musst pünktlich sein. Der Termin ist um neun.* — You have to be on time. The
  appointment is at nine.
- *Wir müssen leider warten.* — Unfortunately we have to wait.
- *Musst du heute noch die Hausaufgabe machen?* — Do you still have to do the homework today?

## dürfen: permission

*Dürfen* says that something is allowed:

- *Darf ich hier rauchen?* — May I smoke here?
- *Kinder dürfen hier spielen.* — Children are allowed to play here.
- *Im Kurs dürfen wir Englisch sprechen.* — In the course we're allowed to speak English.

## nicht müssen vs nicht dürfen

This is the most important trap of the lesson. In English, "must not" means "it's forbidden".
In German, *nicht müssen* only means "not necessary". For "forbidden" you need *nicht dürfen*.

| German | Meaning | English |
|---|---|---|
| *Du musst nicht kommen.* | not necessary, you choose | You don't have to come. |
| *Du darfst nicht kommen.* | forbidden | You mustn't come. / You're not allowed to come. |
| *Man muss hier nicht warten.* | no need to wait | You don't need to wait here. |
| *Man darf hier nicht parken.* | parking is forbidden | You mustn't park here. |

Memory hook: *müssen* is about need. Take the need away (*nicht müssen*) and you are free.
*Dürfen* is about permission. Take the permission away (*nicht dürfen*) and it is forbidden.

## sollen: what someone else wants

*Sollen* passes on an instruction, advice or expectation that comes from another person:

- *Der Arzt sagt, ich soll viel Wasser trinken.* — The doctor says I should drink a lot of
  water.
- *Wir sollen das Formular bis Freitag ausfüllen.* — We're supposed to fill in the form by
  Friday.

In questions with *ich* or *wir*, *sollen* is a friendly offer or a request for instructions:

- *Soll ich das Fenster öffnen?* — Shall I open the window?
- *Wo soll ich unterschreiben?* — Where should I sign?
- *Sollen wir zusammen warten?* — Shall we wait together?

## man: rules for everyone

*Man* is an **[[indefinite pronoun]]**: it means people in general, like English "one", "you" or
"they" in "they say…". It always takes the er/sie/es form of the verb, and it goes very well
with modal verbs when you talk about rules:

- *Hier darf man nicht rauchen.* — You can't smoke here. / Smoking isn't allowed here.
- *Im Kino muss man leise sein.* — In the cinema you have to be quiet.
- *Was muss man hier machen?* — What does one have to do here?
- *Wie schreibt man das?* — How do you spell that? (lesson 1)

Don't confuse *man* (one, people) with *der Mann* (the man): one n, small m.

## Signs and rules

Signs (*das Schild*, plural *die Schilder*) are often very short. Many use *verboten*
(forbidden) or *erlaubt* (allowed) with a verb used as a noun:

| Sign | Meaning | With man + modal |
|---|---|---|
| *Rauchen verboten* | No smoking | *Hier darf man nicht rauchen.* |
| *Parken erlaubt* | Parking allowed | *Hier darf man parken.* |
| *Bitte leise sein!* | Please be quiet! | *Hier muss man leise sein.* |
| *Bitte Ausweis zeigen* | Please show ID | *Man muss den Ausweis zeigen.* |
| *Heute geschlossen* | Closed today | *Man kann heute nicht einkaufen.* |

*Geschlossen* (closed) comes from *schließen* (to close); its opposite on a door is *geöffnet*
(open), from *öffnen*.

## Polite requests

Modal verbs are the normal way to ask for something politely:

- *Kann ich hier warten?* — Can I wait here?
- *Darf ich das Fenster öffnen?* — May I open the window? (a little more polite)
- *Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?* — Could you repeat that, please?
- *Können Sie mir helfen?* — Can you help me? (*mir* = me, lesson 20)

Possible answers: *Ja, natürlich.* — Yes, of course. *Ja, gern.* — Yes, sure. *Nein, leider
nicht.* — No, I'm afraid not.

## Dialogue: Im Bürgeramt

Ana Silva is new in Leipzig and must register her address at the *Bürgeramt* (citizens'
office).

> Herr Krüger: Guten Tag. Haben Sie einen Termin?
>
> Ana: Ja, um zehn Uhr. Ich bin ein bisschen früh. Darf ich hier warten?
>
> Herr Krüger: Natürlich. Aber Sie müssen zuerst dieses Formular ausfüllen.
>
> Ana: Okay. Muss ich alles ausfüllen?
>
> Herr Krüger: Nein, Sie müssen nicht alles ausfüllen. Name, Adresse und Geburtsdatum sind
> wichtig. Und Sie müssen hier unten unterschreiben.
>
> Ana: Gut. Brauchen Sie auch meinen Ausweis?
>
> Herr Krüger: Ja, bitte. Ach, und Sie dürfen hier leider nicht telefonieren. Das ist eine Regel.
>
> Ana: Kein Problem. Soll ich die Tür schließen? Es ist ziemlich laut.
>
> Herr Krüger: Ja, gern. Vielen Dank!

Translation:

> Herr Krüger: Hello. Do you have an appointment?
>
> Ana: Yes, at ten o'clock. I'm a bit early. May I wait here?
>
> Herr Krüger: Of course. But you have to fill in this form first.
>
> Ana: Okay. Do I have to fill in everything?
>
> Herr Krüger: No, you don't have to fill in everything. Name, address and date of birth are
> important. And you have to sign down here.
>
> Ana: Fine. Do you need my ID too?
>
> Herr Krüger: Yes, please. Oh, and I'm afraid you're not allowed to make phone calls here.
> That's a rule.
>
> Ana: No problem. Shall I close the door? It's quite loud.
>
> Herr Krüger: Yes, please. Thanks a lot!

Notice *Sie müssen nicht alles ausfüllen* (no need) next to *Sie dürfen nicht telefonieren*
(not allowed). *Geburtsdatum* (date of birth) and *Problem* come up again in lesson 23.

## Pronunciation

- *müssen, dürfen*: ü is "ee" with rounded lips. Without the umlaut, *muss* has a short u as in
  "put".
- *muss*: the double s after a vowel tells you the vowel is short.
- *schließen*: ie is a long "ee" and ß is a sharp s: "shlee-sen".
- *Ausweis*: both syllables have a diphthong: au as in "how", ei as in "eye": "OWS-vice".
- *unterschreiben*: the stress is on *schrei*: un-ter-SCHREI-ben, because *unter-* here is not
  a separable prefix. Compare *AUS-füllen*, stressed on the separable prefix.
- *Information*: -tion is said "tsyohn" and carries the stress: in-for-ma-TSYOHN.

## Common mistakes

- Using *nicht müssen* for "must not". *Du musst nicht rauchen* means "you don't have to
  smoke". For a ban: *Du darfst nicht rauchen.*
- Adding endings to ich and er: "ich musse", "er darft". Correct: *ich muss, er darf.*
- Keeping the umlaut in the singular: "ich müss", "ich dürf". Correct: *ich muss, ich darf.*
- Using *man* with a plural verb: "man müssen". *Man* takes the er form: *man muss.*
- Spelling the pronoun with two n's. *Der Mann* is a man; *man* is "one, people".
- Splitting *unterschreiben*: "Ich schreibe unter". It is not separable: *Ich unterschreibe.*

## Key points

- *müssen* = must, have to; *dürfen* = may, be allowed to; *sollen* = should, be supposed to.
- ich and er/sie/es forms: *muss, darf, soll*; no umlaut in the singular.
- *nicht müssen* = don't have to; *nicht dürfen* = mustn't, not allowed.
- *man* + modal for rules: *Hier darf man nicht parken.* *Man* takes the er form.
- Polite requests: *Kann ich …? Darf ich …? Können Sie …?* Offers: *Soll ich …?*
- Signs: *verboten* (forbidden), *erlaubt* (allowed), *geschlossen* (closed).

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Dates, seasons, weather and invitations
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lessons 14 and 15 you learned to make plans and talk about what you can, want and have to
do. To make real plans you also need dates (*am dritten Oktober*), months and seasons
(*im Sommer*), and a way to talk about the weather, which in German conversation is almost as
popular as in English. You will also learn four short prepositions that always take the
accusative, and how to accept or turn down an invitation politely.

## Months and seasons

All months are masculine (*der Januar*) and, like all nouns, written with a capital letter.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Januar* | *Februar* | *März* | *April* |
| *Mai* | *Juni* | *Juli* | *August* |
| *September* | *Oktober* | *November* | *Dezember* |

The seasons (*die Jahreszeiten*) are masculine too: *der Frühling* (spring), *der Sommer*
(summer), *der Herbst* (autumn, fall), *der Winter* (winter).

To say "in" a month or season, use *im*: *im Mai* (in May), *im Winter* (in winter). *Im* is
short for *in dem*; for now just learn *im* + month or season as a chunk.

- *Im Sommer fahre ich gern Fahrrad.* — In summer I like cycling.
- *Mein Bruder hat im Januar Geburtstag.* — My brother's birthday is in January.
- *Ein Jahr hat zwölf Monate.* — A year has twelve months.

In Austria January is *Jänner*. On the phone or over a loudspeaker, some people say *Juno*
for *Juni* and *Julei* for *Juli*, so the two aren't confused.

## Ordinal numbers and dates

An **[[ordinal number]]** says the position in a row: first, second, third. German makes them from
the normal numbers you learned in lesson 3:

| Number | Rule | Ordinal |
|---|---|---|
| 1–19 | number + -te | *zweite, vierte, fünfte, zehnte, zwölfte, neunzehnte* |
| 20 and up | number + -ste | *zwanzigste, einundzwanzigste, dreißigste* |
| irregular | learn these | *erste* (1st), *dritte* (3rd), *siebte* (7th), *achte* (8th) |

*Achte* has just one t, because *acht* already ends in t.

In writing, an ordinal is a number with a full stop: *der 3. Oktober* is read *der dritte
Oktober*. Dates are written day first, then month: *3.10.* or *03.10.2026* is the 3rd of
October, never March 10th.

There are two patterns to learn, and the ending tells them apart:

| Use | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| What's the date? | *der* + ordinal with -e | *Heute ist der erste Mai.* — Today is the first of May. |
| On which day? | *am* + ordinal with -en | *Am ersten Mai habe ich frei.* — On the first of May I'm off. |

To ask: *Welches Datum ist heute?* or, more colloquially, *Der Wievielte ist heute?* — What's
the date today? To ask "when": *Wann …?* and answer with *am*:

- *Wann hast du Geburtstag?* — When is your birthday?
- *Ich habe am zwölften März Geburtstag.* — My birthday is on the twelfth of March.
- *Der Kurs fängt am einundzwanzigsten September an.* — The course starts on the twenty-first of
  September.

German says "I have birthday": *Ich habe Geburtstag* (no article). And on the day itself, you
say *Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!* — Happy birthday!

Years up to 1999 are read in hundreds: 1995 is *neunzehnhundertfünfundneunzig*. From 2000 on
they are read as thousands: 2026 is *zweitausendsechsundzwanzig*. Don't put *in* before a
year: say just *2026* or *im Jahr 2026*.

## The weather

*Das Wetter* is talked about with *es*. With weather verbs, *es* doesn't stand for anything;
it is just a placeholder subject, like "it" in "it's raining". These verbs are called
**[[impersonal verbs]]**, and they are used only with *es*.

- *Es regnet.* — It's raining. (*regnen*)
- *Es schneit.* — It's snowing. (*schneien*)
- *Die Sonne scheint.* — The sun is shining. (*scheinen*)
- *Es ist warm / kalt / heiß / kühl.* — It's warm / cold / hot / cool.
- *Es ist windig.* — It's windy. (from *der Wind*)
- *Es sind 25 Grad.* — It's 25 degrees (Celsius).

To ask: *Wie ist das Wetter heute?* — What's the weather like today?

Nouns for the weather: *die Sonne* (sun), *der Regen* (rain), *der Schnee* (snow), *der Wind*
(wind). *Im Winter gibt es oft Schnee.* — In winter there's often snow.

Remember inversion when you start with a time phrase: *Im Herbst regnet es oft* (not "Im
Herbst es regnet").

## Four accusative prepositions: für, ohne, durch, um

A preposition is a little word like "for" or "through" that links a noun to the rest of the
sentence. In German each preposition decides the case of the noun after it. An
**[[accusative preposition]]** is always followed by the accusative, which you know from lesson 9: only the
masculine changes (*der → den*, *ein → einen*, *mein → meinen*).

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *für* | for | *Das Geschenk ist für meinen Bruder.* — The present is for my brother. |
| *ohne* | without | *Ich gehe nie ohne einen Schirm.* — I never go without an umbrella. |
| *durch* | through | *Wir gehen durch den Park.* — We walk through the park. |
| *um* | at (a time), around | *Die Party fängt um acht an.* — The party starts at eight. |

With feminine, neuter and plural nouns nothing changes: *für die Party, ohne das Auto, für
meine Eltern*. *Ohne* is often used with no article at all: *ohne Jacke* (without a jacket).
You also know a fixed phrase with *für*: *Danke für die Einladung!*

## Invitations

An invitation is *die Einladung* (from *einladen*, lesson 14). Here are ways to answer.

Saying yes:

- *Ja, gern! Ich komme gern.* — Yes, I'd love to. I'd be glad to come.
- *Super, danke für die Einladung!* — Great, thanks for the invitation!

Saying no politely, with a reason:

- *Leider kann ich nicht. Ich muss arbeiten.* — Unfortunately I can't. I have to work.
- *Schade, da habe ich keine Zeit.* — What a pity, I don't have time then.

## A message and two answers

> Hallo Sophie, hallo Tom,
>
> ich habe am 14. Juni Geburtstag. Das ist ein Samstag! Ich möchte im Garten feiern und lade
> euch ein. Die Party fängt um 18 Uhr an. Hoffentlich regnet es nicht! Kommt ihr?
>
> Paula

> Hallo Paula,
>
> danke für die Einladung! Ich komme sehr gern. Ich habe auch schon ein Geschenk für dich.
> Bis Samstag!
>
> Sophie

> Hallo Paula,
>
> leider kann ich nicht kommen. Ich muss am 14. Juni zu meiner Oma fahren. Schade! Aber
> herzlichen Glückwunsch schon jetzt und viel Spaß!
>
> Tom

Translation:

> Hi Sophie, hi Tom, my birthday is on the 14th of June. It's a Saturday! I'd like to
> celebrate in the garden and I'm inviting you. The party starts at 6 p.m. Hopefully it won't
> rain! Are you coming? Paula

> Hi Paula, thanks for the invitation! I'd love to come. I've already got a present for you
> too. See you on Saturday! Sophie

> Hi Paula, unfortunately I can't come. On the 14th of June I have to go to my grandma's. What a
> pity! But happy birthday in advance and have fun! Tom

New in passing: *euch* (you, plural object), *dich* (you, object) — both in lesson 20;
*hoffentlich* (hopefully); *zu meiner Oma* (to my grandma's, lesson 18); *schade* (what a
pity); *bis* (until) from lesson 11.

## Pronunciation

- *Juni* and *Juli*: the J is like English y: "YOO-nee", "YOO-lee".
- *März*: ä as in "bed", and z is "ts": "mehrts".
- *Herbst*: say every consonant: "hairpst" (the b sounds like p at the end of a syllable).
- *August* as a month is stressed on the second syllable: au-GUST.
- *Geburtstag*: stress on *-burts-*: ge-BURTS-tag.
- *regnet*: g before n stays a hard g: "RAYG-net".
- *Schnee* is a long "ay": "shnay"; *schneit* has ei as in "eye": "shnite".

## Common mistakes

- Using *in* with months: "in Mai". Correct: *im Mai*.
- Forgetting the ending after *am*: "am drei Oktober" or "am dritte Oktober". Correct: *am
  dritten Oktober*.
- Saying "erste" for 3rd or "dreite". The irregular ones are *erste, dritte, siebte, achte*.
- Reading 3.10. as March 10th. Germans write day.month.
- Dropping *es*: "Regnet." Weather verbs need *es*: *Es regnet.*
- Using the nominative after *für*: "für der Bruder". *Für* takes the accusative: *für den
  Bruder*.
- "Mein Geburtstag ist im 5. Mai." Use *am* with a date: *Mein Geburtstag ist am 5. Mai.*

## Key points

- Months and seasons are masculine; use *im* with them: *im Juli, im Herbst*.
- Ordinals: 1–19 + -te, 20+ + -ste; irregular *erste, dritte, siebte, achte*.
- Date: *Heute ist der dritte Mai.* On a date: *am dritten Mai*. Written *3. Mai* or *3.5.*
- *Wann hast du Geburtstag? — Am …* and *Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!*
- Weather with *es*: *es regnet, es schneit, es ist kalt*; *die Sonne scheint*.
- *für, ohne, durch, um* always take the accusative: *für den Vater, durch den Park*.
- Accept with *Ich komme gern*, decline with *Leider kann ich nicht …* and a reason.

lessons.title: In the city: places, directions and the imperative
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 4 was about free time, plans and rules. Module 5 takes you out of the door: into town, onto
trains, into a flat and, finally, to the doctor. This first lesson gives you the places you find in
any German town, the words for giving and following directions, and a new verb form, the
**[[imperative]]**, which you use to tell or ask someone to do something: *Gehen Sie geradeaus!* — Go
straight ahead! *Nimm die zweite Straße links!* — Take the second street on the left!

You already know most of the pieces. The imperative is built from the present-tense forms you
learned in lesson 4, and the stem changes from lesson 13 (*nehmen → du nimmst*) come back here.
Separable verbs from lesson 12 behave exactly as they do in statements: the prefix goes to the end.

## Places in town

Learn every place with its article; you'll need the gender in the next lesson.

| German | English | German | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *die Straße* | street, road | *die Kirche* | church |
| *der Platz* | square, place | *der Park* | park |
| *die Bank* | bank | *die Brücke* | bridge |
| *die Post* | post office | *das Zentrum* | centre, town centre |
| *die Apotheke* | pharmacy | *die Haltestelle* | stop (bus, tram) |
| *das Krankenhaus* | hospital | *die Ecke* | corner |
| *das Hotel* | hotel | *die Ampel* | traffic lights |
| *das Restaurant* | restaurant | *der Stadtplan* | city map |
| *das Café* | café | *der Weg* | way, path |
| *das Museum* | museum | | |

To ask whether something exists nearby, use *es gibt* (lesson 10) with the accusative:

- *Gibt es hier in der Nähe eine Apotheke?* — Is there a pharmacy nearby?
- *Gibt es hier einen Park?* — Is there a park here?
- *Im Zentrum gibt es viele Cafés.* — There are lots of cafés in the town centre.

To ask where a particular place is, use *Wo ist …?*:

- *Entschuldigung, wo ist die Post?* — Excuse me, where is the post office?
- *Wo ist hier ein Hotel?* — Where is there a hotel around here?

*In der Nähe* (nearby) is a fixed chunk; learn it as a whole. *Im Zentrum* means "in the centre";
you'll see why *in dem* becomes *im* in lesson 19.

## Directions: links, rechts, geradeaus

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *links* | (on the) left |
| *rechts* | (on the) right |
| *geradeaus* | straight ahead, straight on |
| *die erste / zweite / dritte Straße* | the first / second / third street |
| *an der Ampel* | at the traffic lights |
| *an der Ecke* | on the corner |
| *bis zur Ampel* | as far as the traffic lights |
| *weit* | far |
| *nah* | near, close |
| *zu Fuß* | on foot |
| *gegenüber* | opposite, across the street |

Some examples:

- *Die Bank ist links.* — The bank is on the left.
- *Das Hotel ist nicht weit. Sie können zu Fuß gehen.* — The hotel isn't far. You can walk.
- *Der Park ist ganz nah.* — The park is very close.
- *Die Apotheke ist direkt gegenüber.* — The pharmacy is directly opposite.
- *Die Post ist gegenüber der Kirche.* — The post office is opposite the church.
- *Biegen Sie an der Ecke rechts ab.* — Turn right at the corner.

*An der Ampel*, *an der Ecke*, *bis zur Ampel* and *gegenüber der Kirche* use the dative case,
which you'll learn properly in lessons 18 and 19. For now, treat them as ready-made chunks.

### Asking the way: Wie komme ich zum …?

The standard question is *Wie komme ich zum … / zur …?* — How do I get to the …?

- *Wie komme ich zum Museum?* — How do I get to the museum?
- *Wie komme ich zum Bahnhof?* — How do I get to the station? (*der Bahnhof*, station)
- *Wie komme ich zur Post?* — How do I get to the post office?

Use *zum* before masculine and neuter places and *zur* before feminine places. That's why you
learn the gender with every noun. Lesson 18 explains where *zum* and *zur* come from (*zu dem*,
*zu der*). If you want someone to show you the way, say *Können Sie mir den Weg zeigen?* — Can you
show me the way? (*mir* = me, to me; more in lesson 20.)

## The imperative: telling people what to do

German has three imperative forms, one for each way of saying "you": *du*, *ihr* and *Sie*. In all
three, the verb comes first.

### The Sie form: the polite imperative
