Take the *Sie* form of the present tense and swap the order: verb first, then *Sie*.

| Statement | Imperative |
|---|---|
| *Sie gehen geradeaus.* | *Gehen Sie geradeaus!* — Go straight ahead! |
| *Sie nehmen die erste Straße.* | *Nehmen Sie die erste Straße!* — Take the first street! |
| *Sie warten hier.* | *Warten Sie hier!* — Wait here! |

The *Sie* is never dropped. It looks like a yes/no question (*Gehen Sie geradeaus?*); your voice
falls at the end of an instruction instead of rising, and in writing you use *!* or a full stop.

### The du form: drop the pronoun and the ending

Start from the *du* form, drop *du*, and drop the ending *-st* (or just *-t* when the stem ends in
*s*, *ß* or *z*):

| Infinitive | du form | du imperative |
|---|---|---|
| *gehen* | *du gehst* | *Geh!* — Go! |
| *kommen* | *du kommst* | *Komm!* — Come! |
| *zeigen* | *du zeigst* | *Zeig!* — Show! |
| *warten* | *du wartest* | *Warte!* — Wait! |
| *finden* | *du findest* | *Finde!* — Find! |
| *nehmen* | *du nimmst* | *Nimm!* — Take! |
| *sprechen* | *du sprichst* | *Sprich!* — Speak! |
| *lesen* | *du liest* | *Lies!* — Read! |
| *essen* | *du isst* | *Iss!* — Eat! |

Two details:

1. e → i and e → ie verbs keep their change: *nimm*, *sprich*, *lies*, *iss*, *gib*, *hilf*.
   This is why starting from the *du* form works so well.
2. a → ä verbs lose the umlaut: *du fährst → Fahr!*, *du schläfst → Schlaf gut!* — Sleep well!

Verbs whose stem ends in *-t* or *-d* keep an *-e*: *Warte!*, *Finde!*, *Antworte!* — Answer!
With other verbs you may also see an *-e* in careful writing (*Gehe!*, *Komme!*), but in everyday
speech the short form is normal.

### The ihr form: the ihr verb without ihr

For two or more friends, use the normal *ihr* form and drop *ihr*:

| ihr form | ihr imperative |
|---|---|
| *ihr geht* | *Geht!* — Go! |
| *ihr nehmt* | *Nehmt den Bus!* — Take the bus! (*der Bus*, bus) |
| *ihr fahrt* | *Fahrt langsam!* — Drive slowly! |
| *ihr wartet* | *Wartet hier!* — Wait here! |

No stem change appears in the *ihr* imperative, because there is none in the *ihr* form.

### sein is irregular

| du | ihr | Sie |
|---|---|---|
| *Sei!* | *Seid!* | *Seien Sie!* |

- *Sei bitte pünktlich!* — Please be on time!
- *Seid leise, bitte!* — Please be quiet!
- *Seien Sie vorsichtig!* — Be careful! (*vorsichtig*, careful)

### Separable verbs: the prefix goes to the end

*Abbiegen* (to turn) is a separable verb. In the imperative, the verb part comes first and the
prefix goes to the end, just as in a statement:

- *Biegen Sie an der Ampel links ab!* — Turn left at the lights!
- *Bieg an der Ecke rechts ab!* — Turn right at the corner!
- *Biegt hier ab!* — Turn here!

### Making it polite

An imperative on its own can sound blunt. Add *bitte*, at the start or after the verb:

- *Bitte warten Sie hier.* / *Warten Sie bitte hier.* — Please wait here.
- *Zeig mir bitte den Weg.* — Please show me the way.

The word *mal* (roughly "just") also softens a request: *Komm mal!* — Come here a moment! For a
very polite request, a question with a modal verb (lesson 14) is often better: *Können Sie das
bitte noch einmal sagen?* — Could you say that again, please?

## Dialogue: Wie komme ich zum Museum?

A tourist stops a woman on a square.

> Tourist: Entschuldigung, wie komme ich zum Stadtmuseum?
>
> Frau: Zum Stadtmuseum? Das ist nicht weit. Gehen Sie hier geradeaus bis zur Ampel.
>
> Tourist: Bis zur Ampel, okay.
>
> Frau: An der Ampel biegen Sie links ab. Dann nehmen Sie die zweite Straße rechts.
>
> Tourist: Die zweite Straße rechts. Und dann?
>
> Frau: Dann sehen Sie eine Kirche. Das Museum ist direkt gegenüber.
>
> Tourist: Kann ich zu Fuß gehen?
>
> Frau: Ja, natürlich. Das sind nur zehn Minuten.
>
> Tourist: Gibt es dort auch ein Café?
>
> Frau: Ja, das Museum hat ein Café. Es ist sehr schön.
>
> Tourist: Super, vielen Dank!
>
> Frau: Bitte schön!

*Tourist: Excuse me, how do I get to the city museum? — Woman: To the city museum? It's not far. Go
straight ahead as far as the traffic lights. — Tourist: As far as the lights, OK. — Woman: At the
lights you turn left. Then take the second street on the right. — Tourist: The second street on the
right. And then? — Woman: Then you'll see a church. The museum is directly opposite. — Tourist: Can I
walk? — Woman: Yes, of course. It's only ten minutes. — Tourist: Is there a café there too? — Woman:
Yes, the museum has a café. It's very nice. — Tourist: Great, thanks a lot! — Woman: You're welcome!*

Notice that the woman mixes imperatives (*Gehen Sie*, *nehmen Sie*) with plain statements (*An der
Ampel biegen Sie links ab*). Both are normal ways to give directions.

## A text message: the way to Lena's flat

> Hallo Tom! Unser Haus findest du ganz leicht. Nimm am Platz die erste Straße rechts. Geh dann
> geradeaus bis zur Ecke. Dort ist eine Apotheke. Unser Haus ist gegenüber, Nummer 12. Sei bitte
> pünktlich! Bis später, Lena

*Hi Tom! You'll find our house really easily. At the square, take the first street on the right.
Then go straight ahead as far as the corner. There's a pharmacy there. Our house is opposite,
number 12. Please be on time! See you later, Lena*

## Pronunciation

- *geradeaus*: the stress falls on the last part: ge-ra-de-AUS.
- *Café*: stress on the second syllable, ka-FEE, as in French. *Museum* is mu-ZE-um, and
  *Apotheke* is a-po-TE-ke.
- *Straße*: long *a*; the *ß* is a sharp *s*.
- *gegenüber*: ge-gen-Ü-ber; round your lips for *ü*.
- *rechts*: the *ch* is the soft *ich* sound, then *ts*: [rɛçts]. Don't let it become "rex".

## Common mistakes

- Keeping du in the imperative. *Geh du links!* sounds odd; say *Geh links!* or *Bieg links
  ab!* The pronoun appears only for strong emphasis.
- Dropping Sie. *Gehen geradeaus!* is wrong; you need *Gehen Sie geradeaus!* (An infinitive on
  its own, *Bitte nicht rauchen*, is used only on signs and in instructions.)
- Adding an umlaut. *Fähr langsam!* is wrong. The a → ä verbs drop the umlaut: *Fahr langsam!*
- Forgetting the e → i change. *Nehm den Bus!* is a very common mistake. Say *Nimm den Bus!*
- Leaving -st on the verb. *Nimmst den Bus!* is a statement missing its subject, not an
  imperative.
- Putting the prefix in front. *Abbiegen Sie links!* is wrong; say *Biegen Sie links ab!*
- Using bist for sein. *Bist ruhig!* is wrong. The imperative of *sein* is *Sei ruhig!*
- Mixing up rechts and richtig. *Rechts* means "right" as a direction; *richtig* means
  "right" as in correct.

## Key points

- Places: learn every one with *der/die/das*. Ask with *Wo ist …?*, *Gibt es hier in der Nähe …?*
  and *Wie komme ich zum (der, das nouns) / zur (die nouns) …?*
- Directions: *links*, *rechts*, *geradeaus*, *die erste/zweite Straße*, *weit*, *nah*,
  *zu Fuß*, *gegenüber*.
- Imperative, verb first: *Gehen Sie!* (keep *Sie*), *Geh!* (*du* form without *du* and *-st*),
  *Geht!* (*ihr* form without *ihr*).
- In the *du* imperative, e → i/ie stays (*nimm, lies*), a → ä goes (*fahr*), and *-t/-d* stems
  keep *-e* (*warte*).
- *sein*: *Sei! Seid! Seien Sie!* Separable prefixes go to the end: *Biegen Sie links ab!*
- Add *bitte* to sound polite.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Travel and transport: the dative after prepositions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 17 you asked *Wie komme ich zum Museum?* and heard *an der Ampel* and *bis zur Ecke*, and
you were told to treat them as chunks. This lesson explains them. They use the **[[dative]]**, the
third German case after the nominative (the subject) and the accusative (the direct object, lesson
9). At A1 you meet the dative mostly after certain prepositions, and those prepositions are exactly
the ones you need for travelling: *mit dem Zug* (by train), *zum Bahnhof* (to the station), *nach
Wien* (to Vienna), *seit einem Jahr* (for a year).

Along the way you learn the words for trains, buses, planes, tickets and timetables.

## Getting around

| German | English | German | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *der Bahnhof* | station | *die Fahrkarte* | ticket (bus, train) |
| *der Zug* | train | *das Ticket* | ticket (also plane, concert) |
| *der Bus* | bus | *der Fahrplan* | timetable |
| *die U-Bahn* | underground, subway | *das Gleis* | platform, track |
| *die S-Bahn* | suburban train | *die Abfahrt* | departure |
| *die Straßenbahn* | tram, streetcar | *die Ankunft* | arrival |
| *das Auto* | car | *die Verspätung* | delay |
| *das Taxi* | taxi | *die Reise* | trip, journey |
| *das Flugzeug* | plane | *der Urlaub* | holiday, vacation |
| *der Flughafen* | airport | *der Koffer* | suitcase |

Five useful verbs. All except *fliegen* are separable:

- *abfahren* — to leave, to depart: *Der Zug fährt um 8 Uhr ab.* — The train leaves at 8.
  (Stem change like *fahren*: *du fährst ab, er fährt ab*.)
- *einsteigen* — to get on, to get in: *Bitte schnell einsteigen!* — Please get on quickly!
- *aussteigen* — to get off, to get out: *Wir steigen hier aus.* — We're getting off here.
- *umsteigen* — to change (trains, buses): *Sie müssen in Köln umsteigen.* — You have to change in
  Cologne.
- *fliegen* — to fly: *Ich fliege nach Rom.* — I'm flying to Rome.

## The dative articles

After a dative preposition, the article changes. Compare the nominative (lesson 5) and the dative:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nominative | *der / ein* | *die / eine* | *das / ein* | *die / –* |
| dative | *dem / einem* | *der / einer* | *dem / einem* | *den / –* (+ *n*) |

The same endings appear on *kein* and on the possessives (lesson 6): *keinem, keiner, keinen*;
*meinem Bruder*, *meiner Schwester*, *meinem Kind*, *meinen Eltern*.

Three memory hooks:

1. Masculine and neuter are the same in the dative: both end in *-m*: *dem, einem, meinem*.
   Think "m for masculine and the middle gender".
2. Feminine dative ends in *-r*: *der, einer, meiner*. Yes, *der* is also the masculine nominative;
   the preposition in front tells you which one you have.
3. Plural is *den*, and the noun itself takes an extra *-n* if it doesn't already end in *-n* or *-s*:
   *mit den Kindern*, *seit zwei Jahren*, *zu meinen Freunden*; but *mit den Eltern* (already *-n*)
   and *mit den Autos* (plural in *-s*).

## Prepositions that always take the dative

Seven common prepositions always take the dative, whatever the verb. Learn them as a chant:
*aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu*. (*Gegenüber* from lesson 17 is one too.)

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *aus* | out of, from (origin) | *Er kommt aus dem Bahnhof.* — He's coming out of the station. |
| *bei* | at (someone's place), at (a company), near | *Ich wohne bei meinen Eltern.* — I live with my parents. |
| *mit* | with, by (transport) | *Ich fahre mit dem Bus.* — I go by bus. |
| *nach* | to (cities, countries); after | *Wir fliegen nach Spanien.* — We're flying to Spain. |
| *seit* | since, for (time up to now) | *Ich lerne seit einem Monat Deutsch.* — I've been learning German for a month. |
| *von* | from, of | *Ich komme von der Arbeit.* — I'm coming from work. |
| *zu* | to (people, buildings, places) | *Ich gehe zu meiner Freundin.* — I'm going to my girlfriend's. |

You already know *aus* (*Ich komme aus Kanada*) and *von … bis* (lesson 11), and *nach* meaning
"after" (*nach dem Frühstück* — after breakfast). Same word, same dative.

### Contractions: zum, zur, vom, beim

Some preposition + article pairs are almost always fused into one word, a **[[contraction]]**:

| Long form | Contraction | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *zu dem* | *zum* | *zum Bahnhof, zum Flughafen, zum Hotel* |
| *zu der* | *zur* | *zur Haltestelle, zur Post, zur Arbeit* |
| *von dem* | *vom* | *vom Bahnhof, vom Hotel* |
| *bei dem* | *beim* | *beim Arzt, beim Frühstück* (at breakfast) |

So *Wie komme ich zum Museum?* is really *zu dem Museum*, and *zur Post* is *zu der Post*. Use the
contraction in normal speech; the long form only stresses "that particular one". There is no
contraction for *mit dem* or *aus dem*.

### mit for transport

*Mit* + dative is how you say how you travel:

- *mit dem Zug / Bus / Auto / Taxi / Fahrrad* — by train / bus / car / taxi / bike
- *mit der U-Bahn / S-Bahn / Straßenbahn* — by underground / suburban train / tram
- *mit dem Flugzeug* — by plane (but usually just *fliegen*)

On foot is different: *zu Fuß* (no article). *Ich gehe zu Fuß.* — I'm walking.

### nach, zu or in?

English uses "to" for everything; German chooses:

- *nach* + towns, cities and countries without an article: *nach Berlin*, *nach Österreich*, *nach
  Italien*. And the set phrase *nach Hause* — (to) home: *Ich gehe jetzt nach Hause.*
- *zu* + people and places with an article: *zu Anna*, *zum Arzt*, *zur Bank*, *zum Bahnhof*.
- Countries that have an article (*die Schweiz*, *die Türkei*, *die USA*) take *in* + accusative:
  *in die Schweiz*, *in die USA*. Learn these as chunks for now.

This table shows "where to", "where" and "where from" side by side. *Wohin?* means "where to?":

| *Wohin?* (where to) | *Wo?* (where) | *Woher?* (where from) |
|---|---|---|
| *zum Arzt* | *beim Arzt* | *vom Arzt* |
| *zu Anna* | *bei Anna* | *von Anna* |
| *nach Berlin* | *in Berlin* | *aus Berlin* |
| *nach Hause* | *zu Hause* | *von zu Hause* |

*Aus* is for coming out of somewhere or for where you are from; *von* is for the place or person
you've just left: *Ich komme aus Berlin* (I'm from Berlin) but *Ich komme vom Bahnhof* (I've just
come from the station).

### seit with the present tense

*Seit* describes something that started in the past and is still going on. German uses the present
tense here, where English uses "have been":

- *Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren in Köln.* — I've been living in Cologne for two years.
- *Wir warten seit zehn Minuten.* — We've been waiting for ten minutes.
- *Er ist seit Montag im Urlaub.* — He's been on holiday since Monday.

## A text: Marks Weg zur Arbeit

> Ich heiße Mark und wohne seit drei Jahren in Köln. Ich arbeite bei einer Firma im Zentrum. Jeden
> Morgen fahre ich mit dem Fahrrad zum Bahnhof. Dort nehme ich die S-Bahn. Ich steige am Neumarkt aus
> und gehe zu Fuß zum Büro. Nach der Arbeit gehe ich oft zu meinen Freunden. Am Wochenende fahre ich
> mit dem Zug nach Bonn, zu meinen Eltern.

*My name is Mark and I've been living in Cologne for three years. I work for a company in the town
centre. Every morning I cycle to the station. There I take the S-Bahn. I get off at Neumarkt and walk
to the office. After work I often go to my friends' place. At the weekend I take the train to Bonn,
to my parents'.* (*jeden Morgen* — every morning.)

## Dialogue: Am Bahnhof

Anna is at the ticket counter in Stuttgart.

> Anna: Guten Tag. Eine Fahrkarte nach Salzburg, bitte.
>
> Mitarbeiter: Einfach oder hin und zurück?
>
> Anna: Hin und zurück, bitte. Für heute.
>
> Mitarbeiter: Der nächste Zug fährt um 10:15 Uhr ab, von Gleis 7.
>
> Anna: Muss ich umsteigen?
>
> Mitarbeiter: Ja, Sie steigen in München um. Die Ankunft in Salzburg ist um 13:40 Uhr.
>
> Anna: Hat der Zug heute Verspätung?
>
> Mitarbeiter: Nein, im Moment nicht. Das macht 96 Euro, bitte.
>
> Anna: Kann ich mit Karte bezahlen?
>
> Mitarbeiter: Natürlich. Hier ist Ihre Fahrkarte. Gute Reise!

*Anna: Hello. A ticket to Salzburg, please. — Clerk: Single or return? — Anna: Return, please. For
today. — Clerk: The next train leaves at 10:15, from platform 7. — Anna: Do I have to change? —
Clerk: Yes, you change in Munich. Arrival in Salzburg is at 13:40. — Anna: Is the train delayed
today? — Clerk: No, not at the moment. That's 96 euros, please. — Anna: Can I pay by card? — Clerk:
Of course. Here's your ticket. Have a good trip!*

*Hin und zurück* means "there and back" (a return ticket); *einfach* here means "one way";
*nächste* means "next". *Gute Reise!* is what you wish anyone who is setting off.

## Pronunciation

- *Zug*: the *z* is always *ts*, and the final *g* sounds like *k*: [tsuːk].
- *Bahnhof*: the *h* after *a* is silent and only makes the vowel long; the stress is on BAHN.
- *Flughafen*: *Flug* ends in a *k* sound; stress on *Flug*.
- *U-Bahn* and *S-Bahn*: say the letters the German way: "oo-bahn", "ess-bahn".
- *Gleis*: *ei* rhymes with English "rice": [glaɪs].
- Separable verbs are stressed on the prefix: UM-steigen, AUS-steigen, AB-fahren.

## Common mistakes

- Using the nominative after a dative preposition: *mit der Bus* is wrong; *Bus* is masculine, so
  it's *mit dem Bus*.
- Using the accusative because English has no case: *mit den Zug* is wrong; it's *mit dem Zug*.
- Forgetting the plural *-n*: *mit den Freunde* should be *mit den Freunden*.
- Saying *zu Berlin* or *nach dem Arzt*. Cities and countries take *nach*; people and places with an
  article take *zu*: *nach Berlin*, *zum Arzt*.
- Saying *Ich gehe zu Hause*. Going home is *nach Hause*; being at home is *zu Hause*.
- Translating "for" with *für* for time up to now: *Ich wohne hier für zwei Jahre* is English word
  for word. Say *Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren hier.*
- Writing *zu dem* and *bei dem* in ordinary sentences. Use *zum* and *beim*.

## Key points

- The dative articles: *dem/einem* (masculine and neuter), *der/einer* (feminine), *den* + *-n*
  (plural). *Kein* and possessives follow the same pattern.
- Always dative: *aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu* (and *gegenüber*).
- Contractions: *zum* (*zu dem*), *zur* (*zu der*), *vom* (*von dem*), *beim* (*bei dem*).
- Travel: *mit dem Zug*, *mit der U-Bahn*, but *zu Fuß*.
- To: *nach* + cities and countries, *zu* + people and places, *nach Hause*. At home: *zu Hause*.
- *Seit* + present tense: *Ich wohne seit einem Jahr hier.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: At home: rooms, furniture and where things are
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 18 you learned the dative articles (*dem, der, dem, den*) after prepositions like *mit*
and *zu*. This lesson uses the same dative for a new job: saying where something is. *Der Schlüssel
ist auf dem Tisch.* — The key is on the table. *Wir sind im Wohnzimmer.* — We're in the living room.

You'll also learn the rooms and furniture of a flat, how to talk about rent, and how to refer to a
thing with *er*, *sie* or *es*, or *ihn* in the accusative: *Der Schrank? Ich finde ihn schön.*

## Rooms and furniture

| German | English | German | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *die Wohnung* | flat, apartment | *das Sofa* | sofa, couch |
| *das Haus* | house | *der Schrank* | cupboard, wardrobe |
| *das Zimmer* | room | *das Regal* | shelf, bookcase |
| *die Küche* | kitchen | *der Kühlschrank* | fridge |
| *das Bad* | bathroom | *die Wand* | wall |
| *das Wohnzimmer* | living room | *der Boden* | floor (that you walk on) |
| *das Schlafzimmer* | bedroom | *die Treppe* | stairs, staircase |
| *der Balkon* | balcony | *der Stock* | floor, storey |
| *der Garten* | garden, yard | *die Miete* | rent |

From earlier lessons you already know *der Tisch*, *der Stuhl*, *die Lampe*, *das Fenster*, *die Tür*
(lesson 5) and *das Bett* (lesson 12).

Two useful facts about German flats:

- A *Drei-Zimmer-Wohnung* (three-room flat) has three rooms plus a kitchen and a bathroom. The
  kitchen and bathroom aren't counted.
- Floors are counted from the ground floor, *das Erdgeschoss*. So *im ersten Stock* is the first
  floor in British English but the second floor in American English.

Describing a flat uses adjectives after *sein* (lesson 8): *hell* (bright, light), *dunkel* (dark),
*modern* (modern), *ruhig* (quiet), *gemütlich* (cosy, comfortable). *Gemütlich* is a favourite
German word: a room that is warm, relaxed and pleasant to be in.

To say what a flat has, use *es gibt* or *haben* with the accusative (lesson 9):

- *Die Wohnung hat einen Balkon.* — The flat has a balcony.
- *In der Küche gibt es einen Kühlschrank.* — There's a fridge in the kitchen.
- *Es gibt leider keinen Garten.* — Unfortunately there's no garden.

The verb *mieten* means to rent: *Wir mieten eine Wohnung.* — We're renting a flat. And *zu Hause*
means at home: *Ich bin heute zu Hause.* — I'm at home today.

## Where is it? Prepositions + dative

To say where something is, answer the question *Wo?* with one of these prepositions and the
dative:

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *in* | in, inside | *Die Milch ist im Kühlschrank.* — The milk is in the fridge. |
| *an* | on (a vertical surface), at, by | *Das Foto ist an der Wand.* — The photo is on the wall. |
| *auf* | on (top of) | *Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch.* — The book is on the table. |
| *unter* | under, below | *Die Katze ist unter dem Bett.* — The cat is under the bed. |
| *über* | over, above | *Die Lampe ist über dem Tisch.* — The lamp is above the table. |
| *neben* | next to, beside | *Das Regal ist neben dem Schrank.* — The shelf is next to the cupboard. |
| *zwischen* | between | *Der Stuhl ist zwischen dem Sofa und dem Fenster.* — The chair is between the sofa and the window. |
| *hinter* | behind | *Der Garten ist hinter dem Haus.* — The garden is behind the house. |
| *vor* | in front of | *Das Taxi ist vor dem Haus.* — The taxi is in front of the house. |

You know *vor* from lesson 11 as "before" (*vor dem Essen*); with places it means "in front of".

These nine prepositions are called **[[two-way prepositions]]**. With *Wo?* (location, no movement),
they take the dative. With *Wohin?* (movement to a place), they take the accusative: *Ich lege das
Buch auf den Tisch* (I put the book onto the table). That second use is for later; at A1 you only
need location, so: *Wo?* → dative.

### Contractions: im and am

Just as *zu dem* becomes *zum*, two more pairs fuse:

| Long form | Contraction | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *in dem* | *im* | *im Wohnzimmer, im Bad, im Garten, im ersten Stock* |
| *an dem* | *am* | *am Fenster, am Tisch* |

Feminine nouns have no contraction: *in der Küche*, *an der Wand*, *an der Tür*.

### in, an or auf?

English often says "on" or "at" where German makes a finer choice:

- *auf* — on top of a horizontal surface: *auf dem Tisch*, *auf dem Sofa*, *auf dem Boden*, *auf dem
  Balkon*.
- *an* — touching a vertical surface, or right next to an edge: *an der Wand*, *am Fenster*, *an der
  Tür*.
- *in* — inside something closed or a room: *im Schrank*, *in der Küche*, *im Garten*.

*Im Garten* but *auf dem Balkon*: a garden is an area you are inside; a balcony is a platform you
stand on.

## Pronouns for things: er, sie, es and ihn

In English every thing is "it". In German, a pronoun takes the gender of the noun it replaces, so a
table is "he" and a lamp is "she":

| Noun | Nominative (subject) | Accusative (object) |
|---|---|---|
| *der Schrank* | *er* | *ihn* |
| *die Lampe* | *sie* | *sie* |
| *das Sofa* | *es* | *es* |
| *die Stühle* (plural) | *sie* | *sie* |

Only the masculine changes in the accusative: *er → ihn*, just as *der → den*.

- *Wo ist der Schlüssel? — Er ist auf dem Tisch.* — Where's the key? It's on the table.
- *Wie findest du den Schrank? — Ich finde ihn toll.* — What do you think of the cupboard? I think
  it's great.
- *Die Wohnung ist schön. Ich möchte sie mieten.* — The flat is nice. I'd like to rent it.
- *Das Regal ist neu. Ich finde es praktisch.* — The shelf is new. I find it practical.

*Wie findest du …? — Ich finde … + adjective* is the normal way to ask for and give an opinion.

## A text: Mein Zimmer

> Ich wohne in einer Wohnung im zweiten Stock. Mein Zimmer ist klein, aber hell und gemütlich. Das
> Bett ist an der Wand, neben dem Fenster. Unter dem Bett ist mein Koffer. Der Schrank ist hinter der
> Tür. Über dem Tisch ist eine Lampe, und auf dem Regal sind viele Bücher. Am liebsten bin ich aber im
> Wohnzimmer auf dem Sofa.

*I live in a flat on the second floor. My room is small but bright and cosy. The bed is against the
wall, next to the window. My suitcase is under the bed. The wardrobe is behind the door. There's a
lamp above the table, and there are lots of books on the shelf. But my favourite place is the living
room, on the sofa.*

## Dialogue: Eine Wohnung besichtigen

Mr Okafor is viewing a flat. The landlady (*die Vermieterin*) shows him round.

> Vermieterin: Guten Tag, Herr Okafor. Kommen Sie herein!
>
> Herr Okafor: Guten Tag. Die Wohnung ist im dritten Stock, oder?
>
> Vermieterin: Ja, und es gibt leider keinen Aufzug. Hier links ist die Küche.
>
> Herr Okafor: Oh, die Küche ist schön hell. Gibt es auch einen Kühlschrank?
>
> Vermieterin: Ja, der Kühlschrank ist dort, neben dem Fenster.
>
> Herr Okafor: Und wo ist das Bad?
>
> Vermieterin: Das Bad ist rechts, zwischen dem Schlafzimmer und dem Wohnzimmer.
>
> Herr Okafor: Das Wohnzimmer ist wirklich gemütlich. Hat die Wohnung einen Balkon?
>
> Vermieterin: Ja, hier hinter der Tür ist der Balkon.
>
> Herr Okafor: Toll! Und wie hoch ist die Miete?
>
> Vermieterin: 930 Euro warm.
>
> Herr Okafor: Ich finde die Wohnung super. Ich möchte sie mieten!

*Landlady: Hello, Mr Okafor. Come in! — Mr Okafor: Hello. The flat is on the third floor, isn't it? —
Landlady: Yes, and unfortunately there's no lift. Here on the left is the kitchen. — Mr Okafor: Oh,
the kitchen is nice and bright. Is there a fridge too? — Landlady: Yes, the fridge is over there,
next to the window. — Mr Okafor: And where's the bathroom? — Landlady: The bathroom is on the right,
between the bedroom and the living room. — Mr Okafor: The living room is really cosy. Does the flat
have a balcony? — Landlady: Yes, the balcony is here behind the door. — Mr Okafor: Great! And how
much is the rent? — Landlady: 930 euros including heating and bills. — Mr Okafor: I think the flat
is great. I'd like to rent it!*

*Herein* means "in" (into here), *der Aufzug* is the lift (elevator), and *wie hoch* means "how high".
*Warm* rent includes heating and service costs; *kalt* rent doesn't. Always ask which one you are
being told.

## Pronunciation

- *Küche* and *Kuchen* (cake, lesson 9) are a famous pair. *Küche* has *ü* and the soft *ich*
  sound; *Kuchen* has *u* and the throaty *ach* sound.
- *Regal*: stress on the second syllable, re-GAAL. *Balkon* is stressed on *-kon*; many Germans say
  it like French, bal-KONG.
- *gemütlich*: ge-MÜT-lich, long *ü*, soft *ch* at the end.
- *Kühlschrank*: long *ü* (the *h* makes it long), then *sch*.
- *zwischen*: *z* = *ts*, then *w* = English *v*: TSVI-shen.

## Common mistakes

- Using the nominative or accusative for location: *Das Buch ist auf der Tisch* or *auf den Tisch* is
  wrong. *Tisch* is masculine, so: *auf dem Tisch*.
- Using *es* for every thing: *Der Schrank ist groß. Es ist neu.* should be *Er ist neu.*
- Forgetting *ihn*: *Ich finde er schön* is wrong; the object form is *Ich finde ihn schön.*
- Saying *auf der Wand*: pictures hang *an der Wand*. *Auf* is for horizontal surfaces.
- Writing *in dem* and *an dem* where Germans say *im* and *am*.
- Mixing up *der Boden* (the floor you stand on) and *der Stock* (a storey of a building).

## Key points

- *Wo?* + *in, an, auf, unter, über, neben, zwischen, hinter, vor* + dative: *auf dem Tisch*, *an der
  Wand*, *im Bad*.
- Contractions: *im* = *in dem*, *am* = *an dem*; none for feminine *in der*, *an der*.
- *Auf* = on top, *an* = on a wall or at an edge, *in* = inside.
- Pronouns follow the noun's gender: *der Schrank → er / ihn*, *die Lampe → sie*, *das Sofa → es*.
- *Wie findest du …? — Ich finde ihn/sie/es …* for opinions.
- A *Drei-Zimmer-Wohnung* has three rooms plus kitchen and bathroom; *im ersten Stock* is one floor up.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Body, health and personal pronouns
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Sooner or later every traveller needs a pharmacy or a doctor. This last lesson of module 5 gives
you the parts of the body, ways to say what hurts (*Ich habe Kopfschmerzen. Mein Rücken tut weh.*),
and the phone call for a doctor's appointment.

It also completes the personal pronouns. You know the subject pronouns (*ich, du, er …*) from
lesson 4 and met *ihn* for things in lesson 19. Here you get the full set of object pronouns: *mich,
dich, ihn …* in the accusative and *mir, dir, ihm …* in the dative, the dative ones mostly as
ready-made chunks like *Wie geht es dir?* and *Kannst du mir helfen?*

## The body

| German | English | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| *der Körper* | body | *die Körper* |
| *der Kopf* | head | *die Köpfe* |
| *das Auge* | eye | *die Augen* |
| *das Ohr* | ear | *die Ohren* |
| *die Nase* | nose | *die Nasen* |
| *der Mund* | mouth | *die Münder* |
| *der Zahn* | tooth | *die Zähne* |
| *der Hals* | neck, throat | *die Hälse* |
| *der Arm* | arm | *die Arme* |
| *die Hand* | hand | *die Hände* |
| *der Bauch* | stomach, belly | *die Bäuche* |
| *der Rücken* | back | *die Rücken* |
| *das Bein* | leg | *die Beine* |
| *der Fuß* | foot | *die Füße* |

Many body parts come in pairs, so learn the plurals too: *zwei Augen, zwei Ohren, zwei Hände, zwei
Füße*. Note *der Hals*: it is both the outside (neck) and the inside (throat).

## Saying what's wrong

There are three common patterns. Learn them as chunks.

### 1. Ich habe … Schmerzen / Fieber

*Die Schmerzen* means pain or pains. Put a body part in front and you get a compound noun, which is
almost always plural:

- *Ich habe Kopfschmerzen.* — I have a headache.
- *Ich habe Bauchschmerzen.* — I have a stomach ache.
- *Er hat Rückenschmerzen.* — He has back pain.
- *Sie hat Halsschmerzen.* — She has a sore throat.
- *Ich habe Zahnschmerzen.* — I have toothache.
- *Das Kind hat Fieber.* — The child has a temperature.

### 2. … tut weh / … tun weh

*Wehtun* (to hurt) is a separable verb: *weh* goes to the end. Use *tut* for one body part and
*tun* for several:

- *Mein Kopf tut weh.* — My head hurts.
- *Meine Füße tun weh.* — My feet hurt.
- *Tut dein Arm noch weh?* — Does your arm still hurt?

You'll often hear the same idea with a dative pronoun: *Mir tut der Rücken weh.* — My back hurts
(literally "To me the back hurts").

### 3. Mir geht es … / Mir ist …

How you feel uses the dative *mir* (to me), not *ich*:

- *Mir geht es nicht gut.* — I'm not well.
- *Mir ist kalt.* — I'm cold. (*Ich bin kalt* would describe your character.)
- *Mir ist schlecht.* — I feel sick.

And the simple adjectives: *Ich bin krank.* — I'm ill. *Ich bin wieder gesund.* — I'm healthy
again. When someone is ill, say *Gute Besserung!* — Get well soon!

## Personal pronouns in the accusative

When a person is the direct object, use an **[[accusative pronoun]]**:

| Nominative | Accusative | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *ich* | *mich* | *Verstehen Sie mich?* — Do you understand me? |
| *du* | *dich* | *Ich rufe dich morgen an.* — I'll call you tomorrow. |
| *er* | *ihn* | *Kennst du ihn?* — Do you know him? |
| *sie* | *sie* | *Ich sehe sie jeden Tag.* — I see her every day. |
| *es* | *es* | *Das Radio ist laut. Hörst du es?* — The radio is loud. Can you hear it? |
| *wir* | *uns* | *Holst du uns ab?* — Will you pick us up? |
| *ihr* | *euch* | *Ich lade euch ein.* — I'm inviting you. |
| *sie* | *sie* | *Die Kinder sind krank. Ich bringe sie zum Arzt.* — The children are ill. I'm taking them to the doctor. |
| *Sie* | *Sie* | *Ich verstehe Sie nicht.* — I don't understand you. |

Only four are new words: *mich, dich, uns, euch*, plus *ihn*, which you know. The others look the same
as the nominative.

## Personal pronouns in the dative

A **[[dative pronoun]]** is used after dative prepositions (*mit mir*, *zu dir*, *bei uns*), with some
verbs, and for the person who receives something:

| Nominative | Dative | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *ich* | *mir* | *Kannst du mir helfen?* — Can you help me? |
| *du* | *dir* | *Wie geht es dir?* — How are you? |
| *er* | *ihm* | *Wie geht es ihm?* — How is he? |
| *sie* | *ihr* | *Ich fahre mit ihr.* — I'm going with her. |
| *es* | *ihm* | *Das Baby hat Fieber. Wie geht es ihm?* — The baby has a temperature. How is it? |
| *wir* | *uns* | *Kommst du zu uns?* — Are you coming to our place? |
| *ihr* | *euch* | *Ich fahre mit euch.* — I'm going with you. |
| *sie* | *ihnen* | *Wir wohnen bei ihnen.* — We live with them. |
| *Sie* | *Ihnen* | *Wie geht es Ihnen?* — How are you? (formal) |

*Uns* and *euch* are the same in both cases. *Helfen* always takes the dative: *Hilf mir!* — Help
me!

The person who receives something is the **[[indirect object]]**, and it is in the dative. The thing
given is the direct object, in the accusative:

- *Gib mir bitte das Medikament.* — Please give me the medicine.
- *Zeig mir deine Hand.* — Show me your hand.
- *Ich gebe dir eine Tablette.* — I'll give you a tablet.

At A1 you don't need to master the dative. Learn these chunks well: *Wie geht es dir/Ihnen?*, *Mir
geht es gut*, *Kannst du mir helfen?*, *Mir ist kalt*, *Mir tut … weh*, *Gib mir …*, *mit mir*.

## Dialogue: Einen Termin machen

Leon calls a doctor's practice (*die Praxis*).

> Praxis: Praxis Dr. Weber, guten Morgen.
>
> Leon: Guten Morgen, mein Name ist Leon Brandt. Mir geht es nicht gut. Kann ich heute kommen?
>
> Praxis: Was fehlt Ihnen denn?
>
> Leon: Ich habe seit gestern Fieber, und mein Hals tut sehr weh.
>
> Praxis: Haben Sie auch Kopfschmerzen?
>
> Leon: Ja, ein bisschen.
>
> Praxis: Können Sie um 11:30 Uhr kommen?
>
> Leon: Ja, das geht. Vielen Dank.
>
> Praxis: Bringen Sie bitte Ihre Versichertenkarte mit. Bis später, Herr Brandt.
>
> Leon: Bis später. Auf Wiederhören!

*Practice: Dr Weber's practice, good morning. — Leon: Good morning, my name is Leon Brandt. I'm not
well. Can I come today? — Practice: What's the matter? — Leon: I've had a temperature since
yesterday, and my throat really hurts. — Practice: Do you have a headache too? — Leon: Yes, a bit. —
Practice: Can you come at 11:30? — Leon: Yes, that works. Thanks a lot. — Practice: Please bring your
health insurance card. See you later, Mr Brandt. — Leon: See you later. Goodbye!*

*Was fehlt Ihnen?* (What's the matter with you?) is a fixed question from doctors; *die
Versichertenkarte* is your health insurance card; *mitbringen* means to bring along; *Auf
Wiederhören!* is goodbye on the phone.

## At the doctor's

> Der Arzt untersucht Leon und sagt: „Sie haben eine Erkältung. Nehmen Sie dreimal am Tag eine
> Tablette und trinken Sie viel Tee. Bleiben Sie zwei Tage zu Hause und rufen Sie mich am Freitag an.
> Gute Besserung!"

*The doctor examines Leon and says: "You have a cold. Take a tablet three times a day and
drink lots of tea. Stay at home for two days and call me on Friday. Get well soon!"* (*untersuchen* — to
examine; *die Erkältung* — a cold; *dreimal* — three times.)

Notice the *Sie* imperatives from lesson 17: the doctor's instructions are all verb-first.

## Pronunciation

- *Bauch*: *au* as in "how", then the throaty *ach* sound. *Kopf*: say both *p* and *f*.
- *Auge*: OW-geh. *Ohr*: one long *o*. *Zahn*: *ts* + long *a*.
- *Rücken*: short *ü*; *Fieber*: long *ie*, like "fever" with an *ee*.
- *Medikament* is stressed on the last syllable, me-di-ka-MENT; *Tablette* on the middle, ta-BLET-te.
- *mich*, *dich*: soft *ich* sound; *mir*, *dir*: long *i*, the *r* almost a vowel, "meer", "deer".

## Common mistakes

- *Ich habe einen Kopfschmerz* sounds odd. Say *Ich habe Kopfschmerzen* (plural).
- *Ich bin kalt* means you are a cold person. Say *Mir ist kalt.*
- *Mich geht es gut* is wrong; it's *Mir geht es gut* (dative).
- *Kannst du mich helfen?* is wrong; *helfen* takes the dative: *Kannst du mir helfen?*
- *Mein Kopf wehtut* or *Meine Füße tut weh*: *tun* is the verb, so it's in position 2 and agrees
  with the subject: *Mein Kopf tut weh. Meine Füße tun weh.*
- Mixing up *mich* (accusative) and *mir* (dative): *Ruf mich an* (accusative) but *Gib mir das
  Buch* (dative).

## Key points

- Body parts with articles and plurals: *der Kopf, das Auge (die Augen), der Fuß (die Füße)* …
- *Ich habe Kopfschmerzen / Fieber.* — *Mein Bauch tut weh. Meine Füße tun weh.*
- *Mir geht es nicht gut. Mir ist kalt. Mir ist schlecht.* — *Gute Besserung!*
- Accusative: *mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie*.
- Dative: *mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen*; *helfen* and dative prepositions
  take the dative.
- The person who receives is the indirect object, in the dative: *Gib mir das Buch.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Talking about the past: the perfect with haben
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Until now every sentence in this course has been about the present or the future: what you
do, what you can do, what you will do tomorrow. In this module you finally learn to talk
about the past: what you did at the weekend, where you went on holiday, what happened.

Spoken German uses one main past tense for almost everything: the **[[perfect tense]]**
(*das Perfekt*). This lesson shows you how to build it with *haben*, which is the auxiliary
for most verbs. Lesson 22 adds the verbs that use *sein* instead, plus the two short past
forms *war* and *hatte*.

The good news: you already know the sentence pattern. The perfect works exactly like the
modal verbs from lesson 14. One verb sits in position 2, and a second verb waits at the end
of the sentence.

## How the perfect is built

The perfect has two parts:

1. a form of *haben* in the present tense (ich habe, du hast, er hat…). This is the
   **[[auxiliary verb]]**: a helper that carries the person and the ending;
2. the **[[past participle]]** of the main verb, which goes to the very end of the sentence and
   never changes.

| | haben (position 2) | … | participle (end) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | habe | Pizza | gegessen. |
| du | hast | ein Buch | gelesen. |
| er/sie/es | hat | gestern | gearbeitet. |
| wir | haben | einen Ausflug | gemacht. |
| ihr | habt | den Film | gesehen. |
| sie/Sie | haben | das Haus | gekauft. |

- *Ich habe Pizza gegessen.* — I ate pizza. / I've eaten pizza.
- *Hat er gestern gearbeitet?* — Did he work yesterday?

English has two tenses here ("I ate" and "I have eaten"), but in
everyday German the perfect covers both. *Ich habe Pizza gegessen* can answer "What did you
have for lunch?" and "Have you ever eaten pizza?" alike. So don't try to match the English
tense: if it happened in the past and you are speaking, use the perfect.

### The sentence bracket again

The two parts form a bracket around the rest of the sentence, just like *kann … spielen* in
lesson 14. Everything else (the object, the time, the place) goes inside.

- *Ich habe am Samstag meine Oma besucht.* — I visited my grandma on Saturday.
- *Am Samstag habe ich meine Oma besucht.* — On Saturday I visited my grandma.
- *Hast du die Postkarte bekommen?* — Did you get the postcard?
- *Was habt ihr am Wochenende gemacht?* — What did you do at the weekend?

When a time phrase starts the sentence, *haben* still stays in position 2 and the subject
follows it (lesson 12). In a yes/no question *haben* moves to position 1. In a W-question
the question word comes first and *haben* second. The participle is always last.

## Building the past participle

### Pattern 1: regular verbs, ge- + stem + -t

Most verbs are **[[weak verbs]]**: their stem doesn't change, and the participle is *ge-* +
stem + *-t*. Take the infinitive, remove *-en*, put *ge-* in front and *-t* at the end.

| infinitive | stem | participle | |
|---|---|---|---|
| machen | mach | gemacht | done, made |
| kaufen | kauf | gekauft | bought |
| spielen | spiel | gespielt | played |
| hören | hör | gehört | heard |
| lernen | lern | gelernt | learned |
| sagen | sag | gesagt | said |
| lachen | lach | gelacht | laughed |
| weinen | wein | geweint | cried |
| glauben | glaub | geglaubt | believed |
| schenken | schenk | geschenkt | given (as a present) |

If the stem ends in *-t* or *-d*, add an extra *e* so you can pronounce it, the same way as
*er arbeitet* in the present:

- *arbeiten* → *gearbeitet* (worked)
- *antworten* → *geantwortet* (answered)
- *warten* → *gewartet* (waited)

Examples:

- *Wir haben viel gelacht.* — We laughed a lot.
- *Das Baby hat die ganze Nacht geweint.* — The baby cried all night.
- *Ich habe meinem Bruder ein Buch geschenkt.* — I gave my brother a book (as a present).
- *Sie hat lange auf den Bus gewartet.* — She waited a long time for the bus.

*Lange* means "for a long time". *Meinem Bruder* is "to my brother", a dative chunk like
*mir* and *dir* in lesson 20.

### Pattern 2: irregular verbs, ge- + stem + -en

**[[Strong verbs]]** end in *-en*, and the vowel often changes. You can't work these out from
the infinitive, so learn each participle with its verb. Here are the ones you need most with
*haben*:

| infinitive | participle | | infinitive | participle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| sehen | gesehen | | schreiben | geschrieben |
| lesen | gelesen | | sprechen | gesprochen |
| essen | gegessen | | nehmen | genommen |
| geben | gegeben | | helfen | geholfen |
| schlafen | geschlafen | | treffen | getroffen |
| waschen | gewaschen | | finden | gefunden |
| trinken | getrunken | | singen | gesungen |

- *Hast du den Film gesehen?* — Have you seen the film?
- *Ich habe meinen Freund im Park getroffen.* — I met my friend in the park.
- *Er hat mir geholfen.* — He helped me.

A memory hook: the verbs that change their vowel in the present (*sieht, liest, isst,
spricht*) are almost always strong, so they end in *-en* in the participle too.

### Pattern 3: mixed verbs

A small group of **[[mixed verbs]]** change the vowel like strong verbs but end in *-t* like weak
ones. At A1 you need four:

| infinitive | participle | |
|---|---|---|
| bringen | gebracht | brought |
| denken | gedacht | thought |
| kennen | gekannt | known (a person or place) |
| wissen | gewusst | known (a fact) |

- *Hast du Brot gebracht?* — Did you bring bread?
- *Das habe ich nicht gewusst!* — I didn't know that!
- *Ich habe an dich gedacht.* — I thought of you.

*Wissen* is also unusual in the present: *ich weiß, du weißt, er/sie/es weiß, wir wissen,
ihr wisst, sie/Sie wissen*. Note that ich and er have the same form, with no *-e* or *-t*.

*Kennen* or *wissen*? Both mean "to know". Use *kennen* for people, places and things you
are familiar with, and *wissen* for facts and information.

- *Kennst du Frau Weber?* — Do you know Ms Weber?
- *Weißt du ihre Telefonnummer?* — Do you know her phone number?
- *Ich kenne Berlin gut.* — I know Berlin well.
- *Das weiß ich nicht.* — I don't know (that).

### Pattern 4: separable verbs, -ge- in the middle

For separable verbs (lesson 12), *ge-* goes between the prefix and the stem, and the whole
participle is written as one word:

| infinitive | participle |
|---|---|
| einkaufen | eingekauft |
| aufräumen | aufgeräumt |
| abholen | abgeholt |
| anrufen | angerufen |
| fernsehen | ferngesehen |
| anfangen | angefangen |
| einladen | eingeladen |
| kennenlernen | kennengelernt |

- *Ich habe gestern eingekauft.* — I went shopping yesterday.
- *Hast du deine Mutter angerufen?* — Did you call your mother?
- *Wir haben Anna im Kurs kennengelernt.* — We got to know (met) Anna on the course.

*Kennenlernen* means "to get to know" or "to meet for the first time". Use *treffen* for
meeting someone you already know.

### Pattern 5: no ge- at all

Two groups of verbs have no *ge-* in the participle.

Verbs ending in *-ieren* end in *-t*: *studieren* → *studiert*, *fotografieren* →
*fotografiert*, *telefonieren* (to talk on the phone) → *telefoniert*.

Verbs with an **[[inseparable prefix]]**. The prefixes *be-*, *ver-*, *er-* (and a few
others such as *ent-* and *ge-*) never separate from the verb, are never stressed, and block
the *ge-*. The participle may be weak or strong.

| infinitive | participle | |
|---|---|---|
| besuchen | besucht | visited |
| bezahlen | bezahlt | paid |
| benutzen | benutzt | used |
| bekommen | bekommen | got, received |
| erzählen | erzählt | told |
| verkaufen | verkauft | sold |
| verstehen | verstanden | understood |
| vergessen | vergessen | forgotten |
| verlieren | verloren | lost |

- *Wir haben das Auto verkauft.* — We sold the car.
- *Ich habe meinen Schlüssel verloren.* — I've lost my key.
- *Hast du das verstanden?* — Did you understand that?
- *Opa hat eine Geschichte erzählt.* — Grandpa told a story.
- *Ich habe den Brief bekommen.* — I got the letter.

A quick test: if you can hear the stress on the first syllable of the verb (*EIN-kaufen*,
*AN-rufen*), the prefix is separable and *ge-* goes inside. If the stress is on the stem
(*be-SU-chen*, *ver-KAU-fen*), there is no *ge-*. *Bekommen* and *vergessen* look the same
in the infinitive and the participle; only the sentence tells you which one it is.

## Time words for the past

These words tell you a sentence is about the past:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| gestern | yesterday |
| vorgestern | the day before yesterday |
| gestern Abend | last night, yesterday evening |
| letzte Woche | last week |
| letzten Montag | last Monday |
| letztes Wochenende | last weekend |
| vor zwei Tagen | two days ago |
| damals | back then, at that time |
| gerade | just (a moment ago) |
| schon | already, ever |

*Letzte* ("last") takes the ending of the noun's gender: *letzte Woche* (die Woche),
*letzten Monat* (der Monat), *letztes Wochenende* (das Wochenende). Learn them as chunks.
*Vor* + a time means "ago" and the time comes after it, not before: *vor drei Jahren*
(three years ago). The *-n* on *Jahren* and *Tagen* is the dative plural; just copy it.

- *Ich habe gerade gegessen.* — I've just eaten.
- *Hast du schon die Hausaufgabe gemacht?* — Have you done the homework yet?
- *Vorgestern habe ich einen Brief geschrieben.* — The day before yesterday I wrote a letter.
- *Damals habe ich in Wien gewohnt.* — Back then I lived in Vienna.

## Dialogue: Monday morning

Lena and Tom work in the same office.

> Lena: Hallo Tom! Na, wie war dein Wochenende?
>
> Tom: Super! Am Samstag habe ich meine Eltern besucht.
>
> Lena: Schön. Was habt ihr gemacht?
>
> Tom: Wir haben einen Ausflug gemacht und im Park ein Picknick gemacht. Mein Vater hat
> viele Geschichten von damals erzählt. Wir haben viel gelacht.
>
> Lena: Und am Sonntag?
>
> Tom: Da habe ich lange geschlafen und dann eingekauft. Aber ich habe mein Handy im
> Supermarkt vergessen!
>
> Lena: Oh nein! Hast du es verloren?
>
> Tom: Nein, eine Verkäuferin hat es gefunden und mich angerufen.
>
> Lena: Da hast du aber Glück gehabt!

Translation:

> Lena: Hi Tom! So, how was your weekend?
>
> Tom: Great! On Saturday I visited my parents.
>
> Lena: Nice. What did you do?
>
> Tom: We went on an outing and had a picnic in the park. My dad told lots of stories from
> the old days. We laughed a lot.
>
> Lena: And on Sunday?
>
> Tom: I slept in and then went shopping. But I left my phone in the supermarket!
>
> Lena: Oh no! Have you lost it?
>
> Tom: No, a shop assistant found it and called me.
>
> Lena: You were lucky there!

Notes: *wie war …?* means "how was …?"; *war* comes in lesson 22. *Glück haben* means "to be
lucky", and its perfect is *Glück gehabt*. German says *ein Handy vergessen* for leaving
something behind by accident.

## Pronunciation

- The prefix *ge-* is never stressed and its *e* is a weak, short sound, like the "a" in
  "about": *ge-MACHT*, *ge-SE-hen*. Stress the stem.
- In *-ieren* verbs the stress is on *-ie-*: *stu-DIERT*, *fo-to-gra-FIERT*.
- *Gewusst* has a short *u* and a sharp *ss*: [gəˈvʊst]. Compare *weiß* with a long
  diphthong and *ß*.

## Common mistakes

- Putting the participle in the middle. *Ich habe gegessen Pizza* is English word order.
  The participle goes last: *Ich habe Pizza gegessen.*
- Adding ge- to inseparable verbs. Not *gebesucht* or *geverkauft*, but *besucht*,
  *verkauft*. Not *gestudiert* either, but *studiert*.
- ge- in the wrong place. Not *geeinkauft* or *eingekaufen*, but *eingekauft*.
- Weak endings on strong verbs. Not *gesehet* or *getrinkt*, but *gesehen*, *getrunken*.
- Using "did" for questions. German has no "do/did" helper. "Did you see it?" is
  *Hast du es gesehen?*
- Mixing up kennen and wissen. *Ich weiß Anna* is wrong; you *know* a person with
  *kennen*: *Ich kenne Anna.*

## Key points

- The perfect = *haben* (position 2, with the normal present endings) + past participle
  (last). It translates both "I did" and "I have done".
- Weak verbs: *ge- … -t* (*gemacht*, *gearbeitet*). Strong verbs: *ge- … -en*, often with a
  new vowel (*gesehen*, *getrunken*). Mixed: *gebracht, gedacht, gekannt, gewusst*.
- Separable verbs put *-ge-* after the prefix: *eingekauft*, *angerufen*.
- No *ge-* for *-ieren* verbs and verbs with *be-*, *ver-*, *er-*: *studiert*, *besucht*,
  *verloren*, *erzählt*.
- *Kennen* is for people and places, *wissen* for facts.
- Past time words: *gestern, vorgestern, letzte Woche, vor zwei Tagen, damals, gerade,
  schon*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. The perfect tense reference sheet lists all the participles you need at
A1.

lessons.title: The perfect with sein, and war/hatte
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 21 you built the perfect with *haben*: *Ich habe eingekauft*, *Wir haben viel
gelacht*. A smaller but very common group of verbs uses *sein* as the auxiliary instead:
*Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren* (I went to Berlin). These are mostly verbs of going somewhere,
which is exactly what you need for holiday stories.

You also learn *war* and *hatte*, the short past forms of *sein* and *haben*. Germans use
them all the time instead of the perfect of these two verbs. After this lesson you can say
where you were, what you had, where you went and what happened.

## When to use sein

Use *sein* + participle for two kinds of verbs.

Verbs of movement from one place to another:

- *Ich bin nach Hause gegangen.* — I went home.
- *Wir sind nach Spanien geflogen.* — We flew to Spain.
- *Bist du mit dem Zug gefahren?* — Did you go by train?
- *Anna ist schnell zum Bus gelaufen.* — Anna ran quickly to the bus.

Verbs of a change of state, where someone or something becomes different:

- *Ich bin um sechs aufgestanden.* — I got up at six.
- *Er ist Lehrer geworden.* — He became a teacher.

Plus three verbs you just have to learn, because they use *sein* although nothing moves or
changes:

- *sein*: *Ich bin schon in Wien gewesen.* — I've already been to Vienna.
- *bleiben*: *Wir sind zu Hause geblieben.* — We stayed at home.
- *passieren*: *Was ist passiert?* — What happened?

A memory hook: if you can ask "from where to where?", it's *sein*. And verbs that take a
direct object (an accusative: *einen Film sehen*, *ein Buch kaufen*) use *haben*. Almost all
the *sein* verbs at A1 have no object at all.

The word order is the same as with *haben*: the form of *sein* in position 2, the
participle last.

| | sein (position 2) | … | participle (end) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | bin | nach Hamburg | gefahren. |
| du | bist | gestern | gekommen. |
| er/sie/es | ist | ans Meer | geflogen. |
| wir | sind | in die Berge | gewandert. |
| ihr | seid | spät nach Hause | gegangen. |
| sie/Sie | sind | im Hotel | geblieben. |

*Ans Meer* (to the seaside) and *in die Berge* (into the mountains) are chunks for movement
to a place; the grammar behind them comes at A2.

## The sein verbs you need

Most of these are strong verbs, so their participles end in *-en*. Learn them as a group.

| infinitive | perfect | | infinitive | perfect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| gehen | ist gegangen | | bleiben | ist geblieben |
| kommen | ist gekommen | | sein | ist gewesen |
| fahren | ist gefahren | | werden | ist geworden |
| fliegen | ist geflogen | | laufen | ist gelaufen |
| schwimmen | ist geschwommen | | passieren | ist passiert |
| reisen | ist gereist | | wandern | ist gewandert |

*Reisen*, *wandern* and *passieren* are weak or *-ieren* verbs; they only need to be
remembered for the *sein*.

Separable verbs of movement and change also use *sein*, with *-ge-* in the middle as in
lesson 21:

| infinitive | perfect | |
|---|---|---|
| aufstehen | ist aufgestanden | got up |
| ankommen | ist angekommen | arrived |
| abfahren | ist abgefahren | departed |
| einsteigen | ist eingestiegen | got on/in |
| aussteigen | ist ausgestiegen | got off/out |
| umsteigen | ist umgestiegen | changed (trains, buses) |
| mitkommen | ist mitgekommen | came along |
| zurückkommen | ist zurückgekommen | came back |
| umziehen | ist umgezogen | moved (house) |

- *Der Zug ist pünktlich abgefahren.* — The train left on time.
- *Wann seid ihr zurückgekommen?* — When did you come back?
- *Meine Schwester ist nach München umgezogen.* — My sister has moved to Munich.

One small exception you may notice: *fahren* takes *haben* when there is an object, because
then you are driving something: *Ich habe das Auto gefahren* (I drove the car). Without an
object, it's *sein*: *Ich bin nach Köln gefahren.*

*Schwimmen* can also take *haben* when you mean the activity and not going anywhere (*Ich
habe eine Stunde geschwommen*), but *ist geschwommen* is always correct.

In southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland people also say *ich bin gesessen, gestanden,
gelegen* (sat, stood, lain). In the north and in most textbooks these take *haben*.

## war and hatte

*Sein* and *haben* have their own short past forms, called the **[[simple past]]**
(*Präteritum*). With these two verbs Germans much prefer the simple past to the perfect:
*Ich war in Rom* sounds more natural than *Ich bin in Rom gewesen*, and *Ich hatte keine
Zeit* is more common than *Ich habe keine Zeit gehabt*. Both are correct.

| | sein | haben |
|---|---|---|
| ich | war | hatte |
| du | warst | hattest |
| er/sie/es | war | hatte |
| wir | waren | hatten |
| ihr | wart | hattet |
| sie/Sie | waren | hatten |

The pattern is easy: ich and er/sie/es have the same form (*war*, *hatte*), and the other
endings are the ones you know from the present (-st, -en, -t, -en).

- *Wo warst du gestern?* — Where were you yesterday?
- *Ich war krank.* — I was ill.
- *Wie war der Urlaub?* — How was the holiday?
- *Das Wetter war schön, aber wir hatten nicht viel Zeit.* — The weather was nice, but we
  didn't have much time.
- *Hattest du Fieber?* — Did you have a temperature?
- *Wart ihr schon einmal in der Schweiz?* — Have you ever been to Switzerland?

## Holidays and places

Some words for travel stories:

- *die Ferien* (plural only) are the school or university holidays: *In den Sommerferien
  sind wir ans Meer gefahren.* — In the summer holidays we went to the seaside.
- *das Meer* is the sea, *der See* a lake. Same sound, different gender and meaning:
  *Wir sind im See geschwommen.* — We swam in the lake.
- *der Berg, das Dorf, die Insel, der Strand, der Fluss* — mountain, village, island,
  beach, river.
- *im Ausland* means "abroad": *Letztes Jahr war ich im Ausland.* — Last year I was abroad.
- *in der Natur* means "out in nature, outdoors".

Remember *wohin* (where to) from lesson 18 for asking about a destination. *Wo* asks about
a position:

- *Wohin seid ihr gefahren?* — Where did you go?
- *Wo wart ihr?* — Where were you?

And as in lessons 18 and 19, *nach Hause* means "(to) home", with movement; *zu Hause*
means "at home", without it:
*Ich bin nach Hause gegangen*, but *Ich bin zu Hause geblieben*.

## Telling a story

A story needs words that move it along. You know *zuerst, dann, danach* from lesson 12.
Add these:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| früher | in the past, formerly, used to |
| letztes Jahr | last year |
| plötzlich | suddenly |
| endlich | finally, at last |
| zurück | back |

- *Früher habe ich in einem Dorf gewohnt.* — I used to live in a village.
- *Plötzlich ist der Bus gekommen.* — Suddenly the bus came.
- *Endlich sind wir angekommen!* — At last we've arrived!

Remember: when one of these words starts the sentence, the verb (*bin, ist, habe…*) comes
next, in position 2.

## Dialogue: Wie waren die Ferien?

Sara meets her neighbour Herr Klein in the stairwell.

> Herr Klein: Hallo Sara! Sie sind ja wieder da! Wo waren Sie denn?
>
> Sara: Wir waren zwei Wochen in Italien. Wir sind am Samstag zurückgekommen.
>
> Herr Klein: Schön! Sind Sie geflogen?
>
> Sara: Nein, wir sind mit dem Auto gefahren. Zuerst waren wir in den Bergen, dann sind wir
> ans Meer gefahren.
>
> Herr Klein: Und wie war das Wetter?
>
> Sara: Super. Wir waren jeden Tag am Strand und sind viel geschwommen. Nur einmal hatten
> wir Regen.
>
> Herr Klein: Ist etwas passiert? Ihr Auto ist ja ganz schmutzig.
>
> Sara: Ja, plötzlich ist es kaputtgegangen, mitten in einem Dorf. Aber wir hatten Glück:
> Der Mechaniker war sehr nett.

Translation:

> Herr Klein: Hello Sara! You're back! Where were you, then?
>
> Sara: We were in Italy for two weeks. We came back on Saturday.
>
> Herr Klein: Lovely! Did you fly?
>
> Sara: No, we went by car. First we were in the mountains, then we drove to the seaside.
>
> Herr Klein: And how was the weather?
>
> Sara: Great. We were on the beach every day and swam a lot. We only had rain once.
>
> Herr Klein: Did something happen? Your car is really dirty.
>
> Sara: Yes, suddenly it broke down, right in the middle of a village. But we were
> lucky: the mechanic was very nice.

Notes: *wieder da sein* means "to be back"; *in den Bergen* is "in the mountains"; *jeden
Tag* is "every day"; *schmutzig* means "dirty"; *mitten in* is "right in the middle of"; *kaputtgehen* (to break down, to break) is *kaputt* + *gehen*, so it takes *sein*:
*ist kaputtgegangen*.

## Pronunciation

- *war* has a long *a*; *wart* (ihr) is short and ends in a clear *t*.
- *das Meer* sounds exactly like *mehr* (more): a long, closed *e*.
- *der See* is said [zeː], like English "zay" with a long vowel; the *s* is voiced, like
  English z.
- *die Ferien* is stressed on the first syllable, and the *i* glides into the ending:
  FAY-ryen, not "fe-REE-en".
- *plötzlich*: the *ö* is short, and *tz* sounds like "ts": PLÖTZ-lich.

## Common mistakes

- Using *haben* with movement verbs. Not *Ich habe nach Berlin gefahren*, but *Ich bin nach
  Berlin gefahren*. Not *Was hat passiert?*, but *Was ist passiert?*
- Forgetting to change *sein* for the person. *Wir sind gegangen, ihr seid gegangen* (not
  *wir ist*, not *ihr sind*).
- Adding an ending to ich/er in the simple past. Not *ich ware* or *er hatt*, but *ich war,
  er hatte*.
- Using *bekommen* for "become". *Bekommen* means "to get"; "to become" is *werden*: *Er
  ist Arzt geworden* (he became a doctor).
- Mixing up *wo* and *wohin*. *Wo* is the position, *wohin* the direction.
- Mixing up *das Meer* (sea) and *der See* (lake). The gender tells you which is which.

## Key points

- Verbs of movement (*gehen, fahren, fliegen, kommen, laufen*) and change (*aufstehen,
  werden*), plus *sein, bleiben, passieren*, form the perfect with *sein*: *Ich bin
  gefahren.*
- Separable movement verbs too: *ist angekommen, ist zurückgekommen, ist umgezogen*.
- Verbs with an accusative object use *haben*.
- *Sein* and *haben* usually appear in the simple past: *ich war, du warst, wir waren; ich
  hatte, du hattest, wir hatten*.
- *Wohin?* asks where to, *wo?* where. *Nach Hause* is going home, *zu Hause* being at home.
- Story words: *früher, letztes Jahr, plötzlich, endlich, zurück*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. The perfect tense reference sheet has every *sein* verb in one table.

lessons.title: Linking sentences and writing short messages
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far most of your sentences have been short and single: *Ich bin müde. Ich gehe nach
Hause.* That is correct, but it sounds a bit like a robot. In this lesson you learn five
small words that join two sentences into one, and one word that links them in a different
way. Then you put everything to work in two practical skills: writing a short message or
e-mail (to a friend, or to someone you don't know), and filling in a form. Both are tasks
you meet in daily life in a German-speaking country, and both are part of the writing
section of the A1 exam (lesson 24).

## Joining sentences: und, oder, aber, denn, sondern

A **[[conjunction]]** is a word that links words or sentences. The five in this lesson are
easy for one important reason: they don't change the word order. They stand in front of
the second sentence in a slot outside the sentence, called **[[position zero]]**, and the
sentence after them stays exactly as it was, with the verb in position 2.

| conjunction | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| und | and | *Ich koche, und du räumst auf.* |
| oder | or | *Kommst du mit, oder bleibst du hier?* |
| aber | but | *Das Hotel ist alt, aber es ist schön.* |
| denn | because, as | *Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin krank.* |
| sondern | but (rather), instead | *Er kommt nicht heute, sondern morgen.* |

Look at the second half of each example. *Du räumst auf*, *bleibst du hier*, *es ist schön*,
*ich bin krank*: these are complete normal sentences, as if the conjunction weren't there.

- *Ich habe Hunger, aber ich habe kein Geld.* — I'm hungry, but I have no money.
- *Wir können ins Kino gehen, oder wir sehen zu Hause einen Film.* — We can go to the
  cinema, or we can watch a film at home.
- *Ich lerne Deutsch, denn meine Freundin kommt aus Österreich.* — I'm learning German
  because my girlfriend is from Austria.
- *Sie hat die Prüfung bestanden, und jetzt feiert sie.* — She passed the exam, and now
  she's celebrating.

### Leaving words out

When both halves have the same subject, you can drop it after *und*, *oder* and *aber*:

- *Ich stehe auf und dusche.* — I get up and shower.
- *Ich lese am Abend oder höre Musik.* — In the evening I read or listen to music.

Don't do this with *denn*; it always needs a full sentence after it.

### denn: the A1 way to say "because"

*Denn* gives a reason. It always comes second, after the thing it explains: *Ich komme
nicht, denn ich muss arbeiten.* It can't stand alone as the answer to *Warum?* For that,
Germans use *weil*, which sends the verb to the end and comes at A2. For now, answer with
a full sentence: *Warum kommst du nicht? — Ich muss arbeiten.*

### sondern: not this, but that

*Sondern* corrects something negative. You need *nicht* or *kein* in the first half, and
then *sondern* gives the right information. If the first half is not negative, use *aber*.

- *Das ist kein Tee, sondern Kaffee.* — That's not tea, it's coffee.
- *Ich wohne nicht in Berlin, sondern in Hamburg.* — I don't live in Berlin but in Hamburg.
- *Das Zimmer ist klein, aber hell.* — The room is small but bright. (no negative, so
  *aber*)

### Commas

Put a comma before *aber*, *denn* and *sondern*. Before *und* and *oder* a comma is
optional when they join two complete sentences, and there is none when they join single
words: *Brot und Butter*, *Tee oder Kaffee*.

## deshalb: a preview

*Deshalb* (that's why, so, therefore) also links two ideas, but it works differently. It is
not a conjunction but an adverb, so it takes position 1 itself. The verb comes straight
after it, and the subject moves behind the verb, like after *heute* or *dann*.

- *Ich bin krank. Deshalb komme ich nicht.* — I'm ill. That's why I'm not coming.
- *Der Bus ist nicht gekommen, deshalb bin ich zu Fuß gegangen.* — The bus didn't come, so
  I walked.

Compare: *…, denn ich bin krank* (reason, normal order) but *Deshalb komme ich nicht*
(result, verb first). Using *deshalb* correctly in a message shows good control of word
order, but you can always say the same thing with *denn*.

## Writing a short message

Personal messages and e-mails in German follow a simple frame.

| | informal (du) | formal (Sie) |
|---|---|---|
| opening | *Liebe Anna,* / *Lieber Tom,* / *Hallo Anna,* | *Sehr geehrte Frau Weber,* / *Sehr geehrter Herr Klein,* |
| unknown person | — | *Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,* |
| closing | *Viele Grüße* / *Liebe Grüße* / *Bis bald!* | *Mit freundlichen Grüßen* |
| "your" | *dein, deine* | *Ihr, Ihre* |

Some rules that make your message look right:

- *Liebe* is for a woman, *Lieber* for a man. In the formal opening it's *Sehr geehrte*
  for a woman and *Sehr geehrter* for a man.
- After the opening put a comma, and start the next line with a small letter (unless the
  word is a noun or *Sie*): *Liebe Anna, vielen Dank für …*
- No comma after the closing; just put your name on the next line.
- Stay with one form: if you start with *Liebe Anna*, write *du* and *dein* throughout.
  To a stranger, an office or a landlord, use *Sie* and *Ihr*.

### What goes in the message

A good short message has a clear purpose and answers the points it must cover. A typical
pattern is: say why you are writing, give the information or reason, ask a question or
make a suggestion, and close. About 30 words is enough.

Here is an informal message that says no to an invitation (an *Absage*):

> Liebe Julia,
>
> vielen Dank für die Einladung! Leider kann ich am Samstag nicht zur Party kommen, denn
> meine Mutter hat Geburtstag. Hast du am Sonntag Zeit? Wir können zusammen frühstücken.
>
> Viele Grüße
> Marco

Translation: Dear Julia, thanks a lot for the invitation! Unfortunately I can't come to the
party on Saturday, because it's my mother's birthday. Are you free on Sunday? We could have
breakfast together. Best wishes, Marco.

And a formal one that cancels an appointment (*einen Termin absagen*):

> Sehr geehrte Frau Berger,
>
> ich habe am Dienstag um 10 Uhr einen Termin bei Ihnen. Leider kann ich nicht kommen, denn
> ich bin krank. Haben Sie am Freitag Zeit? Bitte schicken Sie mir eine Nachricht.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
> Paul Novak

Translation: Dear Ms Berger, I have an appointment with you on Tuesday at 10 o'clock.
Unfortunately I can't come, because I'm ill. Do you have time on Friday? Please send me a
message. Yours sincerely, Paul Novak.

Notice how both use *denn* for the reason and a question to keep things moving. Useful
building blocks:

- *Vielen Dank für deine Nachricht.* — Thanks for your message.
- *Leider habe ich keine Zeit.* — Unfortunately I don't have time.
- *Ich habe ein Problem.* — I have a problem.
- *Kannst du mir bitte antworten?* — Can you answer me, please?
- *Ich freue mich auf deine Antwort.* — I look forward to your answer.
- *Bis bald!* — See you soon!

## Filling in a form

Forms (*Formulare*, lesson 15) ask for the same facts again and again. Learn the field
names and you can fill in almost any form, from a course registration to a hotel check-in.

| field | meaning | example answer |
|---|---|---|
| Vorname | first name | Elif |
| Familienname / Nachname | surname | Kaya |
| Geburtsdatum | date of birth | 14.03.1995 |
| Geburtsort | place of birth | Izmir |
| Staatsangehörigkeit | nationality | türkisch |
| Familienstand | marital status | ledig / verheiratet / geschieden |
| Geschlecht | sex, gender | männlich / weiblich / divers |
| Adresse (Straße, Hausnummer, PLZ, Ort) | address | Bergstraße 12, 50667 Köln |
| Telefonnummer, E-Mail | | |
| Datum, Unterschrift | date, signature | |

Points to watch:

- Dates are written day, month, year with full stops: *14.03.1995* is 14 March 1995.
- *Staatsangehörigkeit* is usually answered with an adjective: *deutsch*, *amerikanisch*,
  *türkisch*. *PLZ* is short for *Postleitzahl*.
- *Ledig* means single (never married), *verheiratet* married, *geschieden* divorced (lesson
  6). *Divers* is the third official option for gender.
- The *Unterschrift* is your signature, written by hand; *unterschreiben* is to sign.

## Dialogue: help with a course registration

Elif wants to register for a German course and asks at the language school office.

> Elif: Guten Tag. Ich möchte mich für den Kurs am Abend anmelden.
>
> Frau Roth: Gern. Hier ist das Formular. Haben Sie eine Frage?
>
> Elif: Ja. Was heißt „Familienstand“?
>
> Frau Roth: Sind Sie verheiratet oder ledig?
>
> Elif: Ich bin nicht verheiratet, sondern ledig.
>
> Frau Roth: Gut, dann kreuzen Sie hier „ledig“ an. Und unten ist die Unterschrift.
>
> Elif: Wann ist die Prüfung? Ich muss sie unbedingt bestehen, denn ich brauche das Zertifikat.
>
> Frau Roth: Im Juni. Aber keine Sorge, Sie haben genug Zeit!

Translation:

> Elif: Hello. I'd like to sign up for the evening course.
>
> Frau Roth: Of course. Here's the form. Do you have a question?
>
> Elif: Yes. What does "Familienstand" mean?
>
> Frau Roth: Are you married or single?
>
> Elif: I'm not married, I'm single.
>
> Frau Roth: Good, then tick "ledig" here. And the signature goes at the bottom.
>
> Elif: When is the exam? I really have to pass it, because I need the certificate.
>
> Frau Roth: In June. But don't worry, you have enough time!

Notes: *sich anmelden* means "to register, to sign up"; *unbedingt* is "absolutely, really";
*keine Sorge* is "don't worry"; *ankreuzen* (to tick, to put a cross) comes in lesson 24.

## Pronunciation

- *Staatsangehörigkeit* is long but regular: STAATS-an-ge-hö-rig-keit. Stress the first
  part.
- *Unterschrift*: stress on the first syllable, UN-ter-schrift.
- *geehrte* has two separate e sounds: ge-EHR-te.
- *Grüße* has a long *ü* and *ß*: say "ee" with rounded lips.

## Common mistakes

- Putting the verb at the end after *denn*. Not *…, denn ich krank bin*, but *…, denn ich
  bin krank*.
- Normal order after *deshalb*. Not *Deshalb ich komme nicht*, but *Deshalb komme ich
  nicht*.
- Using *sondern* without a negative, or *aber* to correct a negative: *Ich trinke keinen
  Tee, sondern Kaffee.*
- Mixing *du* and *Sie* in one message, or writing *Lieber Anna*. Match the ending to the
  person: *Liebe Anna, Lieber Tom*.
- A capital letter after the opening: *Liebe Julia, Vielen Dank* is wrong; write *vielen
  Dank*.
- Writing dates the American way. 03.04. is the third of April, not March fourth.

## Key points

- *Und, oder, aber, denn, sondern* stand in position zero: the verb stays in position 2.
- *Denn* gives a reason; *sondern* corrects a negative (*nicht/kein … sondern*).
- *Deshalb* is in position 1, so the verb follows it directly.
- Informal messages: *Liebe/Lieber …,* → *Viele Grüße*. Formal: *Sehr geehrte/geehrter
  …,* → *Mit freundlichen Grüßen*.
- Forms: *Vorname, Familienname, Geburtsdatum, Geburtsort, Staatsangehörigkeit,
  Familienstand, Geschlecht, Unterschrift*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The Goethe A1 exam and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last lesson of the course. It does three things. First, it explains what
"A1" actually means and what you can now do. Second, it describes the best-known A1 exam,
the Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1, with strategies for each part. Third, it reviews
the grammar of the whole course and tells you where to look if something is still shaky.
The questions at the end of this lesson cover all 24 lessons, so treat them as a final
check.

You don't have to take an exam. But even if you never sit one, the free official practice
tests are a good way to see whether you have really reached A1.

## What A1 means

The levels A1 to C2 come from the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages
(CEFR), used across Europe and beyond. A1 is the first level. In plain words, a learner at
A1 can:

- understand and use very common phrases from everyday life, as long as they are about
  concrete, immediate needs: shopping, food, times, directions;
- introduce themselves and other people, and ask and answer simple questions about where
  someone lives, who they know and what they have;
- take part in a simple conversation, if the other person talks slowly and clearly and is
  willing to help.

That last point matters. At A1 nobody expects you to follow a fast conversation between two
native speakers. You are expected to manage with patience on both sides, and to ask for help
when you need it. That is a skill too, and this lesson gives you the words for it.

## The Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1

The exam has four parts. Hören, Lesen and Schreiben are written in one block of about 65
minutes; Sprechen is a separate oral exam.

| part | time (about) | what it tests |
|---|---|---|
| Hören (listening) | 20 minutes | short everyday conversations, telephone messages, announcements |
| Lesen (reading) | 25 minutes | short notes and e-mails, signs and notices, small ads |
| Schreiben (writing) | 20 minutes | filling in a form; writing a short message of about 30 words |
| Sprechen (speaking) | 15 minutes | in a small group, with no time to prepare: introducing yourself, asking and answering questions on a topic with word cards, making requests and responding |

There are 100 points in total, and you pass with 60. The grades are:

| points | grade |
|---|---|
| 90–100 | sehr gut (very good) |
| 80–89 | gut (good) |
| 70–79 | befriedigend (satisfactory) |
| 60–69 | ausreichend (sufficient, a pass) |

The Goethe-Institut publishes the official description and free practice material,
including a full model test (*Modellsatz*) with audio and answers:

- [Exam overview: Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1](https://www.goethe.de/ins/si/de/spr/prf/gzsd1.html)
- [Free practice material (Modellsatz and Übungssätze)](https://www.goethe.de/de/spr/prf/ueb/pa1.html)
- [Official exam regulations (Durchführungsbestimmungen, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/resources/files/pdf325/durchfuehrungsbestimmungen_a1_start_deutsch_1.pdf)

Details such as dates, fees and the exact format can change, so always check with the exam
centre where you register. Other A1 exams (for example telc or ÖSD) are similar in level.

## Strategies for each part

### Hören

- Read the questions before you listen. They tell you what to listen for: a time, a price,
  a place, a day.
- You don't need every word. Listen for the key facts: numbers, times and days (lessons 3,
  10, 11, 16) come up again and again.
- Watch out for changes: *Der Termin ist am Montag … nein, am Dienstag.* The second piece of
  information is usually the one that counts.

### Lesen

- Look at the type of text first: a sign, an ad, a short e-mail. Then read the question,
  then look for the part of the text that answers it.
- Signs and notices use the words of lesson 15: *geöffnet, geschlossen, verboten, nicht
  rauchen, bitte warten*.
- Don't panic about unknown words. Many tasks can be answered with the words you know.

### Schreiben

- In the form, copy the information exactly, with correct capital letters and umlauts.
  Dates go day.month.year (lesson 23).
- In the message, cover every point the task gives you. A point you forget costs more than
  a small grammar mistake.
- Use a correct frame: *Liebe …, / Lieber …,* or *Sehr geehrte …,* and a matching closing.
  Link your sentences with *und, aber, denn*.
- Check at the end: verb in position 2? Nouns with capitals? *du* or *Sie* all the way
  through?

### Sprechen

- Prepare your self-introduction at home until it is automatic: name, age, country, where you
  live, languages, job, hobbies. Use lessons 2, 3, 6, 7 and 13.
- When you get a word card, make a simple, correct question: *Was isst du gern zum
  Frühstück?* A short question you can say clearly is better than a long one you can't
  finish.
- For requests, use the polite forms from lessons 14, 15 and 17: *Können Sie bitte …? Gib
  mir bitte …, Darf ich …?* And answer other people's requests: *Ja, gern. / Hier, bitte. /
  Nein, tut mir leid.*
- If you don't understand, ask. That is a normal part of the conversation.

## Words for the classroom and the exam

These phrases help in any lesson, exam or real conversation:

- *Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?* — Could you repeat that, please?
- *Ich verstehe das nicht.* — I don't understand (that).
- *Was bedeutet das?* — What does that mean?
- *Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?* — How do you say that in German?
- *Können Sie das bitte erklären?* — Could you explain that, please?

And these are typical words in exam instructions and textbooks:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| die Aufgabe | task, exercise |
| der Teil | part |
| der Text | text |
| das Beispiel | example |
| die Lösung | answer, solution |
| die Seite | page |
| der Punkt | point |
| der Fehler | mistake |
| ankreuzen | to tick, to mark with a cross |
| ergänzen | to complete, to fill in (a gap) |
| üben | to practise |

- *Lesen Sie den Text und kreuzen Sie an.* — Read the text and tick (the right answer).
- *Ergänzen Sie die Wörter.* — Fill in the words.
- *Wie viele Punkte hast du?* — How many points have you got?
- *Ich habe drei Fehler gemacht.* — I made three mistakes.

### etwas, nichts, jemand, niemand, alle, beide, genug

These small words are everywhere, so they finish off your A1 vocabulary:

- *Hast du etwas gesagt? — Nein, ich habe nichts gesagt.* — Did you say something? — No, I
  didn't say anything.
- *Ist jemand da? — Nein, hier ist niemand.* — Is anybody there? — No, nobody's here.
- *Alle sind gekommen.* — Everybody came.
- *Wir haben beide bestanden.* — We both passed.
- *Hast du genug Zeit?* — Do you have enough time?

Note that German uses one negative word only: *Ich habe nichts gesagt* ("I have nothing
said"), never *nicht nichts*. *Nichts* and *etwas* never change their form.

## Review of the course

Use this table to go back to the lesson you need.

| topic | the core idea | lessons |
|---|---|---|
| sounds and spelling | ä ö ü ß, ei/ie, ch, nouns with capitals | 1 |
| du and Sie, sein | *Wie heißen Sie? Woher kommst du?* | 2 |
| numbers | *einundzwanzig*: ones before tens; prices | 3, 10 |
| present tense | endings -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en; verb in position 2 | 4 |
| questions | yes/no: verb first; W-question: W-word, then verb | 4 |
| nouns | der/die/das, plurals, learn each noun with its article | 5 |
| possessives | *mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr* | 6 |
| negation | *nicht* for verbs and adjectives, *kein* for nouns | 8 |
| accusative | only masculine changes: *den, einen, keinen* | 9 |
| time | *um acht Uhr, am Montag, halb drei* | 11 |
| separable verbs | *Ich stehe um sieben auf.* | 12 |
| stem changes | *fahren → fährt, sprechen → spricht, lesen → liest* | 13 |
| modal verbs | modal in position 2, infinitive at the end | 14, 15 |
| dates and weather | *am dritten Mai, es regnet*; für, ohne | 16 |
| imperative | *Gehen Sie! Geh! Geht!* | 17 |
| dative | *mit dem Bus, zum Bahnhof, bei der Arbeit* | 18 |
| location | *im Wohnzimmer, auf dem Tisch* | 19 |
| pronouns | *mich, dich, ihn; mir, dir* | 20 |
| perfect | *habe gemacht, bin gefahren; war, hatte* | 21, 22 |
| linking | *und, oder, aber, denn, sondern* | 23 |

If you had to remember only three things from this course, make them these: the verb is
always the second element in a statement; every noun has a gender, so learn it with *der*,
*die* or *das*; and the second verb (modal, perfect, separable prefix) goes to the end.

## Dialogue: practising for the speaking test

Ben and Yuki are practising together for the speaking part.

> Ben: Okay, du bist dran. Stell dich bitte vor.
>
> Yuki: Ich heiße Yuki. Ich bin 28 Jahre alt und komme aus Japan. Ich wohne seit einem
> Jahr in Leipzig. Ich spreche Japanisch, Englisch und ein bisschen Deutsch.
>
> Ben: Sehr gut! Jetzt die Karte. Das Thema ist „Freizeit“, das Wort ist „Sport“.
>
> Yuki: Machst du gern Sport?
>
> Ben: Ja, ich spiele Fußball in einem Verein.
>
> Yuki: Entschuldigung, was bedeutet „Verein“?
>
> Ben: Das ist eine Gruppe, zum Beispiel für Sport. Auf Englisch sagt man „club“.
>
> Yuki: Ah, danke!
>
> Ben: Gut, jetzt eine Bitte. Deine Karte zeigt ein Fenster.
>
