> Yuki: Kannst du bitte das Fenster öffnen?
>
> Ben: Ja, natürlich. Siehst du? Die Prüfung ist kein Problem für uns!

Translation:

> Ben: OK, it's your turn. Introduce yourself, please.
>
> Yuki: My name is Yuki. I'm 28 and I'm from Japan. I've been living in Leipzig for a year.
> I speak Japanese, English and a little German.
>
> Ben: Very good! Now the card. The topic is "free time", the word is "sport".
>
> Yuki: Do you like doing sport?
>
> Ben: Yes, I play football in a club.
>
> Yuki: Sorry, what does "Verein" mean?
>
> Ben: It's a group, for example for sport. In English you say "club".
>
> Yuki: Ah, thanks!
>
> Ben: OK, now a request. Your card shows a window.
>
> Yuki: Can you open the window, please?
>
> Ben: Yes, of course. See? The exam is no problem for us!

Notes: *du bist dran* means "it's your turn"; *sich vorstellen* is "to introduce yourself";
*der Verein* is a club or association.

## Pronunciation

- *wiederholen* is stressed on *-ho-*: wie-der-HO-len. The *ie* is a long "ee".
- *jemand* and *niemand* are stressed on the first syllable: JE-mand, NIE-mand.
- *ergänzen*: stress on *-gän-*, and *z* is "ts": er-GÄN-tsen.
- *ankreuzen*: AN-kreu-zen, with *eu* like "oy".

## Common mistakes

- Answering a different question. In the speaking test, listen for the question word: *wo*
  (where), *wohin* (where to), *woher* (where from), *wann* (when), *wie lange* (how long).
- Leaving out a point in the message task. Tick off each point as you write.
- Translating word for word from English: *Ich bin 28 Jahre alt* (not *Ich habe 28 Jahre*),
  *Mir ist kalt* (not *Ich bin kalt*).
- Double negatives: *Ich habe nichts gesagt* (not *Ich habe nicht nichts gesagt*).
- Staying silent. If you didn't understand, say *Wie bitte?* or *Können Sie das bitte
  wiederholen?*

## What comes next

At A2 you will learn to talk about your past in more detail, compare things (*größer, am
größten*), use adjective endings (*ein großes Haus*), say why with *weil* and give opinions
with *dass*, and use more dative and two-way prepositions. Keep your vocabulary reviews
going: the words you learned here are the foundation for everything that follows. Reading
graded readers from the reading list and listening to slow German podcasts are the best
ways to keep growing on your own.

## Key points

- A1 means you can manage simple, everyday situations if people speak slowly and help.
- The Goethe A1 exam has four parts: Hören (about 20 min), Lesen (about 25 min), Schreiben
  (about 20 min), Sprechen (about 15 min, in a group). You need 60 of 100 points to pass.
- Practise with the free official model tests on goethe.de.
- Ask for help in German: *Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? Was bedeutet das?*
- *Etwas/nichts, jemand/niemand, alle, beide, genug* complete your A1 word list.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. Herzlichen Glückwunsch: you have finished German A1!

sections.name: The past and the A1 exam

questions.stem: How is the "w" in "wohnen" (to live) pronounced?
questions.explanation: German w always sounds like English v: wohnen is "VOH-nen", wie is "vee". English speakers often read it as an English w, which Germans hear as a foreign accent at once.

questions.stem: Which of these words has the long "ee" sound?
questions.explanation: ie sounds like English "ee", so sie is "zee". The others are spelled ei, which sounds like English "eye". Hook: say the English name of the second letter (ie ends in e, ei ends in i).

questions.stem: The "ei" in "heißen" (to be called) is a diphthong. Which spelling is correct in Germany?
questions.explanation: After a long vowel or a diphthong like ei, a sharp s is written ß: heißen. A single s between vowels would sound like English z (heisen = "HY-zen"). Only in Switzerland is it written heissen.

questions.stem: Which of these words must always start with a capital letter?
questions.explanation: Name is a noun, and every German noun is capitalized: der Name. Langsam (slow), bitte (please) and schreiben (to write) are not nouns, so they are lowercase unless they start a sentence.

questions.stem: How does the final "d" in "und" (and) sound?
questions.explanation: At the end of a word or syllable, b, d and g lose their voice and sound like p, t and k. So und sounds like "oont" and Tag like "tahk". The letter is still written d.

questions.stem: Where is the stress in "Entschuldigung" (excuse me)?
questions.explanation: German words are usually stressed on the first syllable, but the prefix ent- is never stressed, so the stress moves to the next syllable: ent-SCHUL-di-gung. The same happens with be- and ver- (ver-STE-hen).

questions.stem: It's 8 p.m. and you arrive at a friend's house for dinner. How do you greet her parents?
questions.explanation: Guten Abend is the greeting from about 6 p.m. Gute Nacht looks like the right time of day, but it is only said when someone goes to bed, as a goodbye. Tschüss is also a goodbye.

questions.stem: Someone says "Danke!" to you. What is the usual reply?
questions.explanation: Bitte (or Bitte schön) is the answer to Danke: "You're welcome." Wie bitte? asks someone to repeat, and Entschuldigung is "excuse me" or "sorry".

questions.stem: You didn't catch what someone said. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Wie bitte? means "Pardon?" and asks the speaker to repeat. Wie schreibt man das? asks how a word is spelled, which only helps once you have heard it. Bitte schön means "you're welcome".

questions.stem: You spell the name "Jens" in German. How do you say the first letter?
questions.explanation: The German letter J is called "yot", and it sounds like English y: Jens is "Yens". "Jay" is the English name and isn't a German letter name at all; "ee" is the German I, and "gay" is the German G.

questions.stem: Read the message: "Hallo! Mein Vorname ist Katrin, mein Familienname ist Vogt. Vogt schreibt man V – O – G – T." Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Der Familienname is the surname, so her surname is Vogt; der Vorname (Katrin) is her first name. She spells the surname, not the first name.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake?
questions.explanation: Vorname (first name) is a noun, so it needs a capital letter: Mein Vorname ist Ali. The possessive mein is not a noun, so it is lowercase in the middle of a sentence.

questions.stem: In which word is "ch" the rough sound at the back of the throat, as in Scottish "loch"?
questions.explanation: After a, o, u and au, ch is the rough back sound: Nacht, noch, auch. After other letters (ich, nicht, Milch) it is the soft front sound, like the h in "huge".

questions.stem: You meet your new neighbour, an older woman, for the first time. How do you ask her name?
questions.explanation: With an adult you don't know, use Sie, and the verb form is the same as the infinitive: Wie heißen Sie? Wie heißt du? is correct German but too familiar here. Wer means "who", not "how".

questions.stem: Complete the question: "___ du Lena?"
questions.explanation: The du form of sein is bist: Bist du Lena? (Are you Lena?) Bin goes with ich, ist with er/sie, and sind with Sie.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wie ___ du?" (What's your name?)
questions.explanation:
The du ending is normally -st, but the stem of heißen already ends in ß, so du adds only
-t: du heißt. Heiße goes with ich and heißen with Sie.

questions.stem: Which question asks where someone is from?
questions.explanation: Woher means "where from", so Woher kommst du? asks about origin. Wo wohnst du? asks where someone lives now, which is a different question.

questions.stem: What does "Wer ist das?" mean?
questions.explanation: Wer means "who", even though it looks like English "where". "Where" is wo, "how" is wie and "what" is was.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich komme ___ Kanada."
questions.explanation: Origin is expressed with kommen aus: Ich komme aus Kanada. Von looks like English "from", but Germans don't use it for the country you come from.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich wohne ___ Hamburg."
questions.explanation: Where you live is wohnen in: Ich wohne in Hamburg. Aus goes with kommen, for origin.

questions.stem: Mr Braun asks you: "Wie geht es Ihnen?" What is the best reply?
questions.explanation: He uses the formal Ihnen, so you answer formally and ask back with Und Ihnen? Und dir? is the informal version. Ich bin gut means "I'm good (at something)" or "I'm a good person", not "I'm fine".

questions.stem: Someone introduces himself: "Hallo, ich bin Jonas." What do you say?
questions.explanation: Freut mich means "Nice to meet you", the natural reply when you meet someone, followed by your own name. Auch gut ("fine too") answers Wie geht's? Und dir?

questions.stem: Which question has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Wie heißen du? mixes the Sie form of the verb with du. It must be Wie heißt du? (informal) or Wie heißen Sie? (formal). The other questions match their pronoun.

questions.stem: Read: "Das ist Herr Petrović. Er kommt aus Kroatien, aber er wohnt jetzt in Österreich, in Linz." Where does Mr Petrović live now?
questions.explanation: Er wohnt jetzt in Österreich: he now lives in Austria, in Linz. Croatia (Kroatien) is where he comes from (kommt aus), not where he lives.

questions.stem: How do you greet Ms Wagner, a colleague you call Sie?
questions.explanation: With Sie, use Frau (or Herr) plus the surname: Guten Tag, Frau Wagner! The surname alone sounds rude, and Frau without a name is not a polite form of address.

questions.stem: Which question is correct?
questions.explanation: In a W-question the verb comes straight after the question word, then the subject: Woher kommen Sie? Aus is not needed in the question, because woher already means "where from".

questions.stem: How do you say 25 in German?
questions.explanation: From 21 to 99 German says the unit first, then und, then the ten: fünf-und-zwanzig ("five and twenty"), written as one word. Zweiundfünfzig is 52, the reversed number.

questions.stem: You hear "siebenundvierzig". Which number is it?
questions.explanation: Sieben (7) und vierzig (40) = 47. German says the unit first and the ten second, so you hear 7, then 40. 74 would be vierundsiebzig.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of 30 in Germany?
questions.explanation: 30 is the only ten that doesn't end in -zig: dreißig. Dreizehn is 13. (Switzerland writes dreissig, because it doesn't use ß.)

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of 16?
questions.explanation: Sechzehn drops the s of sechs. Sechszehn is the most common spelling mistake. Sechzig is 60, which also drops the s.

questions.stem: How do you ask a child how old they are?
questions.explanation: German uses sein for age, as English does, and you say du to a child: Wie alt bist du? Wie alt sind Sie? is correct for adults you don't know. Haben is wrong for age.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Age uses sein and the same order as English: Ich bin 30 Jahre alt (or just Ich bin 30). Ich habe 30 Jahre is a direct copy of Spanish or French and is wrong in German.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ du eine Handynummer?"
questions.explanation: The du form of haben is hast, without the b. Hat goes with er/sie, haben with Sie, and habst doesn't exist.

questions.stem: On the phone someone says "null eins sieben zwo". What does "zwo" mean?
questions.explanation: Zwo is another word for zwei (2), used on the phone and in announcements so that it can't be confused with drei (3).

questions.stem: Read the address: "Thomas Berger, Mozartstraße 9, 80336 München". What is the house number?
questions.explanation: In a German address the house number comes after the street name: Mozartstraße 9. The five-digit number before the town, 80336, is the postcode (die Postleitzahl).

questions.stem: What does "die Postleitzahl" mean?
questions.explanation: Die Postleitzahl (PLZ) is the postcode or ZIP code. The phone number is die Telefonnummer and the house number die Hausnummer.

questions.stem: Someone asks: "Wie ist Ihre Telefonnummer?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: Die Telefonnummer is the phone number, so the answer is a number. The other replies answer Wie alt sind Sie?, Wo wohnen Sie? and Woher kommen Sie?

questions.stem: Mia says: "Ich bin einundzwanzig." How old is she?
questions.explanation: Ein(s) und zwanzig = 21. Inside a number eins becomes ein. 12 is zwölf and 31 is einunddreißig.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Ich habe eine Adresse in Köln.
questions.explanation: Haben is slightly irregular: the du form is du hast (and er hat), without the b. Du habst is a regular-looking form that doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir ___ in Berlin." (wohnen)
questions.explanation: The wir ending is -en, so the form is the same as the infinitive: wir wohnen. Wohnt is the er/ihr form, wohnst the du form, wohne the ich form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ihr ___ heute." (arbeiten)
questions.explanation: The ihr ending is -t, and because the stem arbeit- ends in t, an extra e is added: ihr arbeitet. Arbeitest is the du form.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ ihr aus Köln?"
questions.explanation: The ihr form of sein is seid: Seid ihr aus Köln? (Are you from Cologne?) Seit sounds the same but means "since". Sind goes with wir and sie/Sie.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: The verb must be the second element. When heute comes first, the subject ich moves to just after the verb: Heute lerne ich Deutsch. Heute ich lerne copies English word order.

questions.stem: Turn "Du spielst Gitarre." into a yes/no question.
questions.explanation: For a yes/no question, put the verb first and keep its form: Spielst du Gitarre? German has no helper verb like English "do", and the du form stays spielst.

questions.stem: In "sie spielt", who is playing?
questions.explanation: The ending -t shows one person: sie spielt = she plays. "They play" is sie spielen, and formal "you play" is Sie spielen with a capital S.

questions.stem: Choose the question word: "___ lernst du Deutsch? – Ich wohne jetzt in Deutschland."
questions.explanation: The answer gives a reason, so the question is Warum (why)? Wann asks about time and wo about place.

questions.stem: Choose the question word: "___ arbeitest du? – Heute und morgen." (morgen = tomorrow)
questions.explanation: The answer is a time, so the question is Wann (when)? Wo would need a place in the answer, and was a thing.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm learning German"?
questions.explanation: German has no -ing form. The simple present ich lerne covers "I learn", "I'm learning" and "I do learn". Ich bin lernen is a word-for-word copy of the English.

questions.stem: Tom is a student at the university in Munich. Which sentence says that?
questions.explanation: Studieren means studying at a university. Lernen is learning in general (a language, for a test). Arbeitet means he works there, which is not what we want to say.

questions.stem: Read: "Das ist Elif. Sie kommt aus der Türkei, aber sie lebt jetzt in Hamburg. Sie arbeitet in einem Café. Sie hört gern Musik und spielt oft Gitarre." Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Sie hört gern Musik: gern after the verb means she likes doing it. She comes from Turkey but lives in Hamburg now, works in a café, and plays the guitar often (oft).

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: The ihr form of sein is seid: Ihr seid heute hier. Sind is for wir and sie/Sie.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "We like playing"?
questions.explanation: Gern goes after the conjugated verb: Wir spielen gern. In the other sentences the verb is not in second position, and spielt is the wrong ending for wir.

questions.stem: Which article goes with "Tisch" (table)?
questions.explanation: Tisch is masculine: der Tisch. "die" is for feminine nouns and plurals, "das" for neuter nouns. "den" is a different case form you will meet in lesson 9. Learn every noun together with its article.

questions.stem: What is the plural of "das Buch" (book)?
questions.explanation: Buch belongs to the umlaut + -er group: das Buch, die Bücher. German rarely adds -s like English, and every plural takes the article "die", never "das".

questions.stem: Which noun is feminine? Look at the ending.
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in -ung are always feminine: die Zeitung. -chen is always neuter (das Mädchen). -er is a weaker hint: der Computer is masculine but das Fenster is neuter.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: "Das ist ___ Lampe."
questions.explanation: Lampe is feminine (die Lampe), so "a" is eine: Das ist eine Lampe. "ein" is for masculine and neuter nouns. "der" would be "the", and only for masculine nouns.

questions.stem: Which article goes with the compound noun "Handynummer" (das Handy + die Nummer)?
questions.explanation: In a compound noun the last part decides the gender. Nummer is feminine, so it is die Handynummer, even though das Handy is neuter.

questions.stem: You point at three keys on the table. Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: For several things you say "Das sind …". Schlüssel belongs to the no-ending group (der Schlüssel, die Schlüssel), so Schlüssels is wrong, and "ein" has no plural.

questions.stem: What does "das Handy" mean?
questions.explanation: Das Handy is the everyday German word for a mobile (cell) phone. It looks like English "handy" but means something quite different.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: Uhr is feminine (die Uhr), so it must be "Das ist eine Uhr." Heft is neuter and Stift is masculine, so "ein" is correct for them, and Tasche is feminine with "eine".

questions.stem: Read the note: "Lena, hier sind zwei Bücher und ein Heft. Die Bücher sind für Max, das Heft ist für Jana. Danke! Ben" (für = for). What is for Jana?
questions.explanation: The note says "das Heft ist für Jana": the (one) exercise book is for Jana. The two books (die Bücher) are for Max.

questions.stem: Which noun is neuter?
questions.explanation: It is das Fenster. The others are die Brille, der Stuhl and die Tür. Fenster ends in -er, which often suggests masculine, so it is a good example of why you learn every article.

questions.stem: What is the plural of "die Lampe"?
questions.explanation: Most feminine nouns add -n or -en in the plural: die Lampe, die Lampen. German does not form this plural with -s or an umlaut.

questions.stem: Your friend says "Wo ist die Brille?" What is she looking for?
questions.explanation: Die Brille is singular: one pair of glasses. English says "glasses", but German treats it as one thing, so it is "Wo ist die Brille?", not "Wo sind …". Several pairs would be die Brillen.

questions.stem: Complete: "Anna und ___ Vater wohnen in Bonn."
questions.explanation: Anna is the owner, so the word is ihr (her). Vater is masculine, so there is no ending: ihr Vater. "ihre" would be for a feminine or plural noun, and sein/seine means "his".

questions.stem: Complete: "Paul und ___ Schwester wohnen in Wien."
questions.explanation: Paul is the owner, so the word is sein (his). Schwester is feminine, so it takes -e: seine Schwester. "ihre" would mean "her" or "their".

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Bruder ___ zwei Kinder."
questions.explanation: Mein Bruder is the same as er, and the er/sie/es form of haben is hat. "habt" belongs to ihr, "hast" to du and "haben" to wir, sie and Sie.

questions.stem: You ask two friends: "___ ihr ein Tier?"
questions.explanation: With ihr (you, plural) the form of haben is habt: Habt ihr ein Tier? The verb comes first because it is a yes/no question.

questions.stem: You ask two children: "Ist das ___ Katze?"
questions.explanation: Talking to two children you use ihr, so "your" is euer. Katze is feminine, so euer takes -e and drops its second e: eure Katze. "deine" is for one person only.

questions.stem: What does "die Geschwister" mean?
questions.explanation: Die Geschwister means brothers and sisters together: siblings. Parents are die Eltern, grandparents die Großeltern.

questions.stem: What does "Meine Eltern sind geschieden." mean?
choices: My parents are separated by distance.
questions.explanation: Geschieden means divorced. Married is verheiratet and single is ledig.

questions.stem: Read: "Das ist meine Familie. Mein Vater heißt Klaus, meine Mutter heißt Petra. Ich habe einen Bruder, Max. Max ist verheiratet. Seine Frau heißt Lina, und sie haben ein Baby." Who is Lina?
questions.explanation: "Seine Frau heißt Lina": his (Max’s) wife is called Lina. Die Frau means both "woman" and "wife"; after a possessive it usually means wife. The mother is Petra, and the baby’s name isn’t given.

questions.stem: Someone shows you a photo and asks "Wer ist das?" Which answer is correct?
questions.explanation: Schwester is feminine, so "my" is meine. "Das ist" never changes for one person; "Das sind" is only for several people, and "er" means "he".

questions.stem: You speak formally to Frau Berg: "Frau Berg, ist das ___ Hund?"
questions.explanation: The formal "your" is Ihr with a capital I, matching the formal pronoun Sie. Lower-case ihr would mean "her" or "their", and dein is informal.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: Eltern is plural, and possessives take -e in the plural: Meine Eltern wohnen in Köln. The other sentences are correct: meine Tochter (feminine), unser Sohn and dein Opa (masculine).

questions.stem: Lisa und Tom haben einen Hund. "___ Hund heißt Rex."
questions.explanation: The dog belongs to Lisa and Tom, so you need "their": ihr. Hund is masculine, so no ending: Ihr Hund (capital only because it starts the sentence). Sein would mean "his", euer "your".

questions.stem: "Was sind Sie von Beruf?" Which answer is correct for a woman who teaches?
questions.explanation: German uses no article with jobs after sein, and a woman uses the -in form: Ich bin Lehrerin. "Lehrerinnen" is plural, and the verb here is sein (bin), not haben.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Vater ___ Spanisch."
questions.explanation: sprechen changes its stem vowel from e to i in the du and er/sie/es forms: er spricht. "sprecht" is the ihr form, and "sprechen" is for wir, sie and Sie.

questions.stem: Complete the question: "___ du Englisch?"
questions.explanation: The du form also has the stem change: du sprichst. "Sprechst" keeps the e by mistake, and "Spricht" is the er/sie/es form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich ___ ein bisschen Deutsch."
questions.explanation: The stem only changes for du and er/sie/es. The ich form is regular: ich spreche. "spriche" is a common mistake.

questions.stem: What is the feminine form of "der Arzt" (doctor)?
questions.explanation: Feminine job titles add -in, and Arzt also takes an umlaut: die Ärztin. The double n only appears in the plural: die Ärztinnen.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Die Türkei is one of the few countries that always take an article. After aus it becomes der: aus der Türkei (a set phrase for now; the dative comes in lesson 18). Most countries, like Spanien, need no article.

questions.stem: Which language do people speak in Frankreich?
questions.explanation: The language of France is Französisch. Many language names end in -isch, but they aren’t always formed from the country name. Französin means a Frenchwoman.

questions.stem: Read: "Hallo, ich heiße Elif. Ich komme aus der Türkei, aber ich wohne in Berlin. Ich bin Studentin. Ich spreche Türkisch, Deutsch und ein bisschen Englisch. Mein Bruder ist Koch." (aber = but) Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Elif says "Ich bin Studentin": she is a (university) student. Her brother is the cook, she lives in Berlin, and she speaks "ein bisschen Englisch", a little English.

questions.stem: What does "die Firma" mean?
questions.explanation: Die Firma means a company or firm: Meine Firma ist international. It has nothing to do with English "farm".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: The er form is spricht, and the name of a language is capitalized: Deutsch. English names like German are not used in German sentences.

questions.stem: What is the plural of "die Lehrerin" (female teacher)?
questions.explanation: Feminine nouns ending in -in add -nen in the plural: die Lehrerin, die Lehrerinnen.

questions.stem: Daniel is a man who studies at a university. What does he say?
questions.explanation: A man at university is a Student (no article after sein). A Schüler goes to school, Studentin is the female form, and Studenten is plural.

questions.stem: Your new colleague asks: "Welche Sprachen sprichst du?" Which is a fitting answer?
questions.explanation: Welche Sprachen sprichst du? means "Which languages do you speak?", so you name languages. The other answers say where you are from, what your job is, or don’t answer the question.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist ___ Hund, das ist eine Katze!"
questions.explanation: To negate a noun with ein, use kein: ein Hund becomes kein Hund. Hund is masculine, so there is no ending; keine is for feminine and plural nouns. German never says "nicht ein".

questions.stem: Complete: "Tut mir leid, ich habe ___ Zeit." (Tut mir leid = Sorry)
questions.explanation: Zeit has no article here, so you negate it with kein. Zeit is feminine (die Zeit), so it is keine: Ich habe keine Zeit.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist ___ mein Handy."
questions.explanation: A noun with a possessive (mein, dein …) or with der/die/das is negated with nicht, not kein: Das ist nicht mein Handy. "nein" means no as an answer.

questions.stem: A friend asks "Ist das nicht dein Schlüssel?" It is your key. What do you say?
choices: Ja, das ist nicht mein Schlüssel.
questions.explanation: To contradict a negative question you answer doch. "Nein" would agree with the negative ("No, it isn’t"), and "Nicht" is not an answer word.

questions.stem: Complete: "Die Stühle sind ___." (new)
questions.explanation: After sein an adjective never takes an ending, whatever the gender or number: Die Stühle sind neu. Endings only appear when the adjective stands before a noun.

questions.stem: What does "Die Tasche ist zu teuer." mean?
questions.explanation: zu before an adjective means "too", more than you want: zu teuer = too expensive. "Very" is sehr, and "also, too" is auch.

questions.stem: What is the opposite of "langweilig"?
questions.explanation: Langweilig means boring; its opposite is interessant. Lang (long) and langsam (slow) only look similar.

questions.stem: Read the ad: "Verkaufe Fahrrad, rot, 2 Jahre alt, sehr schnell. Das Licht ist kaputt. Nur 90 Euro!" (Verkaufe = I'm selling, Fahrrad = bicycle, Licht = light, nur = only) Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Das Licht ist kaputt: the light is broken. The bike is red (rot), very fast (sehr schnell) and costs only 90 euros.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: To negate a whole simple sentence, nicht usually goes at the end: Ich verstehe das nicht. German doesn’t put nicht before the verb and has no helper like English "don’t".

questions.stem: Which colour is "gelb"?
questions.explanation: Gelb is yellow. Green is grün and grey is grau.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: After sein, adjectives don’t take endings: Das Auto ist rot. The other sentences are correct.

questions.stem: How do you say "I’m bored" in German?
questions.explanation: Mir ist langweilig is the fixed phrase for "I’m bored". "Ich bin langweilig" means "I’m boring", a classic learner mistake.

questions.stem: What does "Die Tasche ist ziemlich schwer." mean?
questions.explanation: Ziemlich means quite or fairly, and schwer means heavy (or difficult). "Too heavy" would be zu schwer.

questions.stem: Complete the order: "Ich möchte ___ Kaffee, bitte." (der Kaffee)
questions.explanation: Kaffee is masculine (der Kaffee) and it is the direct object of möchte, so it takes the accusative: einen Kaffee. "ein Kaffee" is the nominative form, the most common mistake here.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir essen ___ Brot." (das Brot)
questions.explanation: Brot is neuter, and neuter articles don't change in the accusative: das Brot stays das Brot. Only masculine der becomes den, so "den Brot" is wrong.

questions.stem: Complete: "Paul ___ einen Apfel."
questions.explanation: essen changes e to i in the du and er/sie/es forms: er isst. "esst" is the ihr form (ihr esst), and it is the mistake you make if you forget the stem change.

questions.stem: Complete: "Du ___ einen Tee, oder?" (nehmen)
questions.explanation: nehmen changes in the du and er forms: du nimmst, er nimmt. The h disappears and the m doubles. "nimmt" is the er/sie/es form, and "nehmst" forgets the stem change.

questions.stem: Complete: "Er ___ ein Wasser."
questions.explanation: The er/sie/es form of möchten has no -t: er möchte, exactly like ich möchte. "möchtet" is the ihr form, and "möchtest" is the du form.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm hungry" in German?
questions.explanation: German says "I have hunger" with no article: Ich habe Hunger. In the same way, Ich habe Durst means I'm thirsty. "Ich bin Hunger" would mean "I am hunger", and "ich hat" has the wrong verb form (ich habe).

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Wasser is neuter (das Wasser), so its accusative is ein Wasser, not einen Wasser. The -en only goes on masculine words such as Saft and Fisch. "Das ist ein Apfel" is right because sein is followed by the nominative.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I like eating pasta"?
questions.explanation: The verb comes second and gern follows it: Ich esse gern Nudeln. "Ich gern esse" uses English word order, and "Ich essen" has the wrong verb ending.

questions.stem: Read the sign in a café: "Café Sonne. Unser Frühstück: ein Kaffee oder ein Tee, zwei Brötchen mit Butter und Käse, ein Ei. Saft kostet extra." What do you get with the breakfast?
questions.explanation: The breakfast has zwei Brötchen (two rolls) and ein Ei (an egg), plus coffee OR tea (oder = or). Juice (Saft) costs extra, and there is no sausage (Wurst).

questions.stem: The waiter asks: "Was möchten Sie trinken?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: The question is what you would like to drink (trinken), so name a drink: Ich möchte einen Tee, bitte. A cake (Kuchen) is food, and "Ja, ich trinke" doesn't answer a was-question.

questions.stem: What does "Ich habe keinen Durst" mean?
questions.explanation: Durst is thirst, and Durst haben means to be thirsty, so keinen Durst haben means not to be thirsty. Hunger is the word for hunger, and juice is Saft.

questions.stem: Why is it "den" in "Ich trinke den Saft"?
choices: Because the sentence is a question.
Because Saft is masculine and the direct object.
questions.explanation: der Saft is masculine, and here it is the thing being drunk, the direct object. Masculine der becomes den in the accusative. With a feminine or neuter drink the article would not change: Ich trinke die Milch, das Wasser.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wie viel ___ die Äpfel?"
questions.explanation: die Äpfel is plural, so the verb is plural: Wie viel kosten die Äpfel? With one thing you'd say kostet: Wie viel kostet der Apfel?

questions.stem: How do you say the price 3,50 €?
questions.explanation: Say the euros, then the cents, without "und" or "Cent": drei Euro fünfzig. Euro has no plural after a number, so "drei Euros" is wrong.

questions.stem: How is 470 written in words?
questions.explanation: Hundreds first, then the rest: vierhundert + siebzig. Seventy is siebzig, not siebenzig (sieben loses -en). siebzehn is 17.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich möchte ein Kilo ___, bitte."
questions.explanation: German puts the amount straight in front of the food with no word for "of" and no article: ein Kilo Äpfel, eine Flasche Wasser, 200 Gramm Käse. "ein Kilo von Äpfel" copies English.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ Wein nehmen Sie?" (der Wein)
questions.explanation: Wein is masculine and the object of nehmen, so it's accusative: welchen, with the same -n as den. "Welcher" is the nominative (Welcher Wein ist gut?).

questions.stem: Complete: "___ Brot ist frisch." (das Brot)
questions.explanation: dieser takes the endings of der, die, das. Brot is neuter (das), so it's dieses Brot: das ends in -s, and so does dieses.

questions.stem: Complete: "Hier gibt es ___ Supermarkt."
questions.explanation: es gibt is followed by the accusative, and Supermarkt is masculine (der Supermarkt), so: einen Supermarkt. "ein Supermarkt" is the nominative form.

questions.stem: A sign in a supermarket: "Angebot! 500 Gramm Kaffee: nur 4,99 €. Normaler Preis: 6,49 €." How much do you save?
questions.explanation: The normal price (Preis) is 6,49 € and the offer (Angebot) price is 4,99 €: 6.49 − 4.99 = 1.50 euros. German writes the decimal comma where English writes a point.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: After a number, Euro stays singular: zehn Euro. Kilo stays singular too (zwei Kilo), while feminine Flasche takes its plural (zwei Flaschen), so the other sentences are correct.

questions.stem: At the market the saleswoman asks: "Ist das alles?" What is a good answer?
choices: Ja, das ist alles. Was macht das?
questions.explanation: "Ist das alles?" means "Is that everything?" Answer yes, and ask for the total: Was macht das? (What does that come to?). The other answers don't make sense here.

questions.stem: A bike costs 1.500 €. How much is that?
questions.explanation: In German the point separates thousands and the comma marks decimals. 1.500 € is one thousand five hundred euros (tausendfünfhundert Euro). One and a half euros would be 1,50 €.

questions.stem: In a café the waiter asks: "Zusammen oder getrennt?" What does he want to know?
choices: Do you want to pay together or separately?
questions.explanation: zusammen means together and getrennt means separately: the waiter is asking whether one person pays for everyone or each person pays for their own order.

questions.stem: It's 2:30. How do you say this in everyday German?
questions.explanation: halb points to the next hour: halb drei is "half way to three", so 2:30. "halb zwei" is 1:30, the classic mistake for English speakers.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Kurs beginnt ___ neun Uhr."
questions.explanation: Clock times take um: um neun Uhr. am is for days and parts of the day (am Montag, am Abend).

questions.stem: Complete: "___ Montag arbeite ich nicht."
questions.explanation: Days of the week take am: am Montag. um is only for clock times, and "in Montag" copies English "on Monday" with the wrong word.

questions.stem: A train leaves at 19:45. How does the announcement say it?
questions.explanation: Official times are hours, then Uhr, then minutes: neunzehn Uhr fünfundvierzig. Viertel, nach and vor belong to the everyday 12-hour clock, not to the 24-hour clock.

questions.stem: Which everyday time means 8:45?
questions.explanation: 8:45 is a quarter to nine: Viertel vor neun. Viertel nach acht is 8:15, halb neun is 8:30, and Viertel vor acht is 7:45.

questions.stem: Which phrase means "at night"?
questions.explanation: The night is the exception among the parts of the day: in der Nacht. The others take am: am Morgen, am Nachmittag, am Abend.

questions.stem: How do you say "tomorrow morning"?
questions.explanation: German avoids "morgen Morgen" and says morgen früh. Compare heute Morgen (this morning) and morgen Abend (tomorrow evening).

questions.stem: A sign on a door: "Bäckerei Kraus. Montag bis Freitag 6:30 bis 18 Uhr, Samstag 7 bis 13 Uhr, Sonntag geschlossen." (geschlossen = closed) Can you buy bread on Saturday at 2 p.m.?
choices: No, on Saturday it closes at 1 p.m.
No, it's closed all day on Saturday.
questions.explanation: On Saturday (Samstag) the bakery is open from 7 to 13 Uhr, so it closes at 1 p.m. The 18 Uhr closing time is for Monday to Friday, and it is closed (geschlossen) on Sunday.

questions.stem: Complete: "Kaffee? Nein danke, ich trinke ___ Kaffee."
questions.explanation: "Nein danke" tells you the person doesn't drink coffee: ich trinke nie Kaffee, I never drink coffee. immer (always), oft (often) and manchmal (sometimes) don't fit a refusal.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Film ist zwei ___ lang."
questions.explanation: For a length of time use die Stunde, plural Stunden: zwei Stunden. Uhr only gives the time on the clock (Es ist zwei Uhr) and has no plural in times.

questions.stem: Someone asks you: "Wie spät ist es?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: "Wie spät ist es?" means "What time is it?", even though spät means late. Answer with Es ist and the time. "Am Montag" answers wann?, and "Zwei Stunden" answers wie lange?

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: With Uhr, one is ein: Es ist ein Uhr. Without Uhr it's eins: Es ist eins. "eins Uhr" mixes the two. halb eins (12:30) is correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
Ich stehe auf um sieben Uhr.
questions.explanation: aufstehen is separable: the verb part stehe goes in second place and the prefix auf goes to the very end. "Ich stehe auf um sieben Uhr" puts the prefix too early, as in English "I get up at seven".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: When a time phrase comes first, the verb is second and the subject follows it (inversion): Am Montag kaufe ich. The prefix ein still goes to the end. "Am Montag ich kaufe" keeps English word order.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Der Film fangt um acht an.
Der Film fängt um acht an.
Der Film fängst um acht an.
questions.explanation: anfangen splits (fängt … an) and keeps the stem change of fangen in the er/sie/es form: er fängt. "fangt" forgets the umlaut, and "fängst" is the du form.

questions.stem: Which verb is NOT separable?
questions.explanation: frühstücken stays in one piece: Ich frühstücke um acht. früh is not a separable prefix. The others split: ich stehe auf, ich kaufe ein, ich sehe fern.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "He watches TV every evening"?
questions.explanation: fernsehen splits, and sehen changes e to ie in the er form: er sieht … fern. The prefix fern goes to the end of the sentence, after jeden Abend.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I'm phoning my mother"?
questions.explanation: The verb part rufe is second, the person you call comes in the middle, and the prefix an goes to the end: Ich rufe meine Mutter an. "Ich rufe an meine Mutter" follows English "call up my mother".

questions.stem: Complete: "Zuerst dusche ich, dann ___."
questions.explanation: dann takes position 1, so the verb comes next and the subject after it: dann frühstücke ich. frühstücken is not separable, so "ich stücke früh" is wrong.

questions.stem: Read: "Normalerweise steht Maria um sechs Uhr auf. Zuerst duscht sie, dann frühstückt sie. Um sieben holt sie ihre Freundin Eva ab. Die Arbeit fängt um acht an. Um vier hat Maria Feierabend, und danach kauft sie ein." What does Maria do after work?
questions.explanation: Um vier hat Maria Feierabend means she finishes work at four, and danach kauft sie ein means after that she goes shopping. She picks up Eva at seven, before work.

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Ich gehe ins Kino. Kommst du mit?" What does she ask?
choices: Are you coming from the cinema?
questions.explanation: mitkommen means to come along (mit = with). Kommst du mit? is an invitation: "Are you coming along?" To arrive is ankommen.

questions.stem: Complete: "Psst! Das Baby ___."
questions.explanation: schlafen changes a to ä in the du and er/sie/es forms: das Baby (es) schläft. "schläfst" is the du form, and "schlaft" is the ihr form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich möchte heute ___."
questions.explanation: After möchte the second verb is an infinitive at the end, and a separable verb stays in one piece in the infinitive: einkaufen. It only splits when it is the conjugated verb (Ich kaufe heute ein).

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Dann räume ich die Küche auf.
Um acht kommt der Zug an.
questions.explanation: normalerweise fills position 1, so the verb must come next: Normalerweise stehe ich früh auf. The other sentences all have the verb second and the prefix at the end.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Bruder ___ jeden Tag Fahrrad." (fahren)
questions.explanation: Fahren changes a to ä in the du and er/sie/es forms: er fährt. "Fahrt" without the umlaut is the ihr form, "fahre" is the ich form, and "fähren" doesn't exist.

questions.stem: What is the du form of "lesen" (to read)?
questions.explanation: Lesen changes e to ie: du liest. Because the stem ends in -s, du only adds -t, so it is not "liesst". "Lest" is the ihr form, which keeps the plain e.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ihr ___ heute zwei Filme." (sehen)
questions.explanation: The stem change e → ie only happens with du and er/sie/es. The ihr form is regular: ihr seht. "Sieht" (er) and "siehst" (du) are the changed forms; "säht" is not a form of sehen.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: The verb comes in position 2 and gern follows it: Ich spiele gern Fußball. English word order ("Ich gern spiele") puts gern before the verb, which is wrong. "Mehr gern" doesn't exist; the comparative is lieber.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich trinke gern Kaffee, aber ___ trinke ich Tee." (most of all)
questions.explanation: Most of all = am liebsten, the superlative of gern. Lieber means "rather, prefer" (comparative). "Am lieber" mixes the two and is wrong. Note the inversion: am liebsten trinke ich.

questions.stem: What does "Ich jogge lieber." mean?
questions.explanation: Lieber is the comparative of gern: "rather, prefer". "I like jogging" would be Ich jogge gern; "most of all" would be am liebsten.

questions.stem: Which verb form is wrong?
questions.explanation: The stem change (e → i) only happens with du and er/sie/es. With wir the verb is regular: wir sprechen. Du hilfst, er gibt and du triffst are all correct changed forms.

questions.stem: Read: "Ich heiße Ben. In der Freizeit spiele ich gern Gitarre und singe in einer Band. Sport mache ich nicht gern, aber ich wandere manchmal. Am liebsten sehe ich Filme." What does Ben like doing most?
questions.explanation: Am liebsten sehe ich Filme = most of all I like watching films. He also likes playing the guitar and singing (gern), and he hikes only sometimes (manchmal).

questions.stem: Choose the right answer. "Was machst du gern in der Freizeit?"
choices: Ich lese gern und ich male.
questions.explanation: The question asks what you like doing in your free time, so you name activities: Ich lese gern und ich male. A W-question can't be answered with ja or nein, and "Am Wochenende, um acht" answers "when?".

questions.stem: Complete: "Er ___ seine Freunde am Samstag." (treffen)
questions.explanation: Treffen changes e to i in the du and er forms and keeps the double f: er trifft. "Trefft" is the ihr form; "triefft" uses ie, which is the pattern of lesen and sehen, not treffen.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Ihr fährt am Wochenende zusammen, und Lena schläft lange."
questions.explanation: With ihr there is no stem change: ihr fahrt. Lena is er/sie/es, so schläft with ä is correct. "Lange" (for a long time) is the right word here.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm meeting friends and we're going to the cinema"?
choices: Ich trifft Freunde und wir gehen ins Kino.
Ich treffe Freunde und wir fahren Kino.
Ich treffe Freunde und gehen wir ins Kino.
Ich treffe Freunde und wir gehen ins Kino.
questions.explanation: Ich treffe (ich has no stem change) and ins Kino gehen is the fixed chunk for going to the cinema. "Ich trifft" uses the er form; after und the word order doesn't change, so "und gehen wir" is wrong.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ du Klavier spielen?" (können)
questions.explanation: The du form of können is kannst: the vowel changes to a in the singular. "Kann" is the ich/er form, "könnst" keeps the plural vowel, and "kennst" comes from kennen (to know a person).

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: With a modal verb the infinitive goes to the end: Ich will Gitarre lernen. English order ("will lernen Gitarre") is wrong, modals never take zu, and the second verb stays in the infinitive (lernen, not lerne).

questions.stem: Complete: "Er ___ am Wochenende eine Party feiern." (möchten)
questions.explanation: Like all modal forms, the er form is the same as the ich form and has no -t: er möchte. "Möchtet" is ihr, "möchten" is wir/sie, "möchtest" is du.

questions.stem: What does "Ich will morgen kommen." mean?
choices: I would like to come tomorrow, please.
questions.explanation: Wollen means "to want": ich will = I want. It is a false friend: it never means the English future "I will". "I can" would be ich kann, and the polite "would like" is ich möchte.

questions.stem: You are in a café. What is the most polite way to order?
questions.explanation: Möchte is the polite "would like" and is normal for ordering. "Ich will" is direct and sounds demanding; "ich mag" means "I like (tea in general)", and "ich kann" means "I can".

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir ___ leider nicht Ski fahren." (können)
questions.explanation: The plural of a modal is regular and built from the infinitive: wir können. "Kann" is singular, "könnt" is the ihr form, and "kannen" doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Read: "Hallo Tim, ich mache am Freitag eine Party. Kannst du kommen? Du kannst auch deine Gitarre mitbringen. Jana kommt leider nicht. Lisa" What does Lisa ask Tim?
choices: to help Jana with the party
to come to a party and maybe bring his guitar
questions.explanation: Kannst du kommen? asks if he can come, and Du kannst auch deine Gitarre mitbringen invites him to bring (mitbringen) his guitar. Jana is not coming (kommt leider nicht); there is nothing about football or cooking.

questions.stem: Choose the right answer. "Hast du Lust auf Kino?"
questions.explanation: Hast du Lust auf …? means "Do you feel like …?", so a natural answer is Ja, gern! (Yes, I'd love to.) The other answers don't make sense; doch is only used to contradict a negative question.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Meine Schwester kannt sehr gut kochen."
questions.explanation: The er/sie/es form of a modal has no ending: sie kann. Meine is right for a feminine noun, the infinitive kochen at the end is right, and sehr gut is the normal way to say "very well".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I can't come today"?
choices: Ich kann nicht heute kommen nicht.
questions.explanation: The modal is in position 2, the infinitive at the end, and nicht goes just before the infinitive: Ich kann heute nicht kommen. Nicht can't follow the infinitive or stand before the modal.

questions.stem: Which question is correct?
questions.explanation: With a modal, a separable verb is joined again at the end in the infinitive: Willst du mitkommen? Without a modal you would say Kommst du mit?

questions.stem: What does "Ich habe keine Lust." mean?
questions.explanation: Lust haben means to feel like doing something, so keine Lust haben is "not to feel like it". No time = keine Zeit, no idea = keine Ahnung, no plan = keinen Plan.

questions.stem: Complete: "Du ___ morgen früh aufstehen." (müssen)
questions.explanation: Müssen loses its umlaut in the singular: du musst. "Müsst" is the ihr form, "muss" is ich/er, and "müssen" is wir/sie/Sie.

questions.stem: A sign says "Rauchen verboten". What does it mean?
questions.explanation: Verboten means forbidden, so Rauchen verboten = no smoking. "Allowed" would be erlaubt.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "You don't have to fill in the form"?
choices: Sie dürfen das Formular nicht ausfüllen.
Sie müssen das Formular nicht ausfüllen.
Sie können das Formular nicht ausfüllen.
questions.explanation: Nicht müssen means "not necessary": Sie müssen das Formular nicht ausfüllen. The tempting "dürfen nicht" means you are not allowed to fill it in, which is the English "must not".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "You mustn't park here"?
questions.explanation: English "must not" (forbidden) is German nicht dürfen: Hier darf man nicht parken. "Hier muss man nicht parken" only says you don't have to park here.

questions.stem: Complete: "Im Kino ___ man leise sein." (müssen)
questions.explanation: Man always takes the er/sie/es form: man muss. It may feel plural ("people"), but "man müssen" is wrong. "Musst" is du and "müsst" is ihr.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Sie müssen das Formular füllen aus.
questions.explanation: The infinitive goes to the end, and a separable verb is written as one word there: … das Formular ausfüllen. The prefix only separates when ausfüllen itself is the conjugated verb (Sie füllen das Formular aus).

questions.stem: You want to ask politely if you may open the window. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Darf ich …? asks for permission politely. "Ich muss …" says it is necessary for you, and "Du sollst …" tells someone else what to do.

questions.stem: Read the notice: "In der Bibliothek muss man leise sein. Essen und Trinken sind verboten, aber Wasser dürfen Sie trinken. Die Bibliothek schließt um 20 Uhr." (Bibliothek = library) What is allowed?
questions.explanation: Wasser dürfen Sie trinken = you may drink water. Eating is verboten, you must be quiet (leise), and the library closes (schließt) at 20 Uhr, which is 8 p.m.

questions.stem: Your doctor wants you to drink a lot of water. Complete: "Mein Arzt sagt, ich ___ viel Wasser trinken."
questions.explanation: Sollen passes on what another person (here the doctor) wants you to do: ich soll. Darf would mean you are allowed to, and will is your own wish, not the doctor's.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Man müssen hier pünktlich sein."
questions.explanation: Man takes the er/sie/es form: Man muss hier pünktlich sein. "Mann" with two n's is a man (a person), and adjectives after sein have no ending at A1.

questions.stem: Choose the right answer. "Darf ich hier warten?"
questions.explanation: The person asks for permission, so a natural answer gives it: Ja, natürlich. "Du musst nicht" (you don't have to) doesn't fit a request for permission, and the other answers don't answer the question.

questions.stem: What does "pünktlich" mean?
questions.explanation: Pünktlich means on time or punctual: Der Termin ist um neun. Wir müssen pünktlich sein. Quiet is leise or ruhig, important is wichtig, allowed is erlaubt.

questions.stem: How do you say "on the third of October"?
questions.explanation: On a date you use am + ordinal with -en: am dritten Oktober. Dates need the ordinal, not the plain number drei; im is for months alone (im Oktober); and the ordinal of 3 is irregular: dritte, not "dreite".

questions.stem: Complete: "Heute ist der ___ Mai." (1.)
questions.explanation: After der the ordinal ends in -e: der erste Mai. The -en ending (ersten) is used after am: am ersten Mai. The ordinal of 1 is irregular: erste.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe ___ Juli Geburtstag." (in July)
questions.explanation: With months and seasons you use im: im Juli. Am goes with a day or date (am 5. Juli), um with clock times, and "in Juli" without the m is a typical mistake.

questions.stem: What does "Es schneit und es ist sehr kalt." mean?
choices: It is snowing and very cold.
questions.explanation: Es schneit = it is snowing (schneien), kalt = cold. Raining would be es regnet, and the sun shining is die Sonne scheint.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Das Geschenk ist für mein Bruder.
Das Geschenk ist für meinem Bruder.
Das Geschenk ist für meinen Bruder.
Das Geschenk ist für meiner Bruder.
questions.explanation: Für always takes the accusative, and masculine words change: mein → meinen. "Mein Bruder" is the nominative; "meinem" is dative, which für never takes.

questions.stem: A German form shows the date 04.07. Which date is it?
questions.explanation: Germans write the day first, then the month: 04.07. is der vierte Juli, the 4th of July. Reading it the American way (April 7th) is a common mistake.

questions.stem: Which ordinal number is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Siebte (7th) is right. The ordinal of 3 is dritte, of 8 is achte with one t, and numbers below 20 add -te, not -ste: zweite.

questions.stem: Read: "Hallo Max, am Samstag habe ich Geburtstag und ich mache eine Party. Sie fängt um 19 Uhr an. Kannst du Musik mitbringen? Eva" When does the party start?
questions.explanation: Am Samstag = on Saturday, and um 19 Uhr is 7 p.m. in the 24-hour clock. Don't confuse 19 (neunzehn) with 9.

questions.stem: A friend invites you, but you have to work. What do you say?
choices: Leider kann ich nicht. Ich muss arbeiten.
questions.explanation: To decline politely, say leider (unfortunately) and give a reason: Leider kann ich nicht. Ich muss arbeiten. "Ja, gern" accepts, and Herzlichen Glückwunsch is for congratulating.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Im Winter es schneit oft."
questions.explanation: When a time phrase like im Winter comes first, the verb stays in position 2 and the subject follows: Im Winter schneit es oft. Im is right with seasons, and nouns like Winter are capitalized.

questions.stem: What do you say to someone on their birthday?
questions.explanation: The standard phrase is Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag! "Guten Geburtstag" is a word-for-word copy of English and isn't used; Gute Besserung means "get well soon".

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir gehen ___ den Park." (through)
questions.explanation: Through = durch, and like für, ohne and um it takes the accusative: durch den Park. Für means for, ohne without, um at (a time) or around.

questions.stem: A woman gives you directions. Which verb form fits? "___ Sie bitte geradeaus!"
questions.explanation: The polite imperative is the Sie form of the verb, then Sie: Gehen Sie geradeaus! Geht is the ihr imperative and Geh the du imperative, and neither can be used with Sie. Gehst is a present- tense du form, not an imperative.

questions.stem: You tell a friend how to get to your flat. Complete: "___ den Bus Nummer 5!"
questions.explanation: For the du imperative, start from the du form (du nimmst) and drop the ending -st: Nimm! The e to i change stays. Nehm is a very common mistake: it ignores the stem change. Nimmst still has its ending, and Nehmen without Sie is not a polite imperative.

questions.stem: Which is the correct du imperative of "fahren"?
questions.explanation: Verbs with the a to ä change (du fährst) lose the umlaut in the imperative: Fahr langsam! Fähr keeps an umlaut that belongs only to the du and er forms, and Fährst or Fahrst keep the -st ending.

questions.stem: You ask two noisy children to be quiet. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Two children means ihr, and the ihr imperative of sein is Seid! Sei is for one person (du), Seien goes with Sie, and seit (with t) is the preposition "since", not a form of sein.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Abbiegen Sie an der Ampel links!
Biegen Sie an der Ampel links ab!
Sie biegen ab an der Ampel links!
Biegen ab Sie an der Ampel links!
questions.explanation: Abbiegen is separable. In the imperative the verb part comes first, then Sie, and the prefix ab goes to the very end: Biegen Sie an der Ampel links ab! The other choices keep the prefix attached or put it in the middle.

questions.stem: What does "geradeaus" mean?
questions.explanation: Geradeaus means straight ahead, straight on: Gehen Sie geradeaus. It has nothing to do with time, so it does not mean "straight away". On the right is rechts.

questions.stem: Complete the question: "Entschuldigung, wie komme ich ___ Post?"
questions.explanation: Post is feminine (die Post), so you say zur Post. Zum is for masculine and neuter places (zum Bahnhof, zum Museum). Zu die is never correct: after zu the article changes, and zu der is shortened to zur.

questions.stem: Read the message: "Hallo Mia! Geh vom Bahnhof geradeaus bis zum Marktplatz. Nimm dort die zweite Straße rechts. Unser Café ist an der Ecke, gegenüber der Kirche." Where is the café?
choices: on the corner, opposite the church
on the second street on the left
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the café is an der Ecke (on the corner), gegenüber der Kirche (opposite the church). The market square is only where Mia turns, and she turns rechts (right), not left.

questions.stem: You ask: "Entschuldigung, ist das Museum weit?" Which answer fits?
choices: Ja, das Museum hat ein Café.
Nein, nur fünf Minuten zu Fuß.
questions.explanation: Weit means far, so a good answer is about distance: Nein, nur fünf Minuten zu Fuß (No, only five minutes on foot). The other answers say yes or no but talk about something else.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Nehmen changes e to i in the du form (du nimmst), and the du imperative keeps that change: Nimm den Stadtplan! Lies, Sprich and Warte are all correct du imperatives.

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Die Bank ist rechts." What does she mean?
choices: The bank is on the right.
questions.explanation: Rechts is the direction right. Correct is richtig, a different word that English speakers often mix up with rechts. Straight ahead is geradeaus and far is weit.

questions.stem: You ask a stranger in the street for help. Which request is polite and correct?
choices: Zeigen Sie mir bitte den Weg.
questions.explanation: With a stranger you use Sie, and the Sie imperative needs Sie after the verb: Zeigen Sie mir bitte den Weg. Zeig (du) and Zeigt (ihr) are for friends, and Zeigen without Sie is incomplete.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich fahre mit ___ Bus zur Arbeit."
questions.explanation: Mit always takes the dative, and Bus is masculine (der Bus), so the dative article is dem: mit dem Bus. Den is the accusative, which English speakers often choose because English has no difference here.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir fahren mit ___ U-Bahn."
questions.explanation: U-Bahn is feminine (die U-Bahn). After mit you need the dative, and the feminine dative article is der: mit der U-Bahn. Die is the nominative and accusative, and dem is for masculine and neuter nouns.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich gehe heute ___ Arzt."
questions.explanation: Going to a person or place with an article uses zu, and zu dem is shortened to zum: zum Arzt. Zur and zu der are feminine, but Arzt is masculine. Nach is for cities and countries.

questions.stem: Complete: "Im Sommer fliegen wir ___ Spanien."
questions.explanation: Countries and cities without an article take nach: nach Spanien, nach Berlin. Zu is for people and places with an article, and bei means at someone's place.

questions.stem: How do you say "I've been living in Hamburg for two years"?
choices: Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren in Hamburg.
Ich wohne für zwei Jahre in Hamburg.
Ich wohne seit zwei Jahre in Hamburg.
Ich wohne zwei Jahre seit in Hamburg.
questions.explanation: For something that started in the past and is still going on, German uses seit with the present tense. Seit takes the dative, so the plural noun adds -n: seit zwei Jahren. Für zwei Jahre is a word-for-word translation of the English.

questions.stem: Complete: "Am Wochenende bin ich bei meinen ___."
questions.explanation:
Bei takes the dative. In the dative plural the article is den (here meinen), and the noun adds
-n unless it already ends in -n or -s: die Freunde becomes meinen Freunden.

questions.stem: It's late. Which sentence means "I'm going home now"?
questions.explanation: Going home is nach Hause; being at home is zu Hause. Ich bin jetzt zu Hause means "I'm at home now". Zum Haus means "to the house", not home.

questions.stem: Read the announcement: "Achtung an Gleis 5: Der Zug nach München, Abfahrt 14:12 Uhr, hat heute circa 20 Minuten Verspätung." When will the train probably leave?
questions.explanation: The train normally leaves (Abfahrt) at 14:12, but it has about 20 minutes of Verspätung (delay), so it will leave at about 14:32.

questions.stem: "Woher kommst du jetzt?" — "Ich komme ___ der Arbeit."
questions.explanation: Von is for the place you have just left: von der Arbeit, vom Bahnhof. Aus is for where you come from originally (aus Kanada) or for coming out of something. Zu and nach mean "to".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Umsteigen is separable: the verb part steigen is in position 2 and um goes to the end: Wir steigen in Köln um. In Köln wir steigen um breaks the verb-second rule; after In Köln it must be steigen wir.

questions.stem: At the ticket counter the clerk asks: "Einfach oder hin und zurück?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: The question is "single or return?", so you answer with one of the two: Hin und zurück, bitte (a return, please). The other answers talk about transport, platforms or changing trains.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Mit takes the dative, and possessives take dative endings too. Auto is neuter, so it must be mit ihrem Auto. The other sentences correctly use meiner (feminine), dem (masculine) and zur (zu der).

questions.stem: Complete: "Das Buch ist auf ___ Tisch."
questions.explanation: The question is Wo? (where is it?), so auf takes the dative. Tisch is masculine, so the article is dem: auf dem Tisch. Den would be the accusative, used for movement onto the table.

questions.stem: Complete: "Die Milch ist ___ Kühlschrank."
questions.explanation: Kühlschrank is masculine; in + dem becomes im: im Kühlschrank. In alone is missing the article, am means at or on, and ins (in das) is for movement into a place.

questions.stem: The photo is on the wall. Complete: "Das Foto ist ___ der Wand."
questions.explanation: Things on a vertical surface like a wall are an: an der Wand. Auf is for horizontal surfaces such as a table or the floor; English "on" covers both.

questions.stem: "Wie findest du den Schrank?" — "Ich finde ___ schön."
questions.explanation: Schrank is masculine (der Schrank), and here it is the object of finden, so you need the accusative pronoun ihn. Er is the subject form, and es would be for a neuter noun. English "it" covers all three.

questions.stem: "Wo ist die Lampe?" — "___ ist im Wohnzimmer."
questions.explanation: Lampe is feminine (die Lampe), so the pronoun is sie, even though English says "it". Using es for every thing is a common mistake.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Kühlschrank ist in ___ Küche."
questions.explanation: Küche is feminine (die Küche). For location (Wo?) in takes the dative, and the feminine dative article is der: in der Küche. There is no contraction for feminine nouns.

questions.stem: Read the advert: "Schöne 2-Zimmer-Wohnung im 3. Stock, helle Küche, Bad mit Fenster, Balkon. Miete: 750 Euro warm. Kein Aufzug." Which statement is true?
choices: The rent does not include heating.
The flat is on the ground floor.
The flat has two rooms plus a kitchen and a bathroom.
questions.explanation: In German adverts the kitchen and bathroom are not counted, so a 2-Zimmer-Wohnung has two rooms plus kitchen and bathroom. Warm means heating is included, kein Aufzug means there is no lift, and the flat is on the third floor.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "The chair is between the sofa and the window"?
choices: Der Stuhl ist zwischen das Sofa und das Fenster.
Der Stuhl ist neben dem Sofa und dem Fenster.
Der Stuhl ist zwischen dem Sofa und dem Fenster.
Der Stuhl ist zwischen der Sofa und der Fenster.
questions.explanation: Zwischen means between. For location it takes the dative, and Sofa and Fenster are both neuter, so both become dem. Das is the nominative or accusative, der is the wrong gender, and neben means next to.

questions.stem: "Wo ist die Katze?" Which answer is correct?
questions.explanation: Wo? asks about location, so unter takes the dative. Bett is neuter (das Bett), so the dative is dem: unter dem Bett.

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Dein Wohnzimmer ist sehr gemütlich!" What does she mean?
choices: Your living room is very dark.
Your living room is very modern.
Your living room is very expensive.
Your living room is very cosy.
questions.explanation: Gemütlich means cosy, comfortable and pleasant to be in. Dark is dunkel, modern is modern, and expensive is teuer.

questions.stem: Someone says: "Ich wohne im ersten Stock." Where does this person live?
choices: one floor above the ground floor
in the first house on the street
in the first room on the left
questions.explanation: German floors are counted from the ground floor (das Erdgeschoss), so im ersten Stock is one floor up: the first floor in British English, the second floor in American English.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Die Lampe ist über dem Tisch.
Der Garten ist hinter dem Haus.
Das Regal ist neben der Schrank.
Die Tasche ist auf dem Boden.
questions.explanation: Schrank is masculine, so the dative after neben is dem: neben dem Schrank. Der Schrank is the nominative; der before a noun is only dative for feminine nouns.

questions.stem: How do you say "I have a headache"?
questions.explanation: German uses haben with the plural Schmerzen: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen. Or with wehtun: Mein Kopf tut weh (not hat weh).

questions.stem: Complete: "Meine Füße ___ weh."
questions.explanation: Wehtun is separable: tun is the verb in position 2 and weh goes to the end. Füße is plural, so the verb is tun. Tut is for one body part: Mein Fuß tut weh.

questions.stem: "Wie geht es dir?" — "___ geht es nicht gut."
questions.explanation: The answer copies the pattern of the question: es geht + dative. Dir becomes mir: Mir geht es nicht gut. Ich is the nominative and mich the accusative.

questions.stem: Complete: "Kannst du ___ helfen?"
questions.explanation: Helfen always takes the dative, so you need mir: Kannst du mir helfen? Mich is the accusative, a very common mistake because English uses "me" for both.

questions.stem: You say to a friend: "I'll call you tomorrow." Complete: "Ich rufe ___ morgen an."
questions.explanation: Anrufen takes a direct object, so the accusative pronoun is needed: dich. Dir is the dative (Wie geht es dir?), du is the subject form, and dein means your.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm cold"?
questions.explanation: Feeling cold uses the dative: Mir ist kalt. Ich bin kalt describes your character (a cold person). Ich habe kalt is a word-for-word translation from French or Spanish.

questions.stem: Read the sign: "Praxis Dr. Sommer. Sprechzeiten: Mo, Di, Do 8–12 und 15–18 Uhr; Mi, Fr 8–12 Uhr." (Sprechzeiten = opening hours) Can you see the doctor on Wednesday afternoon?
choices: No, on Wednesday the practice is only open in the morning.
No, the practice is closed all day on Wednesday.
questions.explanation: Mi (Mittwoch) is listed with Fr: only 8 to 12. The afternoon hours, 15 to 18, are only on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday.

questions.stem: A colleague says: "Ich bin krank, ich habe Fieber." What do you say?
questions.explanation: Gute Besserung! means Get well soon! Herzlichen Glückwunsch is for birthdays, Guten Appetit before a meal and Gute Reise for someone setting off on a trip.

questions.stem: What is the plural of "die Hand"?
questions.explanation: Hand takes an umlaut and -e in the plural: zwei Hände. The same pattern: der Fuß, die Füße; der Zahn, die Zähne.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Bruder ist krank. Wie geht es ___?"
questions.explanation: Es geht + dative: Wie geht es dir / Ihnen / ihm? The dative of er is ihm. Ihn is the accusative, er the nominative, and sein means his.

questions.stem: Your friend is picking you and your sister up. Complete: "Holst du ___ am Bahnhof ab?"
questions.explanation: You need the object form of wir, which is uns (the same in the accusative and dative). Unser means our, and euch means you (plural).

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Helfen takes the dative: Kannst du mir helfen? The other sentences are correct: Mir ist schlecht (I feel sick), Mein Bauch tut weh (my stomach hurts), Ich verstehe dich nicht (I don't understand you).

questions.stem: Leon says: "Mein Hals tut weh." Where is the pain?
questions.explanation: Der Hals is the neck and throat; Halsschmerzen is a sore throat. Ear is das Ohr, back is der Rücken, and stomach is der Bauch.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: "Ich ___ gestern einen Ausflug gemacht."
questions.explanation: "Machen" forms its perfect with haben, and the subject is "ich", so the form is "habe". "Bin" is the sein auxiliary, used for movement verbs, not for "machen". "Hat" is for er/sie/es and "haben" for wir/sie/Sie.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of "kaufen" (to buy)?
questions.explanation: "Kaufen" is a regular (weak) verb: ge- + stem + -t gives "gekauft". "Gekaufen" mixes in the -en ending of strong verbs, which "kaufen" doesn't have. "Kaufte" is a different past form you don't need at A1.

questions.stem: Complete: "Am Sonntag haben wir unsere Oma ___." (visited)
questions.explanation: "Besuchen" has the inseparable prefix be-, which blocks ge-. The participle is simply "besucht". "Gebesucht" is the most common learner mistake: it adds ge- as if the verb had no prefix.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of the separable verb "einkaufen" (to go shopping)?
questions.explanation: In separable verbs, ge- goes between the prefix and the stem: ein + ge + kauft = "eingekauft", written as one word. "Geeinkauft" puts ge- in front of the whole verb, and "einkauft" leaves it out.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: In the perfect, haben is in position 2 and the participle goes to the very end, with the object in between: "Ich habe eine Pizza gegessen." Putting "gegessen" right after "habe" copies English word order ("I have eaten a pizza").

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Bruder hat in Berlin ___." (studied)
questions.explanation: Verbs ending in -ieren never take ge- in the participle: "studieren" becomes "studiert", like "fotografiert". "Gestudiert" is a very common mistake.

questions.stem: Complete: "Hast du Brot ___?" (brought)
questions.explanation: "Bringen" is a mixed verb: the vowel changes like a strong verb, but the ending is -t like a weak verb. The participle is "gebracht". "Gebringt" treats it as regular, and "gebrungen" copies the pattern of "trinken – getrunken".

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich ___ Frau Müller schon lange." (I've known Ms Müller for a long time.)
questions.explanation: You know a person with "kennen", and the ich form is "kenne". "Wissen" (ich weiß) is for facts and information, not people. "Kennen" without an ending is the infinitive or the wir/sie form.

questions.stem:
Read the postcard:
"Liebe Mia, wir sind in Hamburg! Gestern haben wir den Hafen (the harbour) besucht und Fisch gegessen. Heute habe ich Postkarten gekauft. Leider habe ich meine Brille verloren! Viele Grüße, Jan" What went wrong for Jan?
questions.explanation: "Leider habe ich meine Brille verloren" means "Unfortunately I've lost my glasses". "Verloren" is the participle of "verlieren" (to lose). He did buy postcards ("Postkarten gekauft"), and nothing negative is said about the fish or the harbour.

questions.stem: What does "Ich habe gerade gegessen." mean?
questions.explanation: "Gerade" with the perfect means "just (a moment ago)": I've just eaten. With the present tense ("Ich esse gerade") it would mean "I'm eating right now", but here the verb is in the perfect.

questions.stem: Your friend asks: "Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?" What is the best answer?
questions.explanation: The question is in the perfect and asks what you did, so answer in the perfect: "Ich habe meine Eltern besucht" (I visited my parents). "Ich mache am Wochenende Sport" is present tense and talks about a habit. "Ja" doesn't answer a W-question.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: "Verkaufen" has the inseparable prefix ver-, so its participle has no ge-: "Wir haben das Auto verkauft." The other three are correct: "gesehen" and "geholfen" are strong participles, and "verstanden" also has no ge- because of ver-.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir ___ nach Spanien geflogen."
questions.explanation: "Fliegen" is a verb of movement from one place to another, so it takes sein, and the wir form of sein is "sind". "Haben" is the tempting English-style choice ("we have flown"). "Seid" is for ihr and "ist" for er/sie/es.

questions.stem: Complete: "Was ___ passiert?"
questions.explanation: "Passieren" (to happen) always forms its perfect with sein: "Was ist passiert?" (What happened?). It is one of the verbs you simply have to learn with sein, together with "sein" and "bleiben".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ich habe um sieben Uhr aufgestanden.
Ich bin um sieben Uhr aufgestehen.
Ich habe um sieben Uhr aufgesteht.
Ich bin um sieben Uhr aufgestanden.
questions.explanation: "Aufstehen" is a change of state (from lying to standing), so it takes sein, and its participle is strong: auf + ge + standen = "aufgestanden". The first choice uses the wrong auxiliary; the other two have invented participles.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wo ___ du gestern?"
questions.explanation: The du form of "war" takes the usual -st ending: "du warst". "War" is the ich and er/sie/es form, and "wart" is for ihr.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir ___ leider keine Zeit." (We unfortunately didn't have time.)
questions.explanation: The wir form of "hatte" ends in -en: "wir hatten", just like "wir haben" in the present. "Hatte" is ich/er, "hattest" is du and "hattet" is ihr.

questions.stem: Which of these verbs forms its perfect with haben?
questions.explanation: "Essen" takes an object (etwas essen) and involves no movement, so it uses haben: "Ich habe gegessen." "Kommen" and "fliegen" are movement verbs (ist gekommen, ist geflogen), and "bleiben" is one of the special verbs with sein (ist geblieben).

questions.stem: What does "Wir sind im See geschwommen." mean?
choices: We are swimming in the lake.
questions.explanation: "Der See" (masculine) is a lake; the sea is "das Meer". "Sind … geschwommen" is the perfect, so it describes the past: we swam. "We saw" would be "Wir haben … gesehen".

questions.stem: Complete the question: "___ seid ihr gefahren?" — "Nach Österreich."
questions.explanation: The answer gives a destination ("to Austria"), so the question asks "where to": "Wohin". "Wo" asks about a position (where something is), and "Woher" asks where someone comes from.

questions.stem:
Read the text:
"Letztes Jahr bin ich mit meiner Freundin nach Kroatien gefahren. Wir waren auf einer Insel. Am Strand war es sehr heiß. Nach drei Tagen ist meine Freundin plötzlich krank geworden, und wir sind nach Hause gefahren." Why did they go home?
questions.explanation: "Nach drei Tagen ist meine Freundin plötzlich krank geworden" means "After three days my girlfriend suddenly became ill". "Geworden" is the participle of "werden" (to become), which takes sein. The weather was hot ("sehr heiß"), not bad.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: "Gehen" is a movement verb, so it needs sein: "Wir sind nach Hause gegangen." The other sentences are correct: "bleiben", "werden" and "umziehen" all take sein.

questions.stem: Your neighbour asks: "Wie war der Urlaub?" What is the best answer?
questions.explanation: "Wie war …?" asks how something was, so a past answer that describes it fits: "Super! Das Wetter war toll." The other answers talk about the present or future, and "Ja" doesn't answer a W-question.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Zug ist pünktlich ___." (departed)
questions.explanation: "Abfahren" is separable and "fahren" is strong, so the participle is ab + ge + fahren = "abgefahren", written as one word. "Abgefahrt" gives it a weak ending, and "gefahren ab" splits the participle like a present-tense verb.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ ihr schon einmal in Wien?" (Have you ever been to Vienna?)
questions.explanation: The ihr form of "war" is "wart" (ihr wart), with the -t ending of ihr. "Waren" is for wir and sie/Sie, and "warst" for du. "Wartet" is a form of "warten" (to wait).

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich komme heute nicht, ___ ich bin krank."
questions.explanation: The second half gives the reason, so the linking word is "denn" (because). "Aber" would contrast two ideas, and "sondern" needs to correct a negative. After "denn" the word order stays normal: "ich bin krank".

questions.stem: Which sentence has the correct word order?
choices: Ich gehe nach Hause, denn bin ich müde.
Ich gehe nach Hause, denn ich müde bin.
Ich gehe nach Hause, denn müde ich bin.
Ich gehe nach Hause, denn ich bin müde.
questions.explanation: "Denn" stands in position zero and doesn't change the word order: the second half is a normal sentence with the verb in position 2, "ich bin müde". Putting the verb at the end is the rule for "weil", which comes at A2.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist nicht mein Handy, ___ das Handy von Tom."
questions.explanation: The first half is negative ("nicht mein Handy") and the second half corrects it, so you need "sondern" (but rather). "Aber" is the tempting choice because English uses "but" for both.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das Zimmer ist klein, ___ es ist sehr hell."
questions.explanation: There is a contrast (small, but bright) and no negative to correct, so the word is "aber". "Sondern" only follows "nicht" or "kein". "Denn" would give a reason, which doesn't make sense here.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ich bin krank, deshalb ich bleibe zu Hause.
Ich bin krank, deshalb zu Hause bleibe ich.
Ich bin krank, deshalb ich zu Hause bleibe.
Ich bin krank, deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.
questions.explanation: "Deshalb" is not a conjunction but an adverb in position 1, so the verb comes straight after it and the subject follows: "deshalb bleibe ich". Keeping "ich bleibe" treats deshalb like "denn".

questions.stem: You are writing an e-mail to your friend Tom. How do you start?
questions.explanation: For a man the opening is "Lieber" + name; "Liebe" is for a woman (Liebe Anna). "Sehr geehrte" is formal and is used with Frau/Herr and a surname, never with a first name.

questions.stem: You are writing to an office where you don't know anyone. Which closing is right?
questions.explanation: "Mit freundlichen Grüßen" is the standard formal closing, used with "Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren". "Viele Grüße", "Liebe Grüße" and "Bis bald!" are for friends and people you know.

questions.stem: On a German form, what does the field "Staatsangehörigkeit" ask for?
questions.explanation: "Staatsangehörigkeit" is your nationality or citizenship, usually written as an adjective (deutsch, amerikanisch). Place of birth is "Geburtsort", marital status "Familienstand" and signature "Unterschrift".

questions.stem: A form says "Geburtsdatum: 04.07.1998". When was this person born?
questions.explanation: German dates go day, month, year: 04.07. is the 4th of the 7th month, which is July. Reading it as 7 April is the American month-first order.

questions.stem:
Read the message:
"Hallo Ben, danke für die Einladung! Ich komme gern am Freitag zum Grillen (to the barbecue), aber ich kann erst um acht Uhr kommen, denn ich muss bis sieben arbeiten. Soll ich etwas mitbringen (bring along)? Viele Grüße, Nina" Why is Nina coming late?
choices: She has to work until seven.
She has to buy food first.
