questions.explanation: The reason comes after "denn": "ich muss bis sieben arbeiten" (I have to work until seven). Nina is happy to come ("Ich komme gern"), and she offers to bring something, but she doesn't say she has to buy food.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Ich trinke keinen Tee, sondern Kaffee.
Er ist müde, aber er arbeitet.
Wir bleiben hier, denn es regnet.
Ich wohne in Berlin, sondern in Hamburg.
questions.explanation: "Sondern" needs a negative before it. Correct would be "Ich wohne nicht in Berlin, sondern in Hamburg." The first sentence is fine because "keinen" is negative.

questions.stem: What does "Ich muss den Termin leider absagen." mean?
choices: Unfortunately I have to cancel the appointment.
Unfortunately I have to make an appointment.
I have to confirm the appointment.
I'll be late for the appointment.
questions.explanation: "Absagen" means to cancel (an appointment or event), and "leider" means unfortunately. The noun is "die Absage", a message saying you can't come.

questions.stem: Which answer fits the form field "Familienstand"?
questions.explanation: "Familienstand" is marital status: ledig (single), verheiratet (married) or geschieden (divorced). "Weiblich" answers "Geschlecht", "deutsch" answers "Staatsangehörigkeit" and "Köln" could be your "Geburtsort" or "Ort".

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe die Prüfung ___!" (I passed the exam!)
questions.explanation: "Bestehen" has the inseparable prefix be-, so there is no ge-, and it is strong (like "verstehen – verstanden"): "bestanden". "Gebestanden" adds a ge- that the prefix blocks.

questions.stem: How many points do you need to pass the Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1?
questions.explanation: The pass mark is 60 of 100 points. 60–69 is "ausreichend", 70–79 "befriedigend", 80–89 "gut" and 90–100 "sehr gut".

questions.stem: Which part of the Goethe A1 exam takes place in a small group, without preparation time?
questions.explanation: Sprechen (speaking) is a short oral exam in a small group: you introduce yourself, ask and answer questions with word cards, and make and respond to requests. Hören, Lesen and Schreiben are written together in one block.

questions.stem: The examiner says something and you don't catch it. What do you say?
choices: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
questions.explanation: "Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?" asks the person to say it again. "Was bedeutet das?" asks about the meaning of a word you heard, and "Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?" asks for a German word.

questions.stem: Complete: "Hast du etwas gesagt?" — "Nein, ich habe ___ gesagt."
questions.explanation: The opposite of "etwas" (something) is "nichts" (nothing). "Nicht" negates a verb but can't replace an object, "kein" goes with a noun, and "niemand" means nobody.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich nehme ___ Kaffee." (der Kaffee)
questions.explanation: "Kaffee" is the direct object, so it is in the accusative, and masculine "ein" becomes "einen" (lesson 9). "Ein" is the nominative, and "einem" is the dative.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: The verb is always the second element in a statement. When "Am Montag" comes first, the verb follows and the subject moves behind it: "Am Montag arbeite ich" (lessons 4 and 12). "Am Montag ich arbeite" is English word order.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich kann heute leider nicht ___."
questions.explanation: After a modal verb such as "können", the second verb goes to the end in the infinitive: "kommen" (lesson 14). "Gekommen" is the participle, used with haben or sein in the perfect.

questions.stem: Which question is correct? (anfangen = to start)
questions.explanation: "Anfangen" is separable: the verb "fängt" stays in position 2 and the prefix "an" goes to the end (lesson 12). It also has a stem change, a → ä, in the er/sie/es form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich fahre mit ___ Bus zur Arbeit." (der Bus)
questions.explanation: "Mit" is always followed by the dative, and masculine "der" becomes "dem" (lesson 18). "Den" is the accusative, which is a common mix-up.

questions.stem: Complete: "Gestern ___ wir ins Kino gegangen."
questions.explanation: "Gehen" is a verb of movement, so its perfect uses sein, and the wir form is "sind" (lesson 22). "Haben" is the auxiliary for most other verbs.

questions.stem:
Read the sign:
"Bäckerei Schmidt. Montag bis Freitag 6:30–18:00 Uhr, Samstag 7:00–12:00 Uhr, Sonntag geschlossen." It is Saturday, 2 p.m. Is the bakery open?
choices: No, it is closed all day on Saturday.
questions.explanation: On Saturday ("Samstag") the bakery is open from 7:00 to 12:00, so at 2 p.m. (14:00) it is already closed. The 18:00 closing time is for Monday to Friday, and "geschlossen" (closed) is for Sunday.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist ___ Schwester." (my)
questions.explanation: "Schwester" is feminine (die Schwester), so the possessive takes -e: "meine Schwester" (lesson 6). "Mein" is for masculine and neuter nouns in the nominative.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
questions.explanation: In German the first word of a sentence and every noun start with a capital letter: "Hund" is a noun, so it is capitalized, but verbs and articles are not (lessons 1 and 5).

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe ___ Auto." (I don't have a car.)
questions.explanation: A noun with "ein" is negated with "kein", and "Auto" is neuter, so "kein Auto" (lesson 8). "Nicht" doesn't replace an article, and "keine" is for feminine and plural nouns.

glossary.definition: A letter or sound made with the mouth open and the air flowing freely: a, e, i, o, u, plus ä, ö, ü in German. Every German vowel can be long (Tag, sie) or short (Stadt, bitte), and the length can change the meaning of a word.
A sound made by partly or fully blocking the air with the lips, tongue or throat, such as b, k, s or ch. In German, a vowel before a double consonant (ll, mm, ss, tt) is usually short: Hallo, kommen.

The two dots over a, o or u (ä, ö, ü), which change the vowel's sound. They are part of the spelling: schon (already) and schön (beautiful) are different words. Write ae, oe, ue only if you cannot type the real letters.

Two vowel sounds that glide together in one syllable. German has three: ei/ai (as in eye: nein), eu/äu (as in boy: Deutschland), au (as in cow: Frau). Note that ie is not a diphthong but a long ee sound.
The rule that b, d and g at the end of a word or syllable are pronounced like p, t and k: Tag sounds like "tahk", und like "oont". The spelling stays the same.

The syllable said more strongly than the others. German words are usually stressed on the first syllable (DAN-ke), except after prefixes such as be-, ent-, ver- (ver-STE-hen), in verbs ending in -ieren (stu-DIE-ren) and in many borrowed words (Ad-RES-se).

A word for a person, place, thing or idea: Name, Stadt, Wort. In German every noun starts with a capital letter and has a gender, shown by its article der, die or das, so learn each noun with its article.
The friendly way of addressing someone, with du (one person) or ihr (two or more). Used with friends, family, children, and among students and young people. Goes with first names.

The polite way of addressing someone, with Sie (always capitalized), for one or more people. Used with adults you don't know, staff in shops and offices, and anyone you call Herr or Frau. The verb form is the same as the infinitive: Sie wohnen, Sie heißen (except Sie sind).
A word for an action or state, such as wohnen (to live), kommen (to come) or sein (to be). In a German sentence the verb changes its ending to match the subject: ich wohne, du wohnst.
The basic form of a verb, the one listed in a dictionary. German infinitives end in -en or -n: machen, arbeiten, sein. Remove the -en to find the stem.
The person or thing that does the action of the verb, or that the sentence is about: in Ich wohne in Berlin, the subject is ich. The verb ending must match the subject.

A question that starts with a question word such as wer (who), wie (how), wo (where), woher (where from), was (what), warum (why) or wann (when). The verb comes second, straight after the question word: Wo wohnst du?

A short word that stands for a person or thing. The German subject pronouns are ich (I), du (you, informal), er/sie/es (he/she/it), wir (we), ihr (you, informal plural), sie (they) and Sie (you, formal).

To give a verb the form that matches its subject, usually by adding an ending to the stem: lernen becomes ich lerne, du lernst, er lernt, wir lernen, ihr lernt, sie lernen. The full set of forms is the verb's conjugation.
The part of a verb left when you remove the infinitive ending -en (or -n): mach- from machen, arbeit- from arbeiten. Endings are added to the stem.

The letters added to a stem to show who does the action. The regular present-tense endings are -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en (ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie). Stems ending in -t or -d add an e: du arbeitest.
The verb form for things happening now, in general, or (with a time word) in the future. One German form covers English "I play", "I am playing" and "I do play": ich spiele.
A sentence that tells something rather than asking or ordering: Ich wohne in Köln. In a German statement the conjugated verb is always the second element.

The rule that the conjugated verb is the second element of a German statement. If something other than the subject comes first (a time word, a place), the subject moves to just after the verb: Heute arbeite ich, not Heute ich arbeite.
A question that can be answered with ja or nein. In German the conjugated verb comes first and the subject second, with no helper verb like English "do": Wohnst du hier? (Do you live here?)

The group a German noun belongs to: masculine, feminine or neuter. It is a property of the word, not of the thing, and it decides the form of articles and possessives (der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch). Learn every noun with its article.
One of the three German genders. Masculine nouns take der and ein in the nominative: der Stuhl, ein Stuhl.
One of the three German genders. Feminine nouns take die and eine: die Tür, eine Tür. Nouns ending in -ung, -heit, -keit and -ion, and words for female people in -in (die Lehrerin), are feminine.
One of the three German genders. Neuter nouns take das and ein: das Buch, ein Buch. Nouns ending in -chen and -lein are always neuter.
The word for "the". In the nominative it is der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter) and die (all plurals).
The word for "a" or "an": ein for masculine and neuter nouns, eine for feminine nouns (nominative). It has no plural form.

The form of a noun for more than one. All German plurals take the article die, but the ending varies (die Tische, die Bücher, die Lampen, die Handys, die Schlüssel), so learn each plural with the noun.
A noun made by joining two or more words: die Handynummer = das Handy + die Nummer. The last part decides the gender and the plural.

A word that says whose something is: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr. The owner chooses the word; the noun that follows chooses the ending, which is the same as for ein (meine Mutter, mein Vater, meine Eltern).
The case of the subject, the person or thing doing the action or being described: Der Tisch ist neu. It is the form you find in dictionaries.

The form of an article, pronoun or noun that shows its job in the sentence. German has four cases: nominative (subject), accusative (direct object), dative (indirect object, after some prepositions) and genitive.
A verb whose stem vowel changes in the du and er/sie/es forms of the present tense, while the endings stay regular: sprechen → du sprichst, er spricht; fahren → du fährst, er fährt.
A word that describes a noun: groß, neu, rot. After sein an adjective has no ending (Die Lampe ist neu); before a noun it takes endings, which you learn at A2.
Saying that something is not so. German uses kein to negate nouns that would have ein or no article, and nicht for everything else (verbs, adjectives, nouns with der/die/das or a possessive).
kein, the negative form of ein: "not a", "no", "not any". It takes the same endings as ein and also has a plural: kein Hund, keine Katze, kein Buch, keine Kinder.
A small word that adds a shade of meaning or attitude rather than content, such as doch (yes, contradicting a negative), ja or mal. Particles are very common in spoken German.

The case of the direct object: the person or thing the verb acts on. In German only the masculine article changes: der becomes den, ein becomes einen, kein becomes keinen (Ich trinke einen Kaffee). Feminine, neuter and plural forms are the same as in the nominative.
The person or thing that the action of the verb is done to. In "I eat the apple" the apple is the direct object. In German the direct object is in the accusative: Ich esse den Apfel.
A word that points to a particular thing, like English this or that. German dieser (this, that) takes the same endings as der, die, das: dieser, diese, dieses, masculine accusative diesen.
An adverb that says how often something happens: immer (always), oft (often), manchmal (sometimes), nie (never). It usually comes right after the verb: Ich trinke oft Tee.

A verb with a stressed prefix that splits off in a main clause: the conjugated verb stays in second place and the prefix goes to the end. aufstehen: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf. In the infinitive the verb stays in one piece: Ich möchte einkaufen.
The small front part of a separable verb, such as auf, an, ein, mit, ab or fern. It carries the stress (AUFstehen) and moves to the end of a main clause: Ich rufe meine Mutter an.

Putting the subject after the verb. In a German statement the verb is always the second element, so when something else comes first, such as a time phrase, the subject follows the verb: Am Montag arbeite ich.
The form used to compare two things or options ("more", "-er", "rather"). The comparative of gern is lieber: Ich trinke lieber Tee (I prefer tea).
The form that says something is the most or the best of all. The superlative of gern is am liebsten: Am liebsten lese ich (most of all I like reading).

A verb that adds ability, wish, obligation or permission to another verb: können, wollen, mögen/möchten, müssen, dürfen, sollen. The modal is conjugated and stands in position 2; the other verb goes to the end in the infinitive, without zu: Ich kann schwimmen. The ich and er/sie/es forms are the same and have no ending (ich kann, er kann), except möchte (ich möchte, er möchte).

The German pattern in which the verb is split into two parts: the conjugated verb in position 2 and the rest of the verb (an infinitive, a separable prefix, later a past participle) at the end, with everything else in between. Ich will am Samstag eine Party feiern. Ich stehe um sieben auf.
A pronoun that does not refer to a particular person or thing. Man means people in general (English one, you or they) and always takes the er/sie/es form of the verb: Hier darf man nicht rauchen.

A number that gives a position in a row: first, second, third. In German 1–19 add -te (zweite, vierte) and 20 and up add -ste (zwanzigste); erste, dritte, siebte and achte are irregular. Written with a full stop: der 3. Oktober (der dritte Oktober), am 3. Oktober (am dritten Oktober).
A verb used only with the placeholder subject es, which does not refer to anything, like English "it" in "it is raining". Weather verbs are impersonal: es regnet, es schneit.

A preposition that is always followed by the accusative case. At A1: für (for), ohne (without), durch (through) and um (at a time, around). Only masculine articles change: für den Vater, durch einen Park.

The verb form for telling or asking someone to do something. German has one for each kind of "you", always with the verb first: du (Geh! Nimm!), ihr (Geht! Nehmt!) and Sie (Gehen Sie! Nehmen Sie!). The du form is the present-tense du form without du and its -st ending; the Sie form keeps Sie. Add bitte to sound polite.

The third German case, after the nominative and accusative. It is used after the prepositions aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, after in, an, auf and similar prepositions when they say where something is, and for the indirect object (the person who receives something). Articles: dem/einem (masculine and neuter), der/einer (feminine), den (plural, and the noun adds -n).

A preposition and an article fused into one word: zum (zu dem), zur (zu der), vom (von dem), beim (bei dem), im (in dem), am (an dem), ins (in das). The short forms are the normal ones in speech and writing.

One of nine prepositions (in, an, auf, unter, über, neben, zwischen, hinter, vor) that take the dative for location (Wo? Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch) and the accusative for movement to a place (Wohin? Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch). At A1 you mainly need the location use.
A personal pronoun used as the direct object: mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie. Only mich, dich, ihn, uns and euch differ from the subject forms. Example: Verstehen Sie mich?

A personal pronoun in the dative: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen. Used after dative prepositions (mit mir), with verbs like helfen (Kannst du mir helfen?), in set phrases (Wie geht es dir? Mir ist kalt) and for the indirect object.

The person who receives something or to whom something is done, as in "Give me the book", where me is the indirect object and the book is the direct object. In German the indirect object is in the dative: Gib mir das Buch.

The main past tense of spoken German, made of a present-tense form of haben or sein (the auxiliary, in position 2) and a past participle at the end of the sentence: Ich habe gegessen, Wir sind gefahren. It translates both "I ate" and "I have eaten".

A helper verb that combines with another verb to form a tense. In the German perfect the auxiliary is haben or sein; it takes the person ending and stands in position 2, while the main verb goes to the end as a participle.

The form of a verb used in the perfect tense, placed at the end of the sentence. It never changes its ending. Most have ge- at the front and end in -t (gemacht) or -en (gesehen); separable verbs put -ge- after the prefix (eingekauft), and verbs in -ieren or with an inseparable prefix have no ge- (studiert, besucht).
A regular verb whose stem stays the same in all forms. Its past participle is ge- + stem + -t: machen → gemacht, kaufen → gekauft, arbeiten → gearbeitet. Most German verbs are weak.
A verb whose past participle ends in -en, often with a changed vowel: sehen → gesehen, trinken → getrunken, schreiben → geschrieben. Strong participles have to be learned with the verb.
A verb that changes its vowel like a strong verb but ends in -t like a weak verb in the past participle. At A1: bringen → gebracht, denken → gedacht, kennen → gekannt, wissen → gewusst.

A prefix that always stays attached to its verb and is never stressed, such as be-, ver-, er-, ent- and ge-. Verbs with an inseparable prefix take no ge- in the past participle: besuchen → besucht, verlieren → verloren, erzählen → erzählt.

A one-word past tense, used mainly in writing. In spoken German you need it at A1 only for sein and haben, where it is more common than the perfect: ich war, du warst (was, were); ich hatte, du hattest (had).

A word that joins words or sentences. The coordinating conjunctions und, oder, aber, denn and sondern stand in position zero and do not change the word order of the sentence after them: Ich bleibe hier, denn ich bin müde.

The slot in front of a sentence where und, oder, aber, denn and sondern stand. A word there does not count as position 1, so the next element is position 1 and the verb is still in position 2: …, aber heute habe ich Zeit.

references.title: Articles, possessives and cases
references.body:
## Which case?

| Case | Job in the sentence | Typical triggers | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nominative | subject; after *sein* | who/what does it? | *Der Hund schläft.* — The dog is sleeping. |
| Accusative | direct object | *haben, möchten, es gibt*; *für, ohne, durch, um* | *Ich habe einen Hund.* — I have a dog. |
| Dative | indirect object; after some prepositions | *mit, zu, nach, von, aus, bei, seit*; location with *in, an, auf* … | *Ich fahre mit dem Bus.* — I'm going by bus. |

Only masculine changes between nominative and accusative. In the dative everything changes,
and plural nouns add *-n* if they don't already end in *-n* or *-s* (*mit den Kindern*, but
*mit den Fotos*).

## Definite article: the

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nominative | der | die | das | die |
| Accusative | den | die | das | die |
| Dative | dem | der | dem | den (+ -n) |

## Indefinite article: a / an

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nominative | ein | eine | ein | — |
| Accusative | einen | eine | ein | — |
| Dative | einem | einer | einem | — |

## Negative article: kein (not a, no)

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nominative | kein | keine | kein | keine |
| Accusative | keinen | keine | kein | keine |
| Dative | keinem | keiner | keinem | keinen (+ -n) |

Use *kein* where you would say *ein* or no article: *Das ist kein Kuli. Ich habe keine Zeit.*
Use *nicht* for everything else.

## Possessive articles

Choose the word by the owner:

| Owner | Possessive | English |
|---|---|---|
| ich | mein | my |
| du | dein | your (informal, one person) |
| er / es | sein | his / its |
| sie (she) | ihr | her |
| wir | unser | our |
| ihr (you all) | euer | your (informal, several people) |
| sie (they) | ihr | their |
| Sie | Ihr | your (formal) |

Then add the ending for the noun that follows. The endings are the same as for *kein*:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nominative | mein | meine | mein | meine |
| Accusative | meinen | meine | mein | meine |
| Dative | meinem | meiner | meinem | meinen (+ -n) |

Examples with other possessives: *unser Sohn, unsere Tochter, unseren Sohn (acc.), unserem
Sohn (dat.)*. *euer* drops its second *e* before an ending: *eure Tochter, euren Sohn, eurem
Sohn*.

## Gender hints

Always learn the article with the noun; these endings help you check.

| Ending or group | Gender | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät, -ie | feminine | die Zeitung, die Universität, die Information, die Familie |
| -in (female person) | feminine | die Lehrerin, die Ärztin |
| -e | usually feminine | die Lampe, die Tasche — but der Name, der Käse |
| -chen, -lein | neuter | das Mädchen, das Brötchen |
| -ment, -um | usually neuter | das Medikament, das Museum, das Zentrum |
| -er (person or machine) | usually masculine | der Lehrer, der Computer — but das Fenster |
| -ismus, -ling | masculine | der Tourismus, der Frühling |
| days, months, seasons | masculine | der Montag, der Mai, der Sommer |
| compound nouns | gender of the last part | das Haus + die Tür = die Haustür |

## Plural patterns

| Pattern | Typical nouns | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| -e | many masculine and neuter | der Tisch → die Tische; das Heft → die Hefte |
| ¨ + -e | many masculine | der Stuhl → die Stühle; der Sohn → die Söhne |
| -er | short neuter nouns | das Kind → die Kinder |
| ¨ + -er | short neuter nouns, some masculine | das Buch → die Bücher; der Mann → die Männer |
| -n / -en | most feminine nouns | die Lampe → die Lampen; die Tür → die Türen |
| -nen | feminine nouns in -in | die Lehrerin → die Lehrerinnen |
| -s | loanwords, words ending in a vowel (not -e) | das Handy → die Handys; das Foto → die Fotos |
| no ending | masculine/neuter in -er, -el, -en | der Schlüssel → die Schlüssel; das Fenster → die Fenster |
| ¨ only | some masculine/feminine in -er | der Vater → die Väter; die Mutter → die Mütter |

All plurals take *die* in the nominative and accusative, *den* in the dative.

## Personal pronouns by case

| Nominative | Accusative | Dative | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | mich | mir | I / me |
| du | dich | dir | you (informal, one person) |
| er | ihn | ihm | he / him (also "it" for masculine nouns) |
| sie | sie | ihr | she / her (also "it" for feminine nouns) |
| es | es | ihm | it |
| wir | uns | uns | we / us |
| ihr | euch | euch | you (informal, several people) |
| sie | sie | ihnen | they / them |
| Sie | Sie | Ihnen | you (formal) |

Pronouns follow the noun's grammatical gender, even for things: *Der Tisch ist neu. Er ist
schön.* — The table is new. It's beautiful.

## Short forms (preposition + article)

| Long | Short | Example |
|---|---|---|
| in dem | im | *im Büro* — in the office |
| an dem | am | *am Montag* — on Monday |
| zu dem | zum | *zum Bahnhof* — to the station |
| zu der | zur | *zur Schule* — to school |
| von dem | vom | *vom Arzt* — from the doctor |
| bei dem | beim | *beim Arzt* — at the doctor's |
| in das | ins | *ins Kino* — to the cinema |

references.title: Modal verbs and the sentence bracket
references.body:
## Present tense forms

| | können | wollen | mögen | möchten | müssen | dürfen | sollen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | kann | will | mag | möchte | muss | darf | soll |
| du | kannst | willst | magst | möchtest | musst | darfst | sollst |
| er/sie/es/man | kann | will | mag | möchte | muss | darf | soll |
| wir | können | wollen | mögen | möchten | müssen | dürfen | sollen |
| ihr | könnt | wollt | mögt | möchtet | müsst | dürft | sollt |
| sie/Sie | können | wollen | mögen | möchten | müssen | dürfen | sollen |

Patterns:

- ich and er/sie/es are identical and have no ending: *ich kann, er kann* (*möchte* keeps its
  *-e*: *ich möchte, er möchte*).
- The singular has its own vowel (*können → kann*, *dürfen → darf*, *müssen → muss*,
  *wollen → will*, *mögen → mag*); *sollen* keeps its vowel.
- The plural is regular and built from the infinitive: *wir müssen, ihr müsst*.
- *möchte* is the polite "would like" form of *mögen*; at A1 it is used like a verb of its own.

## Meanings

| Verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *können* | can, be able to; be possible | *Ich kann schwimmen.* — I can swim. |
| *wollen* | want (to); plan to | *Wir wollen im Sommer reisen.* — We want to travel in summer. |
| *mögen* | like (mostly + noun) | *Ich mag Tee.* — I like tea. |
| *möchten* | would like (to), polite | *Ich möchte bitte zahlen.* — I'd like to pay, please. |
| *müssen* | must, have to | *Du musst pünktlich sein.* — You have to be on time. |
| *dürfen* | may, be allowed to | *Darf ich hier parken?* — May I park here? |
| *sollen* | should, be supposed to (someone else wants it) | *Soll ich helfen?* — Shall I help? |

- *will* is direct, *möchte* is polite. *Ich will* means "I want", never "I will".
- For liking an activity, use *gern*: *Ich tanze gern* (not usually *Ich mag tanzen*).
- *können* with a language needs no second verb: *Ich kann Deutsch.*

## nicht müssen vs nicht dürfen

| German | Meaning | English |
|---|---|---|
| *Du musst nicht warten.* | it isn't necessary | You don't have to wait. |
| *Du darfst nicht warten.* | it is forbidden | You mustn't wait. / You're not allowed to wait. |
| *Man muss hier nicht bezahlen.* | free, no need to pay | You don't need to pay here. |
| *Man darf hier nicht rauchen.* | smoking is forbidden | You mustn't smoke here. |

English "must not" = German *nicht dürfen*. German *nicht müssen* = English "don't have to".

## man + modal verb for rules

*Man* (one, people in general) takes the er/sie/es form: *man kann, man muss, man darf, man
soll*.

- *Hier darf man parken.* — You're allowed to park here.
- *Im Kurs muss man pünktlich sein.* — You have to be on time in the course.

## The sentence bracket

The conjugated modal verb stands in position 2; the second verb goes to the end in the
infinitive, without *zu*. Everything else goes in between.

| Position 1 | Position 2 | middle | end |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ich | kann | sehr gut | kochen. |
| Am Samstag | wollen | wir eine Party | feiern. |
| Hier | darf | man nicht | rauchen. |
| Was | möchtest | du | trinken? |
| | Musst | du heute | arbeiten? |

- Statements: modal in position 2, even after a time phrase (*Am Samstag wollen wir …*).
- W-questions: question word, then modal: *Was möchtest du trinken?*
- Yes/no questions: modal first: *Musst du heute arbeiten?*
- *nicht* normally goes directly before the infinitive: *Ich kann heute nicht kommen.*

## Separable verbs

Without a modal, a separable verb is itself a bracket: the stem in position 2, the prefix at
the end. With a modal, the infinitive at the end is written as one word again.

| Without a modal | With a modal |
|---|---|
| *Ich stehe um sieben auf.* | *Ich muss um sieben aufstehen.* |
| *Kommst du mit?* | *Willst du mitkommen?* |
| *Er lädt seine Freunde ein.* | *Er möchte seine Freunde einladen.* |
| *Wir füllen das Formular aus.* | *Wir sollen das Formular ausfüllen.* |
| *Sie ruft ihre Mutter an.* | *Sie kann ihre Mutter morgen anrufen.* |

Inseparable verbs such as *unterschreiben* never split: *Sie unterschreibt hier.* — *Sie muss
hier unterschreiben.*

## Polite requests and offers

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| *Kann ich …?* | *Kann ich hier warten?* — Can I wait here? |
| *Darf ich …?* (more polite) | *Darf ich das Fenster öffnen?* — May I open the window? |
| *Können Sie …?* | *Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren?* — Could you spell that, please? |
| *Soll ich …?* (offer) | *Soll ich die Tür schließen?* — Shall I close the door? |
| *Ich möchte …* | *Ich möchte einen Termin.* — I'd like an appointment. |

references.title: Numbers, prices, dates and time
references.body:
## Numbers 0–20

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 *null* | 6 *sechs* | 11 *elf* | 16 *sechzehn* |
| 1 *eins* | 7 *sieben* | 12 *zwölf* | 17 *siebzehn* |
| 2 *zwei* (*zwo*) | 8 *acht* | 13 *dreizehn* | 18 *achtzehn* |
| 3 *drei* | 9 *neun* | 14 *vierzehn* | 19 *neunzehn* |
| 4 *vier* | 10 *zehn* | 15 *fünfzehn* | 20 *zwanzig* |
| 5 *fünf* | | | |

13–19 are the unit + *zehn*. Two lose letters: *sechzehn* (not sechszehn), *siebzehn* (not siebenzehn). *zwo* is used on the phone and in announcements so it isn't confused with *drei*.

## Tens and 21–99

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 10 *zehn* | 40 *vierzig* | 70 *siebzig* |
| 20 *zwanzig* | 50 *fünfzig* | 80 *achtzig* |
| 30 *dreißig* | 60 *sechzig* | 90 *neunzig* |

Tens end in *-zig*, except *dreißig* (with *ß*). From 21 to 99 the unit comes first, joined by *und*, all in one word:

| Number | German | Literally |
|---|---|---|
| 21 | *einundzwanzig* | one-and-twenty |
| 34 | *vierunddreißig* | four-and-thirty |
| 57 | *siebenundfünfzig* | seven-and-fifty |
| 66 | *sechsundsechzig* | six-and-sixty |
| 99 | *neunundneunzig* | nine-and-ninety |

*eins* becomes *ein-* before *und*: *einundzwanzig*. *sechs* and *sieben* keep their full form before *und* (*sechsundsechzig, siebenundsiebzig*) but shorten in *sechzig* and *siebzig*.

## Hundreds, thousands, a million

| Number | German |
|---|---|
| 100 | *hundert* / *einhundert* |
| 101 | *hunderteins* |
| 115 | *hundertfünfzehn* |
| 199 | *hundertneunundneunzig* |
| 200 | *zweihundert* |
| 486 | *vierhundertsechsundachtzig* |
| 1.000 | *tausend* / *eintausend* |
| 1.001 | *tausendeins* |
| 2.750 | *zweitausendsiebenhundertfünfzig* |
| 10.000 | *zehntausend* |
| 65.000 | *fünfundsechzigtausend* |
| 100.000 | *hunderttausend* |
| 1.000.000 | *eine Million* |
| 2.500.000 | *zwei Komma fünf Millionen* / *zweieinhalb Millionen* |

Pattern: thousands + hundreds + (units *und* tens). Everything below a million is written as one word. *die Million* is a noun: *eine Million, zwei Millionen*.

## Writing numbers

| German | English | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *1.000* or *1 000* | 1,000 | one thousand |
| *2,5* | 2.5 | two point five, said *zwei Komma fünf* |
| *0,75 l* | 0.75 l | three quarters of a litre |

A point (or a space) groups thousands; a comma marks decimals.

## Prices

| Written | Said |
|---|---|
| *1,00 €* | *ein Euro* |
| *2,50 €* | *zwei Euro fünfzig* |
| *9,99 €* | *neun Euro neunundneunzig* |
| *0,60 €* | *sechzig Cent* |
| *15,05 €* | *fünfzehn Euro fünf* |
| *1.200,00 €* | *tausendzweihundert Euro* or *zwölfhundert Euro* |

- No plural after a number: *zehn Euro, fünfzig Cent*.
- No *und* and no *Cent* in the middle: *zwei Euro fünfzig*.
- Questions: *Was kostet …? / Wie viel kostet …?* (one thing), *Was kosten …?* (several). The total: *Das macht 12,40 €.*
- Quantities have no "of": *ein Kilo Äpfel, 200 Gramm Käse, ein Liter Milch, eine Flasche Wasser*. *Kilo, Gramm, Liter, Stück* stay singular after numbers (*zwei Kilo*); *Flasche, Packung* take the plural (*zwei Flaschen*).

## Ordinal numbers and dates

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. *erste* | 6. *sechste* | 11. *elfte* | 20. *zwanzigste* |
| 2. *zweite* | 7. *siebte* | 12. *zwölfte* | 21. *einundzwanzigste* |
| 3. *dritte* | 8. *achte* | 13. *dreizehnte* | 30. *dreißigste* |
| 4. *vierte* | 9. *neunte* | 16. *sechzehnte* | 31. *einunddreißigste* |
| 5. *fünfte* | 10. *zehnte* | 19. *neunzehnte* | 100. *hundertste* |

- 1–19: number + *-te*. Irregular: *erste, dritte, siebte, achte* (*achte* has only one *t*).
- From 20: number + *-ste*.
- In writing, an ordinal is a number with a point: *der 3. Mai* = *der dritte Mai*.

| Use | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| What's the date? | *der* + ordinal + *-e* | *Heute ist der 1. Juli.* (*der erste Juli*) |
| On which day? | *am* + ordinal + *-en* | *am 1. Juli* (*am ersten Juli*) |
| Written date | day. month. year | *01.07.2026* or *1. Juli 2026* |

Questions: *Welches Datum ist heute?* / *Der Wievielte ist heute?* — What's the date today? *Wann hast du Geburtstag? — Am 12. März.*

Years are read in hundreds up to 1999, and as thousands from 2000:

| Year | Said |
|---|---|
| 1989 | *neunzehnhundertneunundachtzig* |
| 2000 | *zweitausend* |
| 2026 | *zweitausendsechsundzwanzig* |

Say *2026* or *im Jahr 2026*, never *in 2026*.

## Clock time

Questions: *Wie spät ist es?* / *Wie viel Uhr ist es?* Answer: *Es ist …*. At what time? *Um wie viel Uhr …? / Wann …? — Um …*

### Official (24-hour)

Hours + *Uhr* + minutes. Used for timetables, opening hours, appointments, radio and TV.

| Written | Said |
|---|---|
| 6:00 | *sechs Uhr* |
| 9:10 | *neun Uhr zehn* |
| 13:30 | *dreizehn Uhr dreißig* |
| 17:45 | *siebzehn Uhr fünfundvierzig* |
| 0:05 | *null Uhr fünf* |

### Informal (12-hour)

| Time | Said | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 8:00 | *acht (Uhr)* | |
| 8:05 | *fünf nach acht* | *nach* = past |
| 8:15 | *Viertel nach acht* | regional: *viertel neun* |
| 8:20 | *zwanzig nach acht* | also *zehn vor halb neun* |
| 8:25 | *fünf vor halb neun* | |
| 8:30 | *halb neun* | half way to nine |
| 8:35 | *fünf nach halb neun* | |
| 8:40 | *zwanzig vor neun* | also *zehn nach halb neun* |
| 8:45 | *Viertel vor neun* | regional: *drei viertel neun* |
| 8:55 | *fünf vor neun* | *vor* = to |
| 1:00 | *ein Uhr* / *eins* | never *eins Uhr* |
| 12:00 | *zwölf Uhr* | *Mittag* (noon), *Mitternacht* (midnight) |

*halb* always points to the next hour: *halb drei* = 2:30. Add *morgens, nachmittags, abends* if needed: *um acht Uhr abends* (8 p.m.).

*die Uhr* = o'clock (no plural in times); *die Stunde* = an hour of time: *Es ist zwei Uhr* vs *Ich warte zwei Stunden*.

## Days of the week

All masculine: *der Montag*.

| German | Short | English |
|---|---|---|
| *Montag* | Mo | Monday |
| *Dienstag* | Di | Tuesday |
| *Mittwoch* | Mi | Wednesday |
| *Donnerstag* | Do | Thursday |
| *Freitag* | Fr | Friday |
| *Samstag* (north also *Sonnabend*) | Sa | Saturday |
| *Sonntag* | So | Sunday |

*das Wochenende* = Saturday and Sunday. With *-s* and a small letter a day means "every": *montags* = on Mondays.

## Parts of the day

| German | Roughly | "in the …" | "every …" |
|---|---|---|---|
| *der Morgen* | 5–9 | *am Morgen* | *morgens* |
| *der Vormittag* | 9–12 | *am Vormittag* | *vormittags* |
| *der Mittag* | 12–14 | *am Mittag* | *mittags* |
| *der Nachmittag* | 14–18 | *am Nachmittag* | *nachmittags* |
| *der Abend* | 18–23 | *am Abend* | *abends* |
| *die Nacht* | 23–5 | *in der Nacht* | *nachts* |

| Today | Yesterday | Tomorrow |
|---|---|---|
| *heute Morgen* | *gestern Morgen* | *morgen früh* |
| *heute Nachmittag* | *gestern Nachmittag* | *morgen Nachmittag* |
| *heute Abend* | *gestern Abend* | *morgen Abend* |

*morgen* (small) = tomorrow; *der Morgen* (capital) = the morning. Tomorrow morning is *morgen früh*.

## Months and seasons

All masculine: *der Januar*, *der Sommer*.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Januar* (Austria: *Jänner*) | *April* | *Juli* | *Oktober* |
| *Februar* | *Mai* | *August* | *November* |
| *März* | *Juni* | *September* | *Dezember* |

| Season | German |
|---|---|
| spring | *der Frühling* |
| summer | *der Sommer* |
| autumn, fall | *der Herbst* |
| winter | *der Winter* |

On the phone people sometimes say *Juno* and *Julei* to keep *Juni* and *Juli* apart.

## Time prepositions

| Preposition | With | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *um* | clock times | *um 8 Uhr, um halb drei* |
| *am* | days, dates, parts of the day, the weekend | *am Montag, am 3. Mai, am Abend, am Wochenende* |
| *in der* | the night | *in der Nacht* |
| *im* | months, seasons | *im Mai, im Sommer* |
| *von … bis* | a period from start to end | *von 9 bis 17 Uhr, von Montag bis Freitag* |
| *bis* | an end point | *bis morgen, bis acht Uhr* |
| no preposition | years | *2026* or *im Jahr 2026* |

Question words: *Wann?* (when?), *Um wie viel Uhr?* (at what time?), *Wie lange?* (how long?), *Wie oft?* (how often?).

How often: *immer* (always) – *oft* (often) – *manchmal* (sometimes) – *nie* (never).

references.title: The perfect tense
references.body:
## How to form it

Perfect = present tense of *haben* or *sein* (position 2) + past participle (end of the
sentence).

| | with haben | with sein |
|---|---|---|
| ich | habe … gemacht | bin … gefahren |
| du | hast … gemacht | bist … gefahren |
| er/sie/es | hat … gemacht | ist … gefahren |
| wir | haben … gemacht | sind … gefahren |
| ihr | habt … gemacht | seid … gefahren |
| sie/Sie | haben … gemacht | sind … gefahren |

- Statement: *Ich habe gestern Fußball gespielt.*
- Time phrase first: *Gestern habe ich Fußball gespielt.*
- Yes/no question: *Hast du gestern Fußball gespielt?*
- W-question: *Wann bist du nach Hause gekommen?*
- Modal verbs are not used in the perfect at A1; their past forms (*ich konnte, ich musste*) come at A2.

## haben or sein?

| use sein | examples |
|---|---|
| movement from one place to another | *gehen, kommen, fahren, fliegen, laufen, reisen, wandern, schwimmen* |
| a change of state | *aufstehen, werden, aufwachen, einschlafen* |
| three special verbs | *sein, bleiben, passieren* |

Everything else uses *haben*, including every verb with an accusative object (*einen Film
sehen*, *ein Buch kaufen*). *Fahren* with an object takes *haben*: *Ich habe das Auto
gefahren.*

## Participle patterns

| pattern | rule | examples |
|---|---|---|
| weak (regular) | ge- + stem + -t | machen → gemacht, kaufen → gekauft, hören → gehört |
| stem ends in -t/-d | ge- + stem + -et | arbeiten → gearbeitet, warten → gewartet, antworten → geantwortet |
| strong (irregular) | ge- + stem + -en, vowel often changes | sehen → gesehen, trinken → getrunken, schreiben → geschrieben |
| mixed | ge- + changed stem + -t | bringen → gebracht, denken → gedacht, kennen → gekannt, wissen → gewusst |
| separable | prefix + ge + participle | einkaufen → eingekauft, anrufen → angerufen, aufstehen → aufgestanden |
| -ieren | no ge-, ends in -t | studieren → studiert, fotografieren → fotografiert |
| inseparable prefix (be-, ver-, er-, ent-, ge-) | no ge- | besuchen → besucht, verstehen → verstanden, erzählen → erzählt |

## Irregular and sein verbs at A1

Regular *haben* verbs are not listed. *Sein* verbs are marked by *ist* in the last column.

| infinitive | er/sie/es (present) | perfect |
|---|---|---|
| abbiegen | biegt ab | ist abgebogen |
| abfahren | fährt ab | ist abgefahren |
| anfangen | fängt an | hat angefangen |
| ankommen | kommt an | ist angekommen |
| anrufen | ruft an | hat angerufen |
| aufstehen | steht auf | ist aufgestanden |
| aussteigen | steigt aus | ist ausgestiegen |
| bekommen | bekommt | hat bekommen |
| bestehen | besteht | hat bestanden |
| bleiben | bleibt | ist geblieben |
| bringen | bringt | hat gebracht |
| denken | denkt | hat gedacht |
| einladen | lädt ein | hat eingeladen |
| einsteigen | steigt ein | ist eingestiegen |
| essen | isst | hat gegessen |
| fahren | fährt | ist gefahren |
| fernsehen | sieht fern | hat ferngesehen |
| finden | findet | hat gefunden |
| fliegen | fliegt | ist geflogen |
| geben | gibt | hat gegeben |
| gehen | geht | ist gegangen |
| haben | hat | hat gehabt |
| heißen | heißt | hat geheißen |
| helfen | hilft | hat geholfen |
| kennen | kennt | hat gekannt |
| kommen | kommt | ist gekommen |
| laufen | läuft | ist gelaufen |

| schlafen | schläft | hat geschlafen |
| schließen | schließt | hat geschlossen |
| schreiben | schreibt | hat geschrieben |
| schwimmen | schwimmt | ist geschwommen |
| sehen | sieht | hat gesehen |
| sein | ist | ist gewesen |

| trinken | trinkt | hat getrunken |

*Schwimmen* can also take *haben* when it means the activity rather than going somewhere
(*Ich habe eine Stunde geschwommen*); *ist geschwommen* is always correct.

## war and hatte

With *sein* and *haben* the simple past is more common than the perfect.

| | sein | haben |
|---|---|---|
| ich | war | hatte |
| du | warst | hattest |
| er/sie/es | war | hatte |
| wir | waren | hatten |
| ihr | wart | hattet |
| sie/Sie | waren | hatten |

references.title: Prepositions and the imperative
references.body:
## Articles after prepositions

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| accusative | *den / einen* | *die / eine* | *das / ein* | *die / –* |
| dative | *dem / einem* | *der / einer* | *dem / einem* | *den / –* (noun + *-n*) |

Possessives and *kein* take the same endings: *für meinen Vater*, *mit meiner Mutter*, *ohne
mein Handy*, *mit meinen Kindern*, *keinem*, *keiner*.

## Prepositions with the accusative

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *durch* | through | *durch den Park* — through the park |
| *für* | for | *für meinen Bruder* — for my brother |
| *gegen* | against | *gegen die Wand* — against the wall |
| *ohne* | without | *ohne einen Koffer* — without a suitcase |
| *um* | around; at (clock time) | *um die Ecke* — round the corner; *um 8 Uhr* — at 8 |

## Prepositions with the dative

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *aus* | out of, from (origin) | *aus dem Haus* — out of the house; *aus der Schweiz* — from Switzerland |
| *bei* | at (someone's place, a company), near | *bei meinen Eltern* — at my parents' |
| *mit* | with, by (transport) | *mit dem Zug* — by train |
| *nach* | to (cities, countries); after | *nach Wien* — to Vienna; *nach dem Essen* — after the meal |
| *seit* | since, for (up to now) | *seit einem Jahr* — for a year |
| *von* | from, of | *von der Arbeit* — from work |
| *zu* | to (people, places) | *zum Arzt* — to the doctor |
| *gegenüber* | opposite | *gegenüber der Post* — opposite the post office |

*Seit* + present tense: *Ich wohne seit 2020 hier.* — I've lived here since 2020.

| Where to? (*Wohin?*) | Where? (*Wo?*) | Where from? (*Woher?*) |
|---|---|---|
| *zum Arzt* | *beim Arzt* | *vom Arzt* |
| *zu Anna* | *bei Anna* | *von Anna* |
| *nach Berlin* | *in Berlin* | *aus Berlin* |
| *nach Hause* | *zu Hause* | *von zu Hause* |

## Two-way prepositions: location with Wo? + dative

| Preposition | Meaning | Example (*Wo?* + dative) |
|---|---|---|
| *in* | in, inside | *im Bad, in der Küche* |
| *an* | on (a wall), at, by | *an der Wand, am Fenster* |
| *auf* | on (top of) | *auf dem Tisch* |
| *unter* | under | *unter dem Bett* |
| *über* | above, over | *über dem Sofa* |
| *neben* | next to | *neben der Tür* |
| *zwischen* | between | *zwischen dem Schrank und dem Regal* |
| *hinter* | behind | *hinter dem Haus* |
| *vor* | in front of | *vor dem Bahnhof* |

With movement to a place (*Wohin?*), the same prepositions take the accusative: *Ich lege das Buch
auf den Tisch.* — I put the book on the table. *Wir gehen ins Kino.* — We're going to the cinema.

## Contractions

| Long form | Short form | Case | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *in dem* | *im* | dative | *im Zentrum* |
| *an dem* | *am* | dative | *am Montag, am Fenster* |
| *zu dem* | *zum* | dative | *zum Bahnhof* |
| *zu der* | *zur* | dative | *zur Post* |
| *von dem* | *vom* | dative | *vom Flughafen* |
| *bei dem* | *beim* | dative | *beim Arzt* |
| *in das* | *ins* | accusative | *ins Kino, ins Bett* |

## The imperative

| Infinitive | du | ihr | Sie |
|---|---|---|---|
| *gehen* | *Geh!* | *Geht!* | *Gehen Sie!* |
| *kommen* | *Komm!* | *Kommt!* | *Kommen Sie!* |
| *warten* | *Warte!* | *Wartet!* | *Warten Sie!* |
| *nehmen* (e → i) | *Nimm!* | *Nehmt!* | *Nehmen Sie!* |
| *sprechen* (e → i) | *Sprich!* | *Sprecht!* | *Sprechen Sie!* |
| *essen* (e → i) | *Iss!* | *Esst!* | *Essen Sie!* |
| *lesen* (e → ie) | *Lies!* | *Lest!* | *Lesen Sie!* |
| *fahren* (a → ä) | *Fahr!* | *Fahrt!* | *Fahren Sie!* |
| *schlafen* (a → ä) | *Schlaf!* | *Schlaft!* | *Schlafen Sie!* |
| *abbiegen* (separable) | *Bieg … ab!* | *Biegt … ab!* | *Biegen Sie … ab!* |
| *sein* | *Sei!* | *Seid!* | *Seien Sie!* |
| *haben* | *Hab!* | *Habt!* | *Haben Sie!* |

- du: the *du* form without *du* and without *-st* (or *-t* after *s, ß, z*). e → i/ie stays, a → ä
  goes. Stems in *-t/-d* keep *-e*.
- ihr: the *ihr* form without *ihr*.
- Sie: the *Sie* form with the verb first; *Sie* is never dropped.
- Separable prefixes go to the end: *Ruf mich an!* Add *bitte* to be polite: *Warten Sie bitte hier.*

references.title: Verbs in the present tense
references.body:
## Personal pronouns

| | Singular | | Plural | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st person | *ich* | I | *wir* | we |
| 2nd person | *du* | you (informal) | *ihr* | you (informal, two or more) |
| 3rd person | *er / sie / es* | he / she / it | *sie* | they |
| formal | *Sie* | you (formal) | *Sie* | you (formal) |

Lowercase *sie* = she or they (the verb ending tells you which); capital *Sie* = formal you.

## Regular endings

Stem = infinitive minus *-en* (or *-n*). Add the ending to the stem.

| | Ending | machen | wohnen | spielen |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | -e | mache | wohne | spiele |
| du | -st | machst | wohnst | spielst |
| er / sie / es | -t | macht | wohnt | spielt |
| wir | -en | machen | wohnen | spielen |
| ihr | -t | macht | wohnt | spielt |
| sie / Sie | -en | machen | wohnen | spielen |

## Spelling adjustments

| Stem ends in | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| -t, -d | add *e* before -st and -t | du arbeitest, er arbeitet, ihr arbeitet; du findest, er findet |
| -s, -ß, -z | *du* adds only -t | du heißt, du tanzt, du reist |
| -el, -er (infinitive in -n) | *wir* and *sie/Sie* add only -n | wir wandern, sie wandern |

## sein and haben

| | sein (to be) | haben (to have) |
|---|---|---|
| ich | bin | habe |
| du | bist | hast |
| er / sie / es | ist | hat |
| wir | sind | haben |
| ihr | seid | habt |
| sie / Sie | sind | haben |

## Stem-changing verbs

Some strong verbs change their stem vowel in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms only. The endings
stay regular, and *ich*, *wir*, *ihr* and *sie/Sie* keep the infinitive's vowel.

### a → ä

| | fahren (to drive, go) | schlafen (to sleep) | waschen (to wash) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | fahre | schlafe | wasche |
| du | fährst | schläfst | wäschst |
| er / sie / es | fährt | schläft | wäscht |
| wir | fahren | schlafen | waschen |

Also *laufen* (to run, to walk): *du läufst, er läuft* (au → äu).

### e → i

| | sprechen (to speak) | essen (to eat) | geben (to give) | helfen (to help) | nehmen (to take) | treffen (to meet) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | spreche | esse | gebe | helfe | nehme | treffe |
| du | sprichst | isst | gibst | hilfst | nimmst | triffst |
| er / sie / es | spricht | isst | gibt | hilft | nimmt | trifft |
| wir | sprechen | essen | geben | helfen | nehmen | treffen |

*nehmen* also changes its consonants: *du nimmst, er nimmt*. *essen*: *du isst* (stem ends in
*s*, so only -t).

### e → ie

| | lesen (to read) | sehen (to see) |
|---|---|---|
| ich | lese | sehe |
| du | liest | siehst |
| er / sie / es | liest | sieht |
| wir | lesen | sehen |

*lesen*: *du liest* (stem ends in *s*, so only -t).

### Other irregular present forms at A1

| | werden (to become) | wissen (to know a fact) | mögen (to like) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | werde | weiß | mag |
| du | wirst | weißt | magst |
| er / sie / es | wird | weiß | mag |
| wir | werden | wissen | mögen |
| ihr | werdet | wisst | mögt |
| sie / Sie | werden | wissen | mögen |

## Word order

### Statements: the verb is second

| Position 1 | Position 2 (verb) | Subject (if not in position 1) | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ich | lerne | | heute Deutsch. |
| Heute | lerne | ich | Deutsch. |
| Deutsch | lerne | ich | heute. |

Anything can stand in position 1 (subject, time, place, object), but only one element. The
conjugated verb always comes next.

### Questions

| Type | Order | Example |
|---|---|---|
| yes/no question | verb – subject – rest | Lernst du Deutsch? |
| W-question | question word – verb – subject – rest | Warum lernst du Deutsch? |

Question words: *wer* (who), *was* (what), *wie* (how), *wo* (where), *woher* (where from),
*wann* (when), *warum* (why).

### One present tense, three English meanings

*Ich spiele* = I play / I'm playing / I do play. With a time word it can also mean the future:
*Morgen spiele ich.* = I'm playing tomorrow.

vocab.note: nein answers a question; 'not any' is kein (Lesson 8).

vocab.exampleEn: Your signature is still missing here.

meanings: cancellation (saying no to an invitation or appointment)
vocab.example: Leider habe ich eine Absage bekommen.
Ich muss den Termin leider absagen.
vocab.exampleEn: Unfortunately I have to cancel the appointment.
vocab.note: Separable: ich sage ab. Perfect: hat abgesagt.
Perfect: hat bestanden.

vocab.example: Kreuzen Sie die richtige Antwort an.
vocab.note: Separable: ich kreuze an. Perfect: hat angekreuzt.
Perfect: hat ergänzt.
Not separable here: ich wiederhole, hat wiederholt.

vocab.exampleEn: Can you explain that to me?
vocab.note: Perfect: hat erklärt.

vocab.example: Ich übe jeden Tag zehn Minuten.
vocab.exampleEn: I practise for ten minutes every day.

meanings: Could you repeat that? (formal, polite request)
vocab.example: Entschuldigung, können Sie das bitte wiederholen?
vocab.exampleEn: Sorry, could you repeat that, please?

vocab.example: Ich verstehe das nicht. Was bedeutet das?
vocab.exampleEn: I don't understand. What does that mean?

vocab.term: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
alt: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch
meanings: How do you say that in German?
how do you say that in German
how does one say that in German
vocab.example: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch? „Club“?
vocab.exampleEn: How do you say that in German? "Club"?

vocab.note: zum Beispiel (z. B.) = for example.

vocab.example: Ich habe nur zwei Fehler gemacht.
Lesen Sie bitte den Text auf Seite zehn.
vocab.exampleEn: Please read the text on page ten.

vocab.example: Für die Prüfung braucht man 60 Punkte.
vocab.exampleEn: You need 60 points for the exam.
Would you like something to drink?

readingList.title: Nicos Weg (A1)
readingList.note: A video course told as a story about Nico, newly arrived in Germany, with short texts and exercises for each episode. A good companion from the first lesson.

readingList.title: Deutsch – warum nicht? Series 1
readingList.note: An older audio course built around a student working in a hotel, with a lesson script for each episode. Some details are dated (prices are in Deutsche Mark).

readingList.title: Leo & Co. – Die Neue (Stufe 1)
readingList.author: Elke Burger and Theo Scherling
readingList.note: A short graded reader set in a café, with audio. Leo & Co. is a long-running series for adult beginners; try it once you're about halfway through the course.

readingList.title: Leo & Co. – Das schnelle Glück (Stufe 1)
readingList.author: Elke Burger and Theo Scherling
readingList.note: Four friends think they've won the lottery, and then the ticket goes missing.

readingList.title: Leo & Co. – Ein Hundeleben (Stufe 1)
readingList.author: Elke Burger and Theo Scherling
readingList.note: A dog-sitting job that lasts much longer than planned.

readingList.title: Lese-Novelas – Tina, Hamburg
readingList.author: Thomas Silvin
readingList.note: A very short novella written for adult beginners. The same series has Anna, Berlin; Eva, Wien; Franz, München and Claudia, Mallorca.

readingList.title: Blinder Passagier (Stadt, Land, Fluss …)
readingList.author: Andrea Maria Wagner
readingList.note: A short adventure for younger readers with a free audio version, set in a real German region.

readingList.title: Café in Berlin (Dino lernt Deutsch 1)
readingList.author: André Klein
readingList.note: Ten short stories about Dino, an Italian newcomer in Berlin, each with a word list and questions.

readingList.title: Goethe-Zertifikat A1 practice tests (reading sections)
readingList.note: The official model test and practice sets. The reading parts are short notes, signs and ads, exactly the kind of text the exam uses. Save these for the end of the course.

readingList.title: Mein Weg nach Deutschland
readingList.note: Free exercises and short texts about everyday life and work in Germany; filter by level A1.

readingList.title: nachrichtenleicht
readingList.level: A2 (a stretch at the end of A1)
readingList.note: Short news articles in plain German with a glossary of harder words. Try one a week once you've finished the course.
